**Pass 1 — Corpus mapping.** Identification of the 34-card case file via VIRIN block analysis, the manifest's `pdf_pairing` field on the two narrative cards, and the declarative pairing language in both card descriptions ("This account is accompanied by infrared imagery..." and "The photos linked... are connected to a set of UAP encounters...").

**Pass 2 — Direct image examination.** All 32 imagery PDFs/PNGs were rendered (300 DPI for B-series PDFs, original PNG resolution for A-series) and examined directly. Per-frame structured observations were recorded into `web/src/data/image-observations/<card_id>.json` files (32 cards) plus an index. Those structured records — covering timestamp, scale, tracked object position and morphology, helicopter visibility, terrain visibility, redaction pattern, and disagreements with the prior augment-from VLM pass — are the canonical machine-readable source for the imagery claims in this entry. The embed and search pipeline quarantines the prior augment-from pass for these 32 cards in favor of the operator-verified observations.

**Pass 3 — Cross-document corroboration.** Narrative claims from the FD-302 and the ODNI Narrative were mapped against the imagery observations and assigned verdicts (corroborated / indeterminate / not in window / not corroborated). The companion finds entries [/finds/fbi-usper-2025-super-hot-orb](/finds/fbi-usper-2025-super-hot-orb) and [/finds/odni-uap-d001-usper-narrative](/finds/odni-uap-d001-usper-narrative) handle the document-grammar work; this entry references their findings rather than re-deriving them.

**What this entry treats as observation:** the imagery's visible content (objects, terrain, helicopter, timestamps, scale markings, redactions) and the narrative documents' explicit text. Cross-document agreement on observable phenomena.

**What this entry treats as inference:** sensor angle from frame composition; twilight versus astronomical-darkness from background brightness; the mapping of the unset-clock 11-minute window onto a specific FD-302 sub-event; the identity of the helicopter visible in B006/B007 as [CALL SIGN 1] rather than [CALL SIGN 2]; the season ("winter or late autumn") from frame ambient brightness; single-incident origin from VIRIN block contiguity plus identical manifest tagging plus sensor signature consistency.

**What this entry does not assert:** the nature of the observed object, the specific incident date or location beyond manifest-given "Late 2025" and "Western United States," any causal mechanism for the observed phenomena, or any conclusion about the underlying physics of what the operator was unable to positively identify.

The augment-from VLM corpus that orients the index's gallery and reader-mode descriptions was used as initial pre-Pass-1 orientation. Direct examination during Pass 2 superseded it for the 32 cards covered here; the supersede is recorded in `web/src/data/image-observations/index.json` and applied in the embed pipeline. Per-frame observations from Pass 2 are committed to the repository alongside this entry and are the citable source for any imagery-derived claim above.

### cia-uap-d001-ussr-1973-iir — A UAP Observation Inside a CIA Sary Shagan Collection Report (Summer 1973)

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/cia-uap-d001-ussr-1973-iir
- Published: 2026-05-22
- Cards: 0f469fcf6fb42875

Card 0f469fcf6fb42875 is the first Central Intelligence Agency document indexed in PURSUE. It is an Intelligence Information Report (IIR) — raw collection, explicitly marked 'not finally evaluated intelligence' — describing the Sary Shagan Weapons Testing Range in the USSR, sourced from a former Soviet citizen who served there. The report's summary on page 1 catalogues facilities, security fencing, the regional headquarters V/Ch 03080, a warhead checkout unit V/Ch 03142, System-75 [SA-2] and System-300/Aldan [ABM-1 GALOSH] warhead details, rumored laser research — and, listed in the same sentence, 'an unidentified aerial phenomenon.' Section 14, spanning pages 2 and 3, records that observation: late summer 1973, at Site 7, a bright green circular object seen at roughly 70 degrees elevation, around which several green concentric circles formed and dissipated within minutes, with no sound. The historical interest is the embedding — a UAP report surfacing inside a standard Cold War collection product, not as a stand-alone study.

## What the document is

Card `0f469fcf6fb42875` is the first Central Intelligence Agency document on the PURSUE index. Three OCR'd pages. Report number **FIRK-311/01638-77**, with distribution date **20 December 1977** and a Date of Information window of **November 1972 – November 1973**. Country covered: **USSR**. Acquired in **Germany**. The source is described on the cover sheet as a former Soviet citizen who served at the location reported on. [cite: card 0f469fcf6fb42875 p.1 "former Soviet citizen"]

The character of the document is stated explicitly at the top of page 1, in bold, above the subject line:

> "THIS IS AN INFORMATION REPORT, NOT FINALLY EVALUATED INTELLIGENCE" [cite: card 0f469fcf6fb42875 p.1 "NOT FINALLY EVALUATED INTELLIGENCE"]

That sentence is the document telling the reader what kind of intelligence object it is. An **Intelligence Information Report** (IIR) is a raw collection product — what a source said, transmitted from the field to the consumers in Washington, prior to evaluation, prior to corroboration, prior to integration into a finished analytical product. The header below it carries a **WARNING NOTICE — SENSITIVE INTELLIGENCE SOURCES AND METHODS INVOLVED** caveat. [cite: card 0f469fcf6fb42875 p.1 "SENSITIVE INTELLIGENCE SOURCES AND METHODS"]

The subject of the report is **the Sary Shagan Weapons Testing Range**.

## What the report is mostly about

The page-1 summary catalogues, in order, the topics the source covered:

> "This report provides limited information on the Sary Shagan weapons testing range, to include facilities, work areas, security fencing, the regional headquarters (V/Ch 03080), and a warhead checkout unit (V/Ch 03142). Also included is limited information on the following: System-75 [SA-2] and System-300/Aldan [ABM-1 GALOSH] warheads; rumored laser research; and an unidentified aerial phenomenon. End of Summary." [cite: card 0f469fcf6fb42875 p.1 "unidentified aerial phenomenon"]

The body sections preserved in pages 2–3 walk through warhead details: System-300/Aldan checked at Site 4 then taken to Site 35 for launching, identified by field comment as the ABM-1/GALOSH (paragraph 10); warhead dimensions, weight, and cassette layouts for the System-300/Aldan and System-75 (paragraph 11); a hearsay note on laser-weapon experiments involving powerful antennas (paragraph 13). [cite: card 0f469fcf6fb42875 p.2 "ABM-1/GALOSH"]

The UAP observation is paragraph 14. It begins on page 2 and continues onto page 3.

## Section 14 — the observation itself

The source's account, as recorded by the reporting officer:

> "On one evening in late Summer 1973, Source observed an unidentified phenomenon at Site 7. While watching a sport competition between Canada and the USSR on television, he stepped outside for some air and observed an unidentified sharp (bright) green circular object or mass in the sky." [cite: card 0f469fcf6fb42875 p.3 "bright"]

The geometry, as reported:

> "The object was situated west of the site at an angle of sighting of approximately 70 degrees. The altitude of the object was undeterminable." [cite: card 0f469fcf6fb42875 p.3 "70"]

A field comment notes that the sky was cloudless that evening and that the source believed the green mass would have been higher than cloud level, but could not estimate the diameter. [cite: card 0f469fcf6fb42875 p.3 "cloud level"]

The evolution of the phenomenon:

> "Within 10 to 15 seconds of observation, the green circle widened and within a brief period of time several green concentric circles formed around the mass. Within minutes the coloring disappeared. There was no sound, such as an explosion, associated with the phenomenon." [cite: card 0f469fcf6fb42875 p.3 "concentric circles"]

A closing field comment:

> "Source had no opinion as to what this phenomenon was. There was no resultant rumors. Source could not provide any further details." [cite: card 0f469fcf6fb42875 p.3 "no opinion"]

That is the entirety of the UAP section. One paragraph. One observation. One unrecalled date in late summer 1973, anchored to a televised Canada-USSR sporting event. No follow-up. No interpretation. No corroboration in the document itself.

## Why the embedding matters

The historical interest of this card is not the observation in isolation — a single secondhand account, recalled years after the fact, of a green circular mass with concentric rings, is too thin to support its own conclusions, and the document does not ask it to. The interest is **what it is sitting inside of**.

This is a CIA Directorate of Operations collection report from a former Soviet citizen who had walked the perimeter of the Sary Shagan range. The reporting officer collected detail on warhead diameters, cassette dimensions, ball-bearing counts in the System-75 fragmentation packages, the V/Ch military unit numbers for the regional headquarters and the warhead checkout unit. The same source, in the same debriefing, in the same numbered-paragraph sequence as the laser-research hearsay, mentioned an evening sighting that had stuck in his memory. The reporting officer wrote it down — verbatim enough that the OCR can recover the field comments without ambiguity — and the CIA distributed the report through the standard channels (NSA, DIA, STATE, FBI, NPIC and the rest are on the cover-sheet distribution list).

The page-1 summary did not bury the observation. It catalogued it in the same sentence as the warhead and laser-research material. The document treats the UAP report as **one of the source's deliverables**, neither inflated into a headline nor dropped from the summary.

That is the historical artifact: a single CIA-formatted line, in a 1977-distributed IIR on a Soviet ABM range, recording that a Soviet defector who served at Sary Shagan reported an unidentified aerial phenomenon as part of his standard debriefing. The phenomenon is not the subject of the report. It is **one entry in the source's catalogue of things he saw at the range**, transmitted with the same plumbing as the rest.

## How to read this document

A reader should hold three things at once:

1. **It is raw collection.** The "NOT FINALLY EVALUATED INTELLIGENCE" stamp at the top of page 1 is not boilerplate; it is the document telling its consumers what it is. An IIR carries what the source said. It does not certify whether the source was right, whether the phenomenon was correctly identified, whether the date was correctly recalled, or whether the observation has any explanation natural, technical, or otherwise.
2. **The DOI is November 1972 – November 1973; the distribution date is December 1977.** The source's recollection of "late summer 1973" was set down in a debriefing some years after the underlying event. Memory degrades; dates anchor to other dates (in this case, a televised sporting event). The temporal precision available from the document is "an evening in late summer 1973."
3. **The source had no theory.** The report records, on the face of it, that the source offered no opinion on what the phenomenon was and that "no resultant rumors" followed. The CIA reporting officer did not propose an interpretation either. The document is a primary-surface record of an observation, nothing more.

## What this is, and is not

This is not a CIA UAP study. The CIA has not, in this document, opened an investigation into the observation. The CIA has done what its Directorate of Operations does — collected what a foreign source said while debriefing him on a topic of operational interest, and transmitted the collection to consumers — and the observation happens to be on the list.

That is the editorial frame. The page-1 summary line — "and an unidentified aerial phenomenon" — is the single most informative phrase on the card, because it shows where in the intelligence cycle this kind of report can surface. It surfaces in collection. Whether anything was done with it after collection is not knowable from this document alone.

## Provenance of this entry

A code-assistant agent walked the three preserved OCR pages of `0f469fcf6fb42875`, verified the page-1 summary line, the "NOT FINALLY EVALUATED INTELLIGENCE" header, the paragraph 10/11/13 weapons-range content, and the paragraph 14 UAP observation against the OCR text (surya engine; page-3 confidence 97.9%, page-1 85.6%, page-2 88.4%), and reported the surface back. The editorial frame — that the historical interest lies in the embedding of the observation within a standard Cold War HUMINT collection product, not in the observation in isolation — is the operator's. The document is preserved at its primary surface; the reader can examine the IIR header, the summary line, and section 14 directly.

### doe-uap-d001-pantex-image — DOE-UAP-D001 — A UCNI-Marked Pantex UAP Report, Enhanced by Sandia

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/doe-uap-d001-pantex-image
- Published: 2026-05-22
- Cards: aaafecbc47103f4b

Card aaafecbc47103f4b is the public release of the back two pages (5 and 6 of 6) of a Department of Energy Pantex Unidentified Object Incident Report. The pages themselves contain almost no body text — they are the image-plate pages of the report — but their surface markings name three things the manifest description does not: the document's handling category (UCNI, Unclassified Controlled Nuclear Information), the FOIA exemption applied to the redaction ((b)(3) UCNI), and the laboratory that performed the image enhancement (Sandia National Labs). This is one of three DOE documents in the 5/22/26 tranche and the only one whose surface ties the incident to the nuclear-weapons assembly site itself.

## What the card actually contains

Card `aaafecbc47103f4b` is a two-page PDF: pages 5 and 6 of a six-page Pantex Unidentified Object Incident Report. The earlier pages of the report — the narrative — are not in the release. What is preserved are the image-plate pages and their captions.

Pantex is the U.S. nuclear-weapons assembly and disassembly facility in Carson County, Texas, managed by Consolidated Nuclear Security, LLC. A UAP incident report from this site is in a different category from a general DOE sighting log: the site's security perimeter is one of the most monitored on the continent.

## What the page surface names that the manifest description does not

**UCNI handling.** Both released pages carry **UCNI** markings at the top and bottom of the page — Unclassified Controlled Nuclear Information. [cite: card aaafecbc47103f4b p.1 "UCNI"] UCNI is a DOE-specific handling category for unclassified information whose unauthorized dissemination could reasonably be expected to have an adverse effect on the health and safety of the public or common defense and security. It is not "classified" in the national-security sense — it is its own category, governed by the Atomic Energy Act. That this report was marked UCNI rather than left unmarked tells you something about how DOE itself classified the sensitivity of a UAP incident on the Pantex perimeter.

**The (b)(3) exemption with UCNI cited as the underlying statute.** The first released page carries a redaction stamp citing **"(b)(3) (UCNI)"** [cite: card aaafecbc47103f4b p.1 "(b)(3) (UCNI)"] — FOIA exemption (b)(3) covers information specifically protected from disclosure by another statute. By citing UCNI as the (b)(3) hook, DOE is invoking the Atomic Energy Act as the statutory basis for the redaction, not the more familiar (b)(1) national-security exemption. This is the same legal mechanism the Department uses to control information about nuclear-weapons design.

**Sandia National Labs performed the image enhancement.** The page-6 caption identifies the enhanced imagery as the product of Sandia, not Pantex itself: **"Sandia National Labs Enhanced Images of the Object."** [cite: card aaafecbc47103f4b p.2 "Sandia National Labs Enhanced Images"] The page-5 caption identifies the original source as a ground surveillance radar tower at the site: **"Image from Ground Surveillance Radar Tower."** [cite: card aaafecbc47103f4b p.1 "Ground Surveillance Radar Tower"] Two different DOE entities are therefore in the document chain: Pantex's ground-surveillance system is the sensor, and Sandia is the post-processor.

## What the card does not contain

The release does not include:

- The date of the incident (the manifest entry's `incident_date` is null).
- The narrative pages of the report (pages 1 through 4).
- The pre-enhancement radar imagery (only the Sandia-enhanced product is on the released pages, and the images themselves are not OCR-recoverable as text).
- The classification authority for the underlying UCNI determination.

A reader who clicks through sees two image-plate pages with UCNI banners and the Consolidated Nuclear Security, LLC management stamp. The actual content of the incident — what was seen, when, by what sensor configuration, with what disposition — is in pages that were not released.

## Why both fragments are in this archive

The two released pages are thin in body text but the *handling surface* of a primary source is itself evidence. The presence of UCNI markings, the choice of (b)(3) UCNI as the redaction citation, and the naming of Sandia as the image-enhancement laboratory are three facts about how DOE processed this incident that survive on the released pages even though the narrative does not. A future release of the full six-page report would slot directly into this card's page sequence at pages 1–4.

DOE-UAP-D001 is one of three DOE documents in the 5/22/26 release (alongside D002 and D003). It is the only one of the three whose surface ties a UAP incident to the Pantex perimeter and to Sandia's analytical chain.

### doe-uap-d002-james-tuck-correspondence-1970s — James Tuck's UAP Correspondence (1970s)

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/doe-uap-d002-james-tuck-correspondence-1970s
- Published: 2026-05-22
- Cards: 8156067f7ff4b983

DOE-UAP-D002 is the first Department of Energy document to enter this archive, and the first time the personal UAP correspondence of a Manhattan Project alumnus has been catalogued here. James L. Tuck — a British physicist who worked on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos under Oppenheimer and later led the Project Sherwood early-fusion program — pursued unidentified aerial phenomena as a personal interest in the 1970s. The four pages preserved in this card include a Los Alamos security-officer's first-person recollection of green-light sightings on 'the Hill' between 1948 and 1951, Tuck's own 16 December 1970 letter requesting the simulated-atomic-bomb vortex recipe used in atmospheric tests referenced in the Condon Report, and a later ball-lightning exchange citing James McCampbell's UFOLOGY. The find is the who and the context, not a smoking-gun claim.

## Why this card matters before its contents

DOE-UAP-D002 is the first Department of Energy document to enter this index, and the first card in which a Manhattan Project alumnus's *personal* — not institutional — UAP correspondence is the primary material. The find is not a disclosure of classified knowledge. It is the documentary fact that **James L. Tuck pursued UAP as a private intellectual interest in the 1970s**, and corresponded with at least one Los Alamos security-force veteran and one ball-lightning correspondent about it.

Tuck was a British-born physicist who joined the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos under Oppenheimer, and after the war led Project Sherwood — the Los Alamos plasma physics effort that founded U.S. controlled-fusion research. He was one of the most credentialed alumni of the wartime weapons program. His extant personal letters about UAP are therefore a small but historically substantive primary source for how scientists with that level of access read the phenomenon.

The card is four pages. Two are a single inbound letter to Tuck recalling Los Alamos sightings from 1948–1951. One is a 16 December 1970 letter Tuck wrote out to the U.S. Army Engineering School. One is a later inbound letter on ball lightning.

## The 1948–1951 Los Alamos sightings — a security officer's recollection

Pages 1–2 of the card are a two-page response addressed *to* Tuck, signed by an individual whose name is redacted under (b)(6). The correspondent identifies themselves as a member of what they call the "Protection Force" — the Los Alamos site security force — during the period in question. The letter regrets they cannot answer Tuck's attached form on specific times and dates, then offers from memory:

> "I can however, tell you that during the years 1948 through 1951 several sightings of green lights were made at Los Alamos. These usually occurred during the early part of the night, nine to eleven, and were usually near the Jemez Mountains." [cite: card 8156067f7ff4b983 p.1 "1948 through 1951"]

The correspondent describes "green light weaving in and out of mountain peaks," notes that all sightings were "reported to the Protection Force Headquarters and should be a matter of record on their logs," and recalls one specific daylight event:

> "I also recall one instance of five objects flying over Los Alamos in the afternoon. They were flying from southeast to northwest and appeared to be flying in formation." [cite: card 8156067f7ff4b983 p.1 "five objects"]

They identify themselves (anonymously, via redaction) as one of "the five or six people" who saw those five objects, and name a second redacted Protection Force member Tuck might also contact. They close by suggesting that if Tuck can obtain access to the Protection Force logs for the period, the time-and-date data will be available there. [cite: card 8156067f7ff4b983 p.2 "Protection Force logs"]

The 1948–1951 timeframe is the same window Dr. Lincoln LaPaz catalogued in his Seventh Report to the OSI 17th District, separately preserved in FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 6 and discussed in the [LaPaz green fireballs entry](/finds/lapaz-green-fireballs-1948-1950). The Tuck correspondence does not add new sightings to that record; it documents that decades later, a security-force veteran was being asked about them by a senior Los Alamos physicist, and that the veteran's recollection of green lights near the Jemez at 2100–2300 hours is independently consistent with the LaPaz catalog.

## Tuck's own 1970 letter — the Condon Report and an atmospheric-vortex recipe

Page 3 is a single-page outbound letter on what appears to be Los Alamos letterhead ("P-DO" header), signed "James L. Tuck" and dated **16 December 1970**. It is addressed to a redacted recipient at the U.S. Army Engineering School, Fort Belvoir, Virginia, Department of Mechanical and Technical Equipment.

The body is short and specific:

> "As agreed in our telephone conversation of today's date, I would like to have the recipe that was used for the simulated atomic bomb demonstrations. We are interested in the large atmospheric vortices which are produced as reported in the book 'Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects' by Dr. Edward U. Condon." [cite: card 8156067f7ff4b983 p.3 "large atmospheric vortices"]

The reference is to the Condon Committee's 1968 *Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects* — the University of Colorado study commissioned by the Air Force that recommended the closure of Project Blue Book. Tuck is asking the Army for the formula used to produce a controlled mushroom-cloud demonstration so he can study the *vortex* it generates. He is not asking about UFOs directly; he is asking about an atmospheric phenomenon discussed in a UFO study report.

This is the most direct documentary evidence in the card of Tuck's personal research interest. He is a senior Los Alamos physicist requisitioning experimental material from a sister agency in order to follow up on a specific physical mechanism cited in the Condon Report. The letter is a working-scientist's request, not an opinion piece.

## The ball-lightning exchange

Page 4 is a one-page inbound letter, undated except for "November 28," addressed "Dear Jim" and signed under a (b)(6) redaction. The text references Tuck's "interesting report on ball Lightning" and encloses comments by James M. McCampbell from McCampbell's *UFOLOGY*, dated to 1976 — "appearing on the new non-fiction shelf at the Mesa Library, call number 629.1338 M125u." [cite: card 8156067f7ff4b983 p.4 "UFOLOGY"]

The correspondent adds a personal aside on Einstein and the unified field theory. [cite: card 8156067f7ff4b983 p.4 "unified field theory"] The 1976 publication date of McCampbell's book places this letter no earlier than that year. The exchange documents that Tuck had himself prepared a report on ball lightning — a recurring scientific candidate for some UFO observations — and was sharing it with at least one correspondent in his personal network.

## What the card does and does not establish

The four pages establish, on the documentary record:

- That James L. Tuck, a Los Alamos physicist of Manhattan Project rank, corresponded in the 1970s with at least one Los Alamos Protection Force veteran and one independent correspondent about UAP and related atmospheric phenomena.
- That he wrote to the U.S. Army Engineering School on 16 December 1970 requesting experimental material specifically to study atmospheric vortices cited in the Condon Report.
- That he authored or contributed a report on ball lightning circulated in his personal correspondence by 1976.
- That a Los Alamos security-force veteran's first-person recollection of 1948–1951 green-light sightings near the Jemez Mountains exists in the document trail — consistent in date range and geography with the LaPaz green-fireball catalog separately documented in FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 6.

The four pages do **not** establish:

- Anything about what Tuck knew or did not know through his Los Alamos classified access about UAP.
- That his interest was an official program responsibility rather than a personal one. The letterhead on page 3 is Los Alamos institutional, but the framing of the request — and the personal-correspondence framing of pages 1–2 and 4 — fits a working scientist following a published-literature lead, not a tasked investigation.
- The identity of any of the redacted correspondents.
- Any institutional Department of Energy position on UAP. DOE-UAP-D002 is *personal* correspondence preserved in DOE custody, not a DOE policy document.

## Why this card is in this archive

It is in this archive because primary correspondence from a working Manhattan Project–era physicist about unidentified aerial phenomena is rare, brief, and historiographically substantive. The Tuck letters are not a revelation. They are documentation. They show that the question "what were the green lights over Los Alamos in 1948–1951" was being asked twenty years later by one of the people most credentialed to ask it, and that the answer trail led through the Condon Report, Project Sherwood–adjacent vortex physics, and ball-lightning literature rather than through any disclosure of classified holdings.

For the institutional context of the 1948–1951 sightings the page-1 correspondent recalls, see the [LaPaz green fireballs entry](/finds/lapaz-green-fireballs-1948-1950). For the broader pattern of the FBI's 17th District file on the same period, see the [reader's guide to FBI 62-HQ-83894](/finds/fbi-62-hq-83894-readers-guide).

### dow-uap-d017-sandia-1948-1950 — Sandia Base, AFSWP, and Project Grudge (1948–1950)

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/dow-uap-d017-sandia-1948-1950
- Published: 2026-05-22
- Cards: 09001c140b97a5db

DOW-UAP-D017 is a 116-page file of general correspondence held at Sandia Base, New Mexico, by the Armed Forces Special Weapons Project — the direct post-WWII successor to the Manhattan Project — and the U.S. Air Force, dated 1948 through May 1950. The file contains a 17th District OSI summary listing 209 sightings of green fireballs, discs, and luminous objects in New Mexico, accompanied by the Mandelkorn trip report of 16 February 1949 in which Edward Teller, Norris Bradbury, John Manley, and Lincoln LaPaz convened at Los Alamos under the codename Project Grudge, and by W. D. Crozier's airborne-particulate collection report identifying copper-bearing particles in the air at Socorro following the fireball of 24 July 1949.

## What the document is

DOW-UAP-D017 (card `09001c140b97a5db`) is 116 pages of general correspondence drawn from the classified documents library of the **Armed Forces Special Weapons Project (AFSWP)** at Sandia Base, Albuquerque. AFSWP was the post-1947 successor organisation to the Manhattan Engineer District — the joint Army-Navy command responsible for the U.S. nuclear stockpile. The file collects intra-agency cables, OSI summaries, weather observations, particle-collection laboratory reports, and the minutes of a February 1949 Los Alamos conference, all relating to unidentified aerial phenomena observed over and around the New Mexico nuclear-weapons complex between December 1948 and May 1950.

The institutional weight of the file is what distinguishes it. This is not a hobbyist collection or a public-relations dossier. It is the operating file of the agency holding custody of the U.S. nuclear stockpile, treating recurrent aerial phenomena near its installations as a matter requiring scientific attention. [cite: card 09001c140b97a5db p.21 "continued occurrence"]

For the narrower scientific framing — Lincoln LaPaz's eleven catalogued differences from meteor behaviour — see the companion entry on the [LaPaz green-fireball reports](/finds/lapaz-green-fireballs-1948-1950). The present entry concerns the institutional record around those events: who else was reading LaPaz, what they were doing about it, and what physical evidence they were attempting to collect.

## The 209-sighting tabulation

Pages 23–60 are a CONFIDENTIAL columnar log: *Summary of Sightings of Unknown Aerial Phenomena, 17th District OSI*. The transmittal cover memo of 25 May 1950 from Lt. Col. Doyle Rees explains that the 17th District had assumed responsibility for collecting and reporting these observations since December 1948 at the direction of a multi-agency liaison meeting that included Fourth Army, AFSWP, the FBI, the Atomic Energy Commission, the University of California, the Air Force Scientific Advisory Board, AMC, and OSI. [cite: card 09001c140b97a5db p.20 "liaison meeting"]

Each row records date, time, number and reliability of observers, general area, apparent direction of flight, apparent altitude, course (horizontal-to-vertical), colour, train, sound, shape, apparent size, apparent speed, and manner of disappearance. Each row terminates with an evaluation key: **(1)** Green Fireball Phenomena, **(2)** Disk or Variation, **(3)** Probable Meteor. The numbered observations run from January 1948 to May 1950 and reach #209 at the close of the table.

Geographic coverage is dense and concentric on the weapons complex: Albuquerque, Sandia Base, Los Alamos, Kirtland AFB, Holloman AFB, Alamogordo, Tularosa, Roswell, Vaughn, Las Vegas (NM), Datil, Window Rock (AZ), El Paso, Camp Hood (TX), Farmington, and others. The reliability column is dominated by "R" (Reliable) entries, with many observers identified as Los Alamos security inspectors, military and commercial pilots, and OSI special agents.

## Three incidents from the table

The catalogue's entries are terse. A representative cross-section:

- **Sighting #179, Los Alamos, 24 February 1950.** A single reliable observer reported an aluminium-coloured spherical object, "rather large," circling at considerable altitude before departing to the east between 1315 and 1400 hours. The phenomenon was evaluated as Green Fireball / Disk. [cite: card 09001c140b97a5db p.55 "Circled"]
- **Sightings #191–192, Farmington, New Mexico, 16 March 1950.** Ten unknown-reliability observers reported a daylight formation of bright, luminous, tin-foil-like discs "turning on their axes and maneuvering up and down," from sizes ranging from one inch to six inches at arm's length, faster than conventional aircraft, in two distinct observations within an hour of each other. Both were evaluated as Disk or Variation. [cite: card 09001c140b97a5db p.57 "turned on their axis"]
- **Sighting #200, Sandia Base, 21 March 1950.** A single unknown-reliability observer reported two silver round objects, dime-sized at arm's length, gradually fading from view at "excessive jet flight" speed about 45° above the horizon. Evaluated as Disk or Variation. [cite: card 09001c140b97a5db p.59 "2 objects"]

These are unremarkable rows within the table. They are unremarkable specifically because the table contains two hundred-odd of them.

## The Mandelkorn trip report (16 February 1949) — and Project Grudge

The most consequential single document in the file is a four-page trip report dated 18 February 1949 by Commander Richard S. Mandelkorn, U.S.N., of AFSWP's Research and Development Division, Sandia Base. The report — Series B, Copy 1 in the Sandia Security and Intelligence Division — minutes a 16 February 1949 conference at Los Alamos convened to consider the green-fireball phenomena.

The attendee list is the most striking feature of the document. For Los Alamos: **Norris E. Bradbury** (Director, Los Alamos), **Marshall Holloway**, **Fred Reines**, **John Manley**, **Edward Teller**, Elmo Morgan (AEC), Sidney Neuberger (Security), Maxwell (AFSS), and Hoyt. For Fourth Army: Major William A. Godsoe and Major Wynn. For USAF: Captain Neef. For the University of New Mexico: **Dr. Lincoln LaPaz**. For Sandia: Commander Mandelkorn. [cite: card 09001c140b97a5db p.90 "Bradbury"]

Captain Neef opened the meeting by stating that "this question had been classified military SECRET under the name, Project 'Grudge', and that the investigation was now the primary responsibility of USAF, Air Materiel Command, T-2." [cite: card 09001c140b97a5db p.90 "Project &quot;Grudge&quot;"] This is one of the earliest extant institutional references to Project Grudge in U.S. government holdings.

Teller's contribution is recorded in unusual detail. He calculated that an object moving at the observed velocity (~8 miles per second) at the observed altitude (~8 to 10 miles) and emitting the observed light output (~10¹⁴ ergs per second) would have to have a mass of roughly twenty grams — and would have produced a shock-wave noise easily audible ten kilometres from the source. No sound had been observed. Teller's tentative opinion, recorded by Mandelkorn, was that the green fireballs were "not material objects passing through the air" and that an explanation should be sought in "electronics and optics" rather than hydrodynamics. [cite: card 09001c140b97a5db p.92 "not material objects"] Bradbury demurred on the electronics hypothesis, observing that it would raise its own intractable problems.

Mandelkorn's conclusion, written for distribution to Fourth Army G-2 and USAF, states: "It is my belief that these phenomena, particularly if there are any further incidents, are deserving of serious consideration until their source and meaning have been satisfactorily explained… there is cause for concern of the continued occurrences of unexplainable phenomena of this nature in the vicinity of sensitive installations." [cite: card 09001c140b97a5db p.93 "sensitive installations"]

## The Crozier copper-particle collections

The file's most concrete physical-trace evidence is W. D. Crozier and Ben K. Seely's 10 August 1949 report from the New Mexico School of Mines, *An Attempt to Collect Airborne Particles Associated with the Fireball of July 24, 1949*. Aerosol-impactment equipment processing 34 litres of air per minute, with rubeanic acid (dithiooxamide) applied to identify copper compounds, was used to make systematic collections at the School of Mines campus starting thirteen and a half hours after a fireball reportedly passed over Socorro at 8:26 p.m. on 24 July 1949.

The collections registered positive copper indications, with particle counts in the smallest size range (1–15 microns) rising sharply some 35 hours after the fireball event. [cite: card 09001c140b97a5db p.6 "copper-bearing particles"] Crozier qualified the result heavily: "it seems very hazardous to draw any definite conclusion associating the copper-bearing particles collected with the fireball of July 24." But he noted the residuum of possibility and recommended continued airborne collection using equipment already on hand and proved in flight.

A subsequent collecting trip (10 August 1949) covering nine locations on Highway 84 north of Highway 66 produced a single anomalous sample, R-104L, containing a large number of copper-bearing particles in a granular matrix unfamiliar to the laboratory. The collection taken immediately afterward at the same location showed practically no copper. Crozier's tentative conclusion: "no widespread significant dispersion of copper-bearing particles was present in the atmosphere in the region covered at the time the collections were made." [cite: card 09001c140b97a5db p.4 "copper-bearing particles"] The copper claim is therefore not a confident affirmative finding. It is a documented attempt by a working aerosol laboratory to falsify, and it produced one anomalous sample its authors could not source.

The relevance for the broader file: LaPaz's Seventh Report noted that laboratory tests had identified the green fireballs' colour as consistent with copper-salt emission in a blowpipe flame, and the Crozier collections are the corresponding attempt to recover physical copper material from the air mass through which a fireball had passed.

## What the file establishes

DOW-UAP-D017 does not establish that the green fireballs, the discs, or the orbs observed near Sandia were exotic. It establishes a different set of facts:

- Between December 1948 and May 1950, the 17th District OSI catalogued 209 reliable-to-unknown-reliability sightings of unidentified aerial phenomena concentrated within and immediately around the New Mexico nuclear-weapons complex.
- The agency holding institutional custody of the U.S. nuclear stockpile — AFSWP, the Manhattan Project's direct organisational successor — kept the resulting paper trail in its own classified documents library, distributed Mandelkorn's trip report to its own Security and Intelligence Division, and was a formal participant in the multi-agency liaison structure responsible for the investigation.
- On 16 February 1949, the Director of Los Alamos, three Manhattan Project veterans (Teller, Manley, Holloway), the discoverer of the neutrino (Reines), the Institute of Meteoritics director (LaPaz), AEC and security representatives, and Fourth Army and USAF intelligence officers sat in the same room at Los Alamos under the codename Project Grudge to consider what the phenomena were. Teller produced a back-of-envelope calculation on the spot.
- A working aerosol laboratory at the New Mexico School of Mines was contracted to look for copper-bearing particles in the wake of fireball passes. The collections produced one anomalous sample its principal investigator declined to characterise.

What the file does not establish is what the phenomena were. Mandelkorn explicitly leaves that question open. Teller leaves it open. LaPaz leaves it open. The 17th District leaves it open and recommends continued scientific study. The reader's takeaway is the institutional shape: the U.S. nuclear establishment, two years removed from Hiroshima, treated 209 recurrent aerial observations near its custody installations as a matter for documented work product — and Edward Teller treated it as worth a calculation.

For the contemporaneous photograph-custody dispute in a parallel UAP file from the same period, see the [Rhodes photographs entry](/finds/rhodes-photographs-phoenix-1947). For LaPaz's own framing of the same phenomena as a problem in observational astronomy, see the [LaPaz green-fireball reports](/finds/lapaz-green-fireballs-1948-1950).

### odni-uap-d001-usper-narrative — ODNI-UAP-D001 — The First-Person Narrative Behind the FBI FD-302

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/odni-uap-d001-usper-narrative
- Published: 2026-05-22
- Cards: fd342b7508668b0e, be533a4ab886eb11, 3893e5d0279db3b1, ba30b5fdb4f6d153, 93cbdaad1d4ac853, 04b9179a7637d6ad, 613dc8ef961f9399, 5a487c793b488382, c142741e8cafc659, 819e725592d1ba79, 1e63919cc6c3daf4, 67ab3ffef2aecf70, 0e3b3ec17a9ae021, 672ae7eab15481ff, 36bcfe2cfb5f3f54, b279eac8e49cf4fe, ccd932b4f40e8de7, 0d7a23b29e6de1bf, fd8286ffc6fbc1fb, af047a976bac0c89, 19d8e1d503211c84, 2b947223739f5bd4, 16fcb501de623b9c, 7d1b50162c29378a, 3a5445e8aa7985d4, 3b36f3dc3b51cf3b, f8bd1f11b7a2ae48, c568aea24f3aef31, eda0a3d37c6dbbc3, bdf033d4a47eaad3, c304734c04357887, dc9f45a9ec6feb00, a417f61b2dbd671f, 6ded7ef20ded84c7

Card fd342b7508668b0e is the first ODNI-released document on the index: a two-page first-person narrative by a serving senior US intelligence official of a late-2025 UAP encounter near a sensitive military facility in the Western United States. It is the same incident the FBI FD-302 in card be533a4ab886eb11 records in third-person interview form — but ODNI released it without the FD-302's redactions: no [WITNESS], no [STATE PARTNER ORGANIZATION], no [BEARING], no [DATE] brackets. The manifest pairs it with thirty-two FBI photographs (A001–A008, B001–B024) and the USPER Statement card. This entry reads what the first-person grammar commits to that the FD-302 grammar does not, and notes what both still hold back.

## What the document is

Card `fd342b7508668b0e` is **"ODNI-UAP-D001, USPER Narrative, Senior USIC Official"** — a two-page first-person narrative carrying the Office of the Director of National Intelligence as releasing agency. The manifest characterizes it as "a first-hand account written by a currently serving (May 2026) senior U.S. intelligence official." The release date on the index is 2026-05-22 (Release 02); the incident date the document recounts is `Late 2025`, in the `Western United States`. The manifest records `redacted: false` — a flag that the rest of this entry treats as load-bearing.

The narrative opens in the first-person voice:

> "In late 2025, during early evening daylight hours, I — a senior U.S. intelligence officer — along with a colleague and two pilots, departed our Joint Operations Center (JOC) in a helicopter." [cite: card fd342b7508668b0e p.1 "senior U.S. intelligence officer"]

This is the same person whose account is summarized, in third-person and with every proper noun redacted, in card `be533a4ab886eb11` — the **FBI FD-302** already documented in this archive at [/finds/fbi-usper-2025-orb](/finds/fbi-usper-2025-super-hot-orb). The manifest's `pdf_pairing` field on `fd342b7508668b0e` lists, explicitly, "USPER Statement about UAP Sighting" alongside thirty-two FBI photographs (A001–A008, B001–B024). The pairing is declared by the corpus, not inferred.

## What the first-person grammar commits to

The FD-302 anonymizes by category — `[WITNESS 1 (a senior US intelligence official)]`, `[STATE PARTNER ORGANIZATION]`, `[FEDERAL PARTNER 4]`, `[MILITARY AIRCRAFT]`, `[CALL SIGN 1]`, `[DATE]`, `[BEARING]`, `[COORDINATES]`. The ODNI narrative carries none of those brackets. What it does *not* fill them in with is also part of how to read it.

The narrative refers to:

- **"I — a senior U.S. intelligence officer."** No agency, no service. The role descriptor matches the FD-302's `[WITNESS 1 (a senior US intelligence official)]` exactly. Which intelligence-community component the author sits inside is not stated. The redactor's category in the FD-302 was preserved as a self-description in the ODNI release.
- **"A colleague and two pilots."** The FD-302's `[WITNESS 2 (a senior US intelligence official)]` and `[STATE PARTNER ORGANIZATION]`-employed aircrew. The ODNI text does not name them either.
- **"Our Joint Operations Center (JOC)."** Named by acronym. The FD-302 has this as `[OPERATIONS CENTER]`. The narrative also references "the test range," "the mountain range," "a prearranged rendezvous point," "a prepositioned tanker on the range," and "base" — terrain by function, not by toponym.
- **"Fighter jets… launched on a training mission in our operating area."** The FD-302's `five [MILITARY AIRCRAFT] from [REDACTED]`. The ODNI text says "fighter jets" by class but neither names the platform nor the operator, and gives a count only later ("the fighter jets") without restating "five."

What the narrative *does* fill in that the FD-302 did not: the **time of day in absolute terms** ("early evening daylight hours" on departure; "the sun had set" before the radar hits; "After landing… I then entered the JOC for a quick debrief before driving home"), the **navigation profile** ("a low-altitude 'map of the earth'[^nap] route through the mountain range"), the **rationale for descent** ("Multiple times, we spotted debris on the ground and descended for closer inspection. Each time, we determined it was remnants from rockets and other projectiles that had crashed during years of weapons testing on the range"), and the **terrain feature that occasioned an orbit** ("we discovered a large cave entrance with no visible end in sight. The terrain around the entrance offered no safe landing spot, so I instructed the pilot to orbit it several times for observation"). [cite: card fd342b7508668b0e p.1 "large cave entrance"]

The FD-302 has none of these. They are details a first-person narrator volunteers; a third-person interview summary, written to a different purpose, does not.

## The two grammars on the same observations

The FD-302 records the LP/OP-relayed FLIR observation as `"super-hot,"` in quotation marks, attributed to a different federal partner. The ODNI narrative records the same observation from the helicopter perspective, in first-person, and quotes the LP/OP's words back:

> "En route, ground teams reported spotting a UAP on FLIR, describing it as 'super-hot,' low to the ground, and moving east then south at high speed. The object then split into two and changed direction." [cite: card fd342b7508668b0e p.1 "super-hot"]

The same quotation marks around `"super-hot"`; the same attribution to a ground team on FLIR. The FD-302 captures the relay as a transcription; the ODNI text captures it as something the narrator *heard over the radio* and recounts. Both grammars agree on the relayed phrase.

The FD-302's 20-mile leg — `"LP/OP reported the orb gained elevation, came within ten feet of [CALL SIGN 1] and then headed east to [REDACTED]"` — is the ODNI narrative's:

> "The ground team suddenly radioed that the object had risen from the ground, approached within ten feet of the helicopter, dropped below us, and then sped away. The pilots observed it through NVGs and saw it split into two as a smaller object emerged before it accelerated out of sight. We briefly pursued but broke off, unable to match its speed." [cite: card fd342b7508668b0e p.1 "ten feet of the helicopter"]

Same ten-foot proximity, same break-off-from-pursuit, same speed-mismatch conclusion. The narrative resolves an ambiguity the FD-302 carried: the "ten feet" event was *radioed in by a ground team*, not observed by the narrator's own platform. ("The ground team suddenly radioed that the object had risen from the ground…") That matches the FD-302's structural attribution — the ten-foot proximity was an LP/OP-reported event, not a sensor observation from the helicopter itself — and the first-person voice makes the relay explicit.

## The "T" formation, in the narrator's own words

The FD-302 records the recurring observation language as `"flared up one at a time in a horizontal formation."` The ODNI narrative is more specific about one instance:

> "Through NVGx, the pilots and I (using the naked eye) observed two large orbs flare up side by side, close to the helicopter — stationary and just above the rotor disk to our right. They were oval-shaped, orange with a white or yellow center, and emitted light in all directions. After a few seconds, a third orb flared up below the pair, followed by a fourth below that, forming a total of four or five in a 'T' formation under the original two. Moments later, they dimmed in reverse order, remaining stationary until they vanished from view. The entire event lasted 10-15 seconds." [cite: card fd342b7508668b0e p.2 "T"]

The geometric description ("oval-shaped, orange with a white or yellow center"), the spatial-relative language ("just above the rotor disk to our right"), the formation count ("a total of four or five"), and the explicit pattern name ("'T' formation") are the narrator's own. The FD-302 captures the *grammar* of the recurring observation — flare-up, formation, sequential dim-down, 10-15 seconds — but not the formation-shape names. A reader can put the FD-302's structural-time-series treatment alongside the ODNI's geometric-prose treatment and see two different ways of writing down the same observed event.

## The chase, as observed from the helicopter

The closing paragraph of page 2 describes the fighter-jet portion of the timeline in the narrator's voice:

> "We then spotted the fighter jets entering visual range at about 23,00 feet AGL, identifiable by their blinking navigation lights. As watched from afar, the same type of orbs appeared directly above the fighters. They flared up one at a time in a horizontal formation, matching the jets' speed and flight path. After 10-15 seconds, they dimmed sequentially and disappeared. This repeated several times as the jets transited the airspace and eventually landed. I remarked to the pilots that it seemed the same orbs we had encountered were now 'chasing' the fighters." [cite: card fd342b7508668b0e p.2 "chasing"]

The FD-302 records the same interpretation in its closing-comments section as the witness's words: "The orbs appeared to break off from [CALL SIGN 1] and pursue the [MILITARY AIRCRAFT]." The ODNI narrative shows where that interpretation came from — a remark the narrator made aloud to the pilots, in the moment, with the word "chasing" placed in scare-quotes by the narrator himself. The phrasing is preserved across both documents at almost identical specificity.

## What the unredacted narrative still does not say

`redacted: false` in the manifest is true at the bracket level — there are no `[REDACTED]` tokens in the OCR text. It is not the same as "fully specified." The ODNI narrative declines to name:

- **The narrator.** A senior US intelligence officer who, per the manifest description, was "currently serving (May 2026)" at the time of release. The narrative is a first-person account whose first-person voice does not include an introduction.
- **The agency or service.** "Senior U.S. intelligence officer" is the only role descriptor used. The intelligence community spans civilian and uniformed components; the narrative does not say which side the narrator sits on.
- **The colleague.** Referred to throughout as "my colleague." The FD-302's `[WITNESS 2 (a senior US intelligence official)]`.
- **The pilots' operator.** "Two pilots" who switched to "Forward Looking Infrared (FLIR) and Night Vision Goggles (NVG)" at sunset. The FD-302 had this as `[STATE PARTNER ORGANIZATION]`. The ODNI narrative does not specify whether the pilots were military or civilian, federal or state.
- **The facility.** The manifest field `incident_location` reads `Western United States`; the narrative uses functional terms ("the test range," "the JOC," "base") rather than a named installation.
- **The date inside late 2025.** The opening phrase is "In late 2025." The FD-302's Zulu timestamps (1700, 1751, 2050, 2052, …, 2320) are absent from the ODNI text, which uses relative phrases ("After a brief search… After this encounter… Minutes later… After a few seconds").
- **The fighter platform.** "Fighter jets" by class only; the FD-302's `[MILITARY AIRCRAFT]` with a count of five. The ODNI narrative does not restate the count.

A reader holding both documents alongside each other can recover more of the operational picture than either supports alone — but a reader holding only one of them should hold its level of specificity at exactly where the document drew it.

## The 24-photo evidence trail

The manifest's `pdf_pairing` field on `fd342b7508668b0e` lists thirty-two FBI photographs by ID — eight A-series (A001–A008) and twenty-four B-series (B001–B024) — alongside the USPER Statement. The A-series and B-series are continuous numerical sequences that the corpus delivered together with this narrative. One of them, **FBI Photo B7** (`ccd932b4f40e8de7`), is the grayscale FLIR-style frame already documented in [/finds/fbi-usper-2025-orb](/finds/fbi-usper-2025-super-hot-orb): a helicopter under a central crosshair reticle with 5/10/15 tick scales, OCR yielding only a corrupted system timestamp. The companion entry's reading of B7 — visually consistent with an LP/OP FLIR display imaging an in-air helicopter, with the manifest-described "second, smaller, dark circular object… visible below the reticle" — applies here without modification. The corpus now declares that frame to be paired with the present narrative; the editorial reading does not need to assert it.

The remaining thirty-one frames in the A/B sequence are released alongside the narrative as a corpus-declared evidence package. This entry surfaces the existence of that pairing rather than re-deriving each frame's reading; per-frame examination of all 32 photographs — including the sensor-system classification that splits the A-series from the B-series, the burst structure of the 24 B-frames, and what the imagery does and does not corroborate against this narrative — is in the companion finds entry at [/finds/helicopter-case-2025-imagery](/finds/helicopter-case-2025-imagery).

## Three grammars, one incident

With the ODNI narrative now on the index, the late-2025 helicopter-orb encounter is documented in this archive through three distinct document grammars:

1. **First-person narrative (ODNI, card `fd342b7508668b0e`)** — the participant's own account, written in prose, two pages, no agency-internal redaction. Names sensors, geometry, terrain function, and the in-the-moment word "chasing."
2. **Third-person interview summary (FBI FD-302, card `be533a4ab886eb11`)** — the agent's transcription of a witness debrief, three pages, SECRET//NOFORN, every proper noun in a redaction category. Names timestamps, personnel counts, sensor types, and the LP/OP's relayed `"super-hot."`
3. **Imagery (FBI Photo A001–A008, B001–B024 — thirty-two cards)** — ground-team FLIR frames captured during the same exercise per the manifest pairing. Per-frame direct examination of all 32 photographs — including the sensor-system classification that splits the A-series from the B-series, the burst structure of the 24 B-frames, and the operator-mediated mid-burst zoom-in — is in [/finds/helicopter-case-2025-imagery](/finds/helicopter-case-2025-imagery).

The three grammars do not perfectly overlap. The FD-302's Zulu timestamps are not in the ODNI narrative; the ODNI narrative's "large cave entrance" is not in the FD-302; the photographs' per-frame embedded data is not in either document. They are useful as three readings of the same event because each grammar commits to a different set of details.

## Provenance of this entry

A code-assistant agent located and verified the document surface — the first-person opening, the role descriptor matching the FD-302's `[WITNESS 1]` token, the verbatim quotation marks around `"super-hot"` and `"chasing,"` the "T" formation language, the absence of redaction brackets, and the corpus-declared pairing of thirty-two FBI photographs and the USPER Statement — by reading the two preserved OCR pages of `fd342b7508668b0e` directly and the manifest entry for the card. The cross-reference to the FD-302 entry at [/finds/fbi-usper-2025-orb](/finds/fbi-usper-2025-super-hot-orb) is to an existing find in this archive on the third-person side of the same incident. The editorial frame — surfacing this card as a sibling-grammar to the existing FD-302 entry, and reading the unredacted first-person voice for what it commits to that the FD-302's redaction categories did not — is the operator's.

[^nap]: ODNI re-released this document on 2026-05-26 with a typo correction: "map-of-the-earth" → "nap-of-the-earth," the standard military aviation term for low-altitude terrain-following flight. The verbatim quote above ("map of the earth") is from the 2026-05-22 release we archived at byte_sha `87297ea7…`; the corrected version is at byte_sha `bef126d8…`. Both are preserved at content-addressed `/archive/<sha>.pdf` URLs. No other text content changed in the May 26 revision — the document was re-paginated to fit an inline footnote ODNI added explaining the correction.

### apollo-11-debriefing — Apollo 11 Technical Crew Debriefing: Three Anomalous Observations and How the Crew Reasoned About Them

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/apollo-11-debriefing
- Published: 2026-05-12
- Cards: d14e0371a5bf0f5e

Card d14e0371a5bf0f5e is the NASA Apollo 11 Technical Crew Debriefing (July 31, 1969), 11 OCR'd pages drawn from Volumes I and II of the post-mission report. The document records Armstrong, Aldrin, and Collins discussing three discrete anomalies on the record: an unidentified object visible roughly a day out from Earth, brief flashes of light seen inside the cabin, and two visual-sighting artifacts during translunar and lunar-orbit observation. In each case the document captures the complete arc — observation, in-conversation analysis, and the crew's working hypothesis. The cabin-flash passage is the document's strongest physical-science moment: Armstrong proposes 'a neutron or some kind of an atomic particle' before the effect had been formally measured.

## What this document is

Card `d14e0371a5bf0f5e` is the **Apollo 11 Technical Crew Debriefing**, dated **July 31, 1969** — eleven days after splashdown — and prepared by the **Mission Operations Branch, Flight Crew Support Division**. [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.1] The 11 OCR'd pages in the archive are drawn from Volumes I and II of the report: pages 1–8 from Volume I (covering the in-flight observation and cabin flashes discussion) and pages 9–11 from Volume II (covering Section 21, Visual Sightings).

The cover pages of both volumes carry the same handling block: **CONFIDENTIAL**, **Group 4**, with an explicit auto-declassification clause — *"Downgraded at 3-year intervals; declassified after 12 years."* [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.1 "Downgraded at 3-year"] The same block appears on the Volume II cover. [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.9 "Downgraded at 3-year"] A FOIA notice is printed directly below it, referencing 5 U.S.C. 552 and NASA Policy Directive 1382.2. This is processing-classification — a document classified on origination with a built-in declassification timeline, automatic by 1981 — not secrecy-classification. Worth saying plainly because the CONFIDENTIAL stamp on the pages can read more dramatic than the cover block intends.

The substantive material in the archive's eleven pages partitions cleanly into three crew discussions of three different anomalies. The editorial through-line, in each case, is the same: the crew sees something, talks about it among themselves and (where applicable) with Houston, and arrives at a hypothesis — sometimes confident, sometimes tentative.

## The object roughly one day out from Earth (pages 2–5)

The first anomaly is opened by Aldrin in the middle of an exchange about pre-LM-separation pacing:

> "The first unusual thing that we saw I guess was 1 day out or something pretty close to the moon. It had a sizeable dimension to it, so we put the monocular on it." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.2 "first unusual thing"]

Collins asks how they first spotted it; Aldrin answers, and immediately reports the first thing the crew did:

> "Yes, and we weren't sure but what it might be the S-IVB. We called the ground and were told the S-IVB was 6000 miles away." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.3 "S-IVB was 6000 miles"]

The S-IVB — the Saturn V third stage — is the obvious candidate for a trailing object in the right phase of the mission, and the crew ruled it out within the first minutes of the observation by consulting Houston for its actual range. With the simplest explanation excluded, they kept looking. The next several exchanges record the three of them in passive thermal control rotation ("PTC"), each taking a turn through the monocular and the sextant, working through what shape they were actually seeing:

> "We looked at it through the monocular and it seemed to have a bit of an L shape to it." (Aldrin) [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.3 "bit of an L shape"]

> "Like an open suitcase." (Armstrong) [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.3 "open suitcase"]

Aldrin then moves to the lower equipment bay to use the sextant optics, and the apparent shape changes again — because the sextant was off focus:

> "So then I got down in the LEB and started looking for it in the optics. We were grossly mislead because with the sextant off focus what we saw appeared to be a cylinder." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.4 "grossly mislead"]

Armstrong corrects to "two rings"; Collins overrides with "hollow cylinder"; Armstrong flags that the object was "right at the limit of the resolution of the eye" and notes explicitly that without independent knowledge of the range or the size, they couldn't determine either. [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.4 "limit of the reso"] The transcript preserves the crew arguing about apparent shape across three optical instruments — naked eye, monocular, off-focus sextant — and explicitly flagging that the off-focus sextant had been misleading them.

Then Collins, on page 5, proposes the working hypothesis:

> "Skipping ahead a bit, when we jettisoned the LM, you know we fired an explosive charge and got rid of the docking rings and the LM went boom. Pieces came off the LM. It could have been some Mylar or something that had somehow come loose from the LM." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.5 "some Mylar or something"]

Aldrin pushes back that "it didn't appear to have that shape" of a panel. Collins answers with a candidate part — the high-gain antenna — and then states his own current view on the record:

> "In the back of my mind, I have some reason to suspect that its origin was from the spacecraft." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.5 "origin was from the spacecraft"]

The whole arc — observation, consultation with Houston, rejection of the S-IVB, debate over apparent shape across three optical instruments, recognition that the sextant focus was an artifact, and the tentative settling on spacecraft-origin debris (Mylar, LM panel, or a high-gain antenna piece) — sits in three contiguous pages of transcript. The crew did not resolve the question, and they say so explicitly: *"we really don't have a conclusion as to what it might have been, how big it was, or how far away it was."*  What the document preserves is not a conclusion but a method.

## The cabin light flashes (pages 6–8)

The second anomaly is internal to the spacecraft. Aldrin opens it:

> "I was trying to go to sleep with all the lights out. I observed what I thought were little flashes inside the cabin, spaced a couple of minutes apart and I didn't think too much about it other than just note in my mind that they continued to be there. I couldn't explain why my eye would see these flashes." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.6 "little flashes inside the cabin"]

His description sharpens over the next page. During transearth coast he had more time to investigate; he reports double flashes "separated by maybe a foot" and "a line with no direction of motion." He proposes a working hypothesis on the record:

> "the only thing that comes to my mind is that this is some sort of penetration. At least that's my guess, without much to support it; some penetration of some object into the spacecraft that causes an emission as it enters the cabin itself." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.6 "some sort of pene"]

He tests his own hypothesis. He moves his hand against the sleep restraint to check whether static electricity could account for the appearance, observes the resulting sparks, and rules static out: *"there was a definite difference between the two as I observed it more and more."* [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.7 "static electricity"] He attempts a directional correlation with the Sun via the window-shade leakage, gets a weak signal, and reports that level of confidence accurately ("a little bit of evidence seemed to support this"). He asks the other two crew members; they hadn't seen it until the last day.

On the last night Armstrong runs the systematic version of the observation:

> "I spent probably an hour carefully watching the inside of the spacecraft and I probably made 50 significant observations in this period." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.7 "50 significant observations"]

Aldrin gives a rate ("on an average, I'd say just as a guess it was maybe something like one a minute") and then writes a sentence about the subjective experience that is unusual for an aeronautics debrief:

> "It did give you a rather funny feeling to contemplate that something was zapping through the cabin. There wasn't anything you could do about it." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.8 "zapping through the cabin"]

And Armstrong, on page 8, proposes the explanation:

> "It could be something like Buzz suggested. Mainly a neutron or some kind of an atomic particle that would be in the visible spectrum." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.8 "neutron or some kind of an atomic particle"]

This passage is the document's strongest physical-science moment, and it deserves to be flagged as such. The phenomenon Aldrin and Armstrong are describing here — brief flashes seen by dark-adapted astronauts, sometimes as points, sometimes as short lines or double events — was later formalized as the **Apollo light flashes**. The accepted physical explanation is that cosmic-ray nuclei (and, in some events, secondary particles) transit the retina or the visual cortex, producing Cherenkov radiation or direct retinal stimulation that the visual system registers as a flash. Apollo 17 in 1972 carried a dedicated experiment, **ALFMED** (Apollo Light Flash Moving Emulsion Detector), specifically to characterize the effect.

In 1969 the Apollo 11 crew did not have the vocabulary "cosmic ray" in this transcript. They had "neutron or some kind of an atomic particle." They were substantively correct. They got there by sequence: notice it → describe it precisely (counts, spacing, double events, lines) → propose a mechanism (penetration) → test an alternative (static electricity) → seek a directional correlation (Sun) → poll the other observers → run a systematic count → name a candidate particle. The transcript captures all of that across three pages, and the candidate particle Armstrong names turns out to be in the right physical regime.

## Section 21, Visual Sightings — Mars and the lake (pages 10–11)

The third set of observations comes from Volume II, **Section 21, Visual Sightings**, which Armstrong opens with the note that most items in the section "have been previously reported." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.10 "previously reported"] Two are recorded in the archive's pages.

The first is an optical illusion during the return leg from the Moon:

> "Looking back at it, at a time after Mars had passed behind the Moon, there was one time period where I imagined that the image of Mars was coming from a region where it couldn't come from, because it was in a dark portion of the Moon. This obviously was an optical illusion of some sort." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.10 "optical illusion of some sort"]

Armstrong adds the resolution in the next breath — Mars must have been "immediately adjacent to the horizon" — and Aldrin agrees they were probably observing the planet as it emerged from occultation. The crew names the illusion, identifies the geometry that probably produced it, and moves on inside the same exchange.

The second is the "possible laser" sighting in lunar orbit, which is also resolved within the document itself. Aldrin reports observing "a fairly bright light source which we tentatively ascribed to a possible laser" while approaching CDH (constant delta height) with the Earth above the lunar horizon. [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.10 "possible laser"] Then:

> "That seemed to be the best possible explanation until we were coming back in the command module approaching the Earth and were able to observe something that gave about the same appearance. When putting the monocular on the light source, it appeared as though it was the reflection of the Sun from a relatively smooth body of water such as a lake. I think we've revised our initial conclusion as to what the source of that light was that we saw coming from the Earth." [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.11 "reflection of the Sun"]

Aldrin closes with a caveat he writes into the record himself: *"If no one owns up to having beamed the laser toward the Moon at that time, it was more probably a reflection off a lake."* [cite: card d14e0371a5bf0f5e p.11 "more probably a reflection off a lake"] The hypothesis is named, the alternative is left open contingent on what someone else can rule in or out, and the residual oddity — that a sun-glint off a lake was bright enough to see from cislunar distance — is noted: *"I still think it's an unusual phenomenon, at that distance, to see so bright a source of light."*

## Why surface this document

The three passages are different in character. Pages 2–5 are about an external object — an unidentified body trailing the spacecraft — that the crew works on across three optical instruments and consults Houston about, and that they leave unresolved while explicitly favoring the spacecraft-debris hypothesis. Pages 6–8 are about a phenomenon internal to the cabin — brief flashes visible even with eyes closed — that the crew correctly diagnoses to particle physics in the absence of the formal terminology. Pages 10–11 are observational artifacts — an occulted-planet illusion and a sun-glint mistaken for a laser — resolved inside the same Section 21 exchange.

What ties them together is the epistemic shape. In each passage the document records the crew collectively reasoning about an anomalous observation in real time, on the record, with the hypotheses preserved alongside the observations. That shape is the editorial value of the document. The Apollo 11 Technical Crew Debriefing is not a record of unexplained phenomena; it is a record of how three trained observers handled the unexplained phenomena they encountered. The cabin-flashes passage, where Armstrong reaches a correct physical regime ahead of the formal measurement, is the strongest example of that shape, but the structure repeats.

The classification arc fits the same reading. A CONFIDENTIAL-stamped technical debriefing with a 12-year auto-declassification clause and a FOIA-handling notice on its cover page is not a withheld document; it is a document on a known timeline, and the timeline ran out in 1981. What survived to be released is the working transcript: not the cleaned-up post-hoc narrative, but the conversation in which three astronauts argue with each other about what they saw.

## A note on the sister entry

This site also carries a finds entry for the [Apollo 17 Technical Crew Debriefing](/finds/apollo-17), which covers the December 1972 mission's three reported visual phenomena: a reentry plasma tunnel, an aircraft carrier seen briefly through fogged windows, and the Apollo light flashes — by then a formal experimental target rather than an in-flight puzzle. The two debriefings together form a useful pair. The light-flash phenomenon Aldrin and Armstrong are *discovering* in the 1969 transcript is the same phenomenon Schmitt is *characterizing* in the 1972 transcript, three and a half years and four crewed missions later. The arc between the two documents is the arc of the phenomenon entering the formal scientific record.

## Provenance of this entry

A code-assistant agent extracted the document's identifying surface (mission, date, preparing organization, classification block, declassification clause) and the three substantive passages from the eleven OCR'd pages, and reported back; the editorial frame is the operator's. The agent was asked to identify the three UAP-relevant passages and to summarize what each records the crew doing in real time; it was not asked to render any judgment about what the document means for any external claim or narrative, and this entry does not.

### fbi-1947-dallas-teletype — The July 8 1947 Wyly Teletype and the March 22 1950 Hottel Memo

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/fbi-1947-dallas-teletype
- Published: 2026-05-12
- Cards: bcf2e688dfbc220d, b246c782b16be168

Card bcf2e688dfbc220d (FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 1, page 70) is a single-page urgent teletype from SAC Dallas, sent at 6:17 PM on July 8, 1947, relaying a same-day phone call from a Major at HQ Eighth Air Force about an object recovered near Roswell. Card b246c782b16be168 (FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 5, page 68) is the March 22, 1950 memorandum from SAC Washington Field Guy Hottel describing three circular saucers recovered in New Mexico, each with three occupants. The two documents are editorially adjacent — both flow through FBI channels, both reference New Mexico recoveries — but their dates, geometries, source chains, and what the Bureau was doing in each case differ substantially. This entry sets them side-by-side so a reader can read both and form their own judgment.

## What's in the case file

FBI 62-HQ-83894 is the Bureau's general flying-disc case file. Two documents in it are editorially adjacent — both mention New Mexico recoveries, both flow through SAC-to-Director channels — but they are different documents with different evidential properties, filed nearly three years apart, in different Sections of the file. This entry walks through each on its own terms.

## Document 1 — The Wyly teletype, July 8, 1947

**Surface.** A single-page urgent teletype, time-stamped **6:17 PM**, dated **7-8-47**, from **FBI Dallas** to **Director and SAC, Cincinnati**. Subject line: **"FLYING DISC, INFORMATION CONCERNING."** Signed at the bottom **WYLY** — Percy Wyly, the Dallas SAC. Card `bcf2e688dfbc220d`, page 70 of FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 1.

**Content.** Wyly is relaying a phone call he received the same day from an Eighth Air Force officer at Fort Worth. The teletype, as typed, names the caller as "MAJOR CURTAN":

> "MAJOR CURTAN, HEADQUARTERS EIGHTH AIR FORCE, TELEPHONICALLY ADVISED THIS OFFICE THAT AN OBJECT PURPORTING TO BE A FLYING DISC WAS RE COVERED NEAR ROSWELL, NEW MEXICO, THIS DATE." [cite: card bcf2e688dfbc220d p.70 "PURPORTING TO BE A FLYING DISC"]

(Historians of the case identify the actual caller as **Major Edwin M. Kirton**, an Eighth Air Force intelligence officer. "CURTAN" is a teletype transmission artifact — a transposition consistent with how Kirton's name was rendered through the period's wire equipment. The teletype's surface preserves the artifact, and the corpus preserves the surface.)

**Geometry described.** Hexagonal. Suspended from a balloon by cable. The balloon, not the disc, is given a diameter of approximately twenty feet:

> "THE DISC IS HEXAGONAL IN SHAPE AND WAS SUSPENDED FROM A BALLON BY CABLE, WHICH BALLON WAS APPROXIMATELY TWENTY FEET IN DIAMETER." [cite: card bcf2e688dfbc220d p.70 "HEXAGONAL IN SHAPE"]

**The weather-balloon comparison, and its limits at time of transmission.** The teletype records Major Kirton's own statement that the object resembled a high-altitude weather balloon with a radar reflector — and, in the same sentence, records that the Eighth Air Force's own check against Wright Field had not, as of 6:17 PM that day, confirmed that identification:

> "MAJOR CURTAN FURTHER ADVISED THAT THE OBJECT FOUND RESEMBLES A HIGH ALTITUDE WEATHER BALLOON WITH A RADAR REFLECTOR, BUT THAT TELEPHONIC CONVERSATION BETWEEN THEIR OFFICE AND WRIGHT FIELD HAD NOT SOUND BORNE OUT THIS BELIEF." [cite: card bcf2e688dfbc220d p.70 "HAD NOT SOUND BORNE OUT THIS BELIEF"]

This is the methodologically interesting line on the page. At the moment of transmission, the AAF's own preferred identification was not yet confirmed by its own internal phone check.

**No bodies.** The teletype mentions no occupants, no human-shaped figures, no biological material of any kind. It describes an object and a balloon.

**Disposition.** The object and balloon are being flown to Wright Field for examination. The reason the FBI is being told at all is institutional housekeeping — press interest:

> "INFORMATION PROVIDED THIS OFFICE BECAUSE OF NATIONAL INTEREST IN CASE AND FACT THAT NATIONAL BROADCASTING COMPANY, ASSOCIATED PRESS, AND OTHERS ATTEMPTING TO BREAK STORY OF LOCATION OF DISC TODAY." [cite: card bcf2e688dfbc220d p.70 "ATTEMPTING TO BREAK STORY"]

The closing line records the Bureau's posture: **"NO FURTHER INVESTIGATION BEING CONDUCTED."** [cite: card bcf2e688dfbc220d p.70 "NO FURTHER INVESTIGATION BEING CONDUCTED"]

**Source chain in one sentence.** A same-day, named-officer phone call from the Eighth Air Force to the Dallas SAC, transmitted to the Director and Cincinnati within hours of the underlying event, while the AAF was still actively processing the recovery.

## Document 2 — The Hottel memo, March 22, 1950

**Surface.** A Standard Form No. 64 Office Memorandum, dated **March 22, 1950**, from **GUY HOTTEL, SAC, WASHINGTON** to **DIRECTOR, FBI**. Subject: **"FLYING SAUCERS — INFORMATION CONCERNING."** Card `b246c782b16be168`, page 68 of FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 5.

**Content.** Hottel is relaying what was passed to one of his agents (SA R. H. Kurtzman) by a Metropolitan Police Department investigator (Karl Howe) who had heard it from an Air Force investigator. The chain is set out explicitly on the page:

> "The following information was furnished to SA R. H. KURTZMAN by KARL HOWE, Special Investigator, Sex Squad, Metropolitan Police Department: An investigator for the Air Forces stated that three so-called flying saucers had been recovered in New Mexico." [cite: card b246c782b16be168 p.68 "An investigator for the Air Forces"]

**Geometry described.** Three saucers, not one object. Each circular with raised centers. Each approximately fifty feet in diameter, not twenty:

> "They were described as being circular in shape with raised centers, approximately 50 feet in diameter." [cite: card b246c782b16be168 p.68 "approximately 50 feet in diameter"]

**Bodies.** Three per saucer, each three feet tall, in metallic-cloth garments:

> "Each one was occupied by three bodies of human shape but only 3 feet tall, dressed in metallic cloth of a very fine texture." [cite: card b246c782b16be168 p.68 "three bodies of human shape"]

**Proposed mechanism.** A radar-interference hypothesis is attributed to Howe's informant:
