> "the saucers were found in New Mexico due to the fact that the Government has a very high-powered radar set-up in that area and it is believed the radar interferes with the controling mechanism of the saucers." [cite: card b246c782b16be168 p.68 "interferes with the controling mechanism"]

**The Bureau's own posture in the memo.** This is the single most important line on the page for assessing the document's evidential weight. Hottel closes the memo with a sentence in which the FBI affirmatively declines to evaluate what it has just relayed:

> "No further evaluation was attempted by SA KURTZMAN concerning the above." [cite: card b246c782b16be168 p.68 "No further evaluation was attempted"]

That sentence is the memo telling the reader what the memo is: a filing of a thirdhand report, by an agent who did not pursue it further. The Bureau is documenting that it heard the story, recording it in the case file, and stating on the face of the document that it did not work it.

**Source chain in one sentence.** Air Force investigator → Karl Howe (DC Metropolitan Police, Sex Squad) → SA Kurtzman → SAC Hottel → Director, with no Bureau investigative action attached at the bottom.

## What the two documents actually differ on

| Property | Wyly teletype (1947) | Hottel memo (1950) |
|---|---|---|
| Date | July 8, 1947 — same day as the Roswell incident | March 22, 1950 — nearly three years later |
| Section of 62-HQ-83894 | Section 1, page 70 | Section 5, page 68 |
| Number of objects | One | Three |
| Geometry | Hexagonal, suspended by cable from a balloon | Circular saucers, raised centers |
| Stated diameter | ~20 ft (the balloon, not the disc) | ~50 ft (each saucer) |
| Occupants mentioned | None | Three per saucer, ~3 ft tall, in metallic cloth |
| Source chain | Same-day named-officer phone call from HQ Eighth Air Force, while AAF was actively processing the event | Thirdhand: AF investigator → DC police investigator → SA → SAC |
| FBI's posture in the document | Routing fresh same-day intelligence to the Director and Cincinnati; "no further investigation being conducted" because the AAF is handling it | Filing a report at the case file, with an explicit on-page statement that "no further evaluation was attempted" |

The geometries do not match each other. The diameters do not match each other. The bodies in one are not in the other. The dates are nearly three years apart. The source chains and the Bureau's posture in each case are different.

## Why both documents are in this archive

The corpus's editorial discipline is to preserve the surface of each primary source — what the document actually says, who signed it, when, through what channel, with what disclaimers — and let the reader judge. These two documents sit adjacent in the case file but are evidence for different propositions filed under different conditions: one a same-day intelligence relay during an active recovery, the other a thirdhand filing the Bureau explicitly declined to evaluate.

A reader who clicks through to card `bcf2e688dfbc220d` can read the Wyly teletype's twelve typed lines and assess for themselves what kind of evidential object a same-day, named-officer wire relay is. A reader who clicks through to card `b246c782b16be168` can read Hottel's eleven-line memo and assess what kind of evidential object a thirdhand filing labeled "no further evaluation was attempted" is. Both judgments are available because both documents are preserved at their primary surface.

## Provenance of this entry

A code-assistant agent located the two documents in the preserved OCR for FBI 62-HQ-83894 (card `bcf2e688dfbc220d` page 70 of Section 1; card `b246c782b16be168` page 68 of Section 5), verified the exact wording cited above against the OCR text at high confidence (surya engine, 94.9% and 95.4% respectively), and reported the document surface back. The editorial frame — placing the two documents side-by-side as different evidential objects in the same case file — is the operator's. The "CURTAN" / Kirton transmission-artifact note is a one-sentence editorial annotation on a teletype-typography fact; the corpus preserves the teletype as transmitted.

### fbi-usper-2025-orb — An FBI FD-302 on a Senior Intelligence Official's UAP Sighting, Late 2025

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/fbi-usper-2025-orb
- Published: 2026-05-12
- Cards: be533a4ab886eb11, ccd932b4f40e8de7

Card be533a4ab886eb11 is a three-page FBI FD-302-style interview narrative classified SECRET//NOFORN on every page, summarizing a senior US intelligence official's first-hand account of a Late-2025 UAP encounter at an unnamed US military facility. The document records a layered sensor chain — a Listening Post/Observation Post FLIR/NVG observation post, a state-partner helicopter intercept, and a late-arriving flight of five military aircraft on an unrelated training mission — and is precise about which platform saw what. Card ccd932b4f40e8de7 is the companion image, FBI Photo B7: a grayscale FLIR-style frame showing a helicopter under a central crosshair reticle with 5/10/15 tick scales, OCR yielding only a corrupted system timestamp. Together the two cards introduce a document grammar — the FD-302 narrative — that the same Release 01 corpus also carries in the structured MISREP form. This entry walks what the 302 commits to and what its redactions deliberately withhold.

## What the documents are

Card `be533a4ab886eb11` is **"USPER Statement about UAP Sighting"** — a three-page FBI document released as part of Release 01. The narrative form (chronological prose, third-person summary of a single witness's first-hand account, indented "Comments" block at the close) is consistent with an FBI **FD-302** interview summary, which is how the FBI's institutional grammar records what an agent was told. The classification banner runs **SECRET//NOFORN** on all three pages (the page-1 OCR captures the banner as `SECRET//NOFORM`, an artifact of the banner underline; pages 2 and 3 OCR cleanly).

Card `ccd932b4f40e8de7` — **"FBI Photo B7"** — is a single grayscale frame: a helicopter in the upper-center-right of the display, a central crosshair reticle, tick-mark scales running `5`, `10`, `15` horizontally on both sides of center. The OCR yields essentially no text — only the tick numerals and a corrupted system timestamp `12/31/99 18:10:02` (the source-system clock was not set). The image-description note recorded for that card describes the frame as a "Grayscale video frame of a helicopter in the upper center-right, overlaid with a central crosshair and tick-mark scale labeled 5, 10, and 15 on both horizontal sides." [cite: card ccd932b4f40e8de7 p.1 "Grayscale video frame of a helicopter"] The manifest description carried with the image notes "a second, smaller, dark circular object… visible below the reticle" and that "an accompanying mission report was not provided."

Both cards carry `redacted: true` in the manifest. The 302 reads as essentially nothing *but* redactions in its proper nouns — and the structure of what the redactor chose to leave in vs. take out is itself the most useful reading of the document.

## What the redactor left in, and what they took out

The 302 anonymizes by category. Each redacted entity is replaced with a bracketed role token, and the categories are kept distinct from each other across all three pages:

- `[WITNESS 1 (a senior US intelligence official)]` and `[WITNESS 2 (a senior US intelligence official)]` — two people, same role descriptor, agencies redacted.
- `[FEDERAL PARTNER 1]` through `[FEDERAL PARTNER 4]` — four separate federal partner agencies, none named.
- `[STATE PARTNER ORGANIZATION]` — the operator of the helicopter at the center of the chase, distinct from the federal partners and from the military aircraft.
- `[MILITARY AIRCRAFT]` — a class of aircraft (five of them, on an unrelated training mission) that appears later in the timeline.
- `[OPERATIONS CENTER]`, `[FACILITY]`, `[MOUNTAIN RANGE NAME]`, `[SITE CODE NAME]`, `[LOCAL TOWN]`, `[NEARBY TOWN NAME]`, `[ROAD NAME]` — every place name redacted.
- `[CALL SIGN 1]`, `[CALL SIGN 2]` — both helicopter call signs redacted.
- `[COORDINATES]` — every coordinate string, on every page.
- The incident date itself: the document opens with `On [DATE], at approximately 1700 hours…`. [cite: card be533a4ab886eb11 p.1 "senior US intelligence official"]

What the redactor *did* leave in: Zulu-style timestamps to the minute (1700, 1751, 2050, 2052, 2141, 2149, 2202, 2207, 2218, 2227, 2228, 2233, 2241, 2249, 2252, 2257, 2306, 2316, 2320), the count of personnel and aircraft, the sensor types in use at each observation (FLIR, NVG, naked eye), and the verbatim radio-relayed language LP/OP used to describe the orb on FLIR (`"super-hot"`, in quotation marks in the document itself).

The document is therefore readable as a precise timeline of *who saw what on which sensor* — with every proper noun, every place, and the date stripped out.

## The witness, as the document characterizes them

The narrative is told from the perspective of WITNESS 1. Both WITNESS 1 and WITNESS 2 are introduced with the same role descriptor:

> "On [DATE], at approximately 1700 hours [WITNESS 1 (a senior US intelligence official)], [FEDERAL PARTNER 1] and [FEDERAL PARTNER 2], accompanied by [WITNESS 2 (a senior US intelligence official)], and two pilots from [STATE PARTNER ORGANIZATION], departed the [OPERATIONS CENTER]…" [cite: card be533a4ab886eb11 p.1 "senior US intelligence official"]

"Senior US intelligence official" is the exact phrase, and it is the only descriptor either witness is given. The agency, and therefore the witness's military-versus-civilian status, is among the things the redactor took out. The intelligence community spans civilian career services and uniformed components; this document does not say which side either witness sits on, and a reader who wants to stay inside what the document supports should hold "senior US intelligence official" at exactly the level of specificity the redactor allowed.

## The sensor chain, in the order the document records it

The structural feature of this 302 is that it carefully segregates which platform observed which event on which sensor. A reader following the chronology can trace the chain:

**1700 hours — composite departure.** Two senior intelligence officials, two FEDERAL PARTNER agencies, and two pilots from a STATE PARTNER ORGANIZATION lift off from the OPERATIONS CENTER in a STATE PARTNER ORGANIZATION helicopter, `[CALL SIGN 1]`, for a daytime aerial search. The mission is prompted by prior eyewitness reports of orbs/lights and personnel "thuds as if something has fallen and hit the ground." [cite: card be533a4ab886eb11 p.1 "thuds as if something has fallen"]

**2141 hours — handover to LP/OP.** `[CALL SIGN 1]` lifts off from refueling and heads toward debris spotted by a **Listening Post/Observation Post** — `[FEDERAL PARTNER 4]` personnel "using Forward Looking Infrared (FLIR) and Night Vision Goggles (NVG)". [cite: card be533a4ab886eb11 p.1 "Forward Looking Infrared"] The LP/OP is a ground observation post operated by a different federal partner than the agencies aboard the helicopter; its instruments — not the helicopter's — are what carry the next phase of the encounter.

**2202 hours — the "super-hot" relay.** `[CALL SIGN 1]` arrives at LP/OP-provided coordinates and "spotted a possible aircraft on the horizon moving away to the west." Then:

> "LP/OP confirmed the sighting then relayed they spotted an orb under FLIR and described as 'super-hot' hovering at ground level before heading [BEARING] from LP/OP." [cite: card be533a4ab886eb11 p.1 "super-hot"]

Two structural details to preserve. The word `"super-hot"` is in quotation marks in the document — it is the relayed FLIR-observation language from LP/OP, transcribed by the 302 as quoted speech, not the 302's own characterization. And the observation is a **thermal description of what LP/OP saw on the FLIR display**, not an instrument temperature reading; the document does not say what temperature `"super-hot"` corresponds to.

**2207 hours — the military aircraft appear, separately.** Page 2 opens by introducing a different platform category:

> "JOC reported five [MILITARY AIRCRAFT] from [REDACTED] were in the air space conducting a training mission." [cite: card be533a4ab886eb11 p.2 "MILITARY AIRCRAFT"]

The 302 is consistent across all three pages about this distinction: `[CALL SIGN 1]` is a STATE PARTNER ORGANIZATION helicopter; the `[MILITARY AIRCRAFT]` are a separate flight of five aircraft on an unrelated training mission, who later "JOC relayed they contacted… enroute to assist, eta two minutes." The helicopter and the military aircraft are two different things, with two different operators, in two different roles in the timeline.

**The 20-mile leg, as LP/OP reports it.** This is the most-quoted detail and the one the document is most precise about. After `[CALL SIGN 1]` is on station and finds nothing on its own sensors:

> "Once on station, [CALL SIGN 1] searched the location with FLIR, NVG, and the naked eye but did not locate the orb. LP/OP reported the orb gained elevation, came within ten feet of [CALL SIGN 1] and then headed east to [REDACTED]. [CALL SIGN 1] moved to intercept but LP/OP reported the orb continued southeast and estimated it to be past [ROAD NAME], some 20 miles from the current position at [REDACTED]. [CALL SIGN 1], unable to match speed, broke off pursuit…" [cite: card be533a4ab886eb11 p.2 "20 miles from the current"]

The paragraph rewards a slow read. The helicopter, with FLIR, NVG, and naked-eye observers, "did not locate the orb" on its own sensors. The orb's gaining elevation and ten-foot proximity to `[CALL SIGN 1]` are recorded as **LP/OP-reported** events. The orb's southeast continuation and 20-mile estimate are **LP/OP's estimate of distance from `[CALL SIGN 1]`'s position**, made over the period after the helicopter had lost contact, not a continuous track flown by the helicopter. The helicopter "unable to match speed, broke off pursuit" — but the pursuit it broke off was one it had not, on its own instruments, been able to reacquire.

The co-pilot does record a brief second-sensor observation in that same window — "the co-pilot reported seeing under NVG something emerge from the two objects and then travel in a different direction and a high rate of speed" — but this is an NVG note, not a tracked extended observation.

## The eight further structured observations

The 20-mile leg is one item on a much longer timeline. Across the rest of pages 2 and 3, between 2218 and 2257 hours, the 302 records eight further structured observations of orbs, each by `[CALL SIGN 1]` with WITNESS 1 on the naked eye and the pilots on NVG. The recurring pattern is the document's own vocabulary:

> "The orbs flared up one at a time in a horizontal formation and after approximately ten – fifteen seconds, flared down in the opposite order and lost visual." [cite: card be533a4ab886eb11 p.2 "flared up one at a time"]

Variations on that sentence — sometimes with `ten seconds` instead of `ten – fifteen`, sometimes with `three distinct orbs in a triangle formation`, sometimes with `four or five in total below the original two` — recur five times across the two pages, each anchored to a Zulu timestamp and a position relative to a redacted site code name. The form of the observation is part of what makes it sit oddly with the structured-form MISREPs in the same corpus: the 302 has no checkbox for `flared up`, no numeric kinetic block, no Observer Assessment field. It is prose.

WITNESS 1's closing comment on page 3, set off from the timeline as a separate "Comments" section:

> "Pilots indicated they were recording however many sightings were above the helicopter which was outside of the helicopters FLIR camera angle. Some things I could not see with the naked eye, but I recall the pilots calling out sightings. The orbs appeared to break off from [CALL SIGN 1] and pursue the [MILITARY AIRCRAFT]." [cite: card be533a4ab886eb11 p.3 "break off"]

The closing sentence is WITNESS 1's interpretation of what was observed; the 302 records the interpretation as the witness's words, without adjudicating it.

## The FD-302 grammar vs. the MISREP grammar

The 302 and the DOW MISREPs ([D23](/finds/dow-d23-arabian-gulf-october-2023), [D32](/finds/dow-d32-syria-october-2024), [D33](/finds/dow-d33-aegean-sea-october-2023)) all sit in the same Release 01 corpus, and all are modern (2020s) primary-source UAP documents. They commit to different things because they are different document types.

A MISREP is **a structured form filled out by aircrew**. Its commitments are check-box selections and numeric block entries. When a MISREP says `UAP Physical State: Solid`, it is the aircrew's selection from the menu `Solid | Gas | Plasma | UNK`. When it says `Kinetic Velocity: 320 MPH`, it is an estimated number written into a labeled field. The form's range — what fields it offers, what menus it constrains the selection to — is part of what makes any given entry readable.

An FD-302 is **a prose narrative summary, written by an agent, of what a witness said**. It does not have field menus; the structure is chronological. Its commitments are at a different layer — *what the document chose to write down as direct quotation*, *what redaction category each anonymized noun was sorted into*, and *what observational language the agent transcribed as the witness's own*. There is no `UAP Physical State: Solid` field here; there is `"super-hot"` in quotation marks, attributed to LP/OP, on FLIR. There is no `Observer Assessment: Benign` field; there is the closing-comments paragraph in which WITNESS 1 says the orbs "appeared to break off from [CALL SIGN 1] and pursue the [MILITARY AIRCRAFT]" and the document records that as the witness's interpretation, not as a finding.

The two grammars also redact differently. A MISREP that records an Iranian guard call leaves the call sign of the friendly aircraft as `[callsign]` and otherwise commits to numbers (FL230, 158 KIAS) and proper-noun adversary identifications (`IRANIAN AIR DEFENSE`). A 302 takes out every proper noun in the witness's account and leaves the *categories* (`STATE PARTNER ORGANIZATION`, `FEDERAL PARTNER 4`, `MILITARY AIRCRAFT`) so the structure of the operation is legible even when none of its participants are. A reader interested in modern UAP documents has both grammars to work with, and they are usefully different ways of writing down what happened.

## The companion image — what it does and does not show

Card `ccd932b4f40e8de7` is a single grayscale frame depicting a helicopter under a central crosshair reticle with tick scales — visually consistent with an LP/OP FLIR display imaging an in-air helicopter, though the document chain does not assert this. The image carries no embedded metadata except the corrupted system timestamp; OCR returns essentially nothing.

The 302 and the photo are both FBI-released, both dated `Late 2025`, both carry `redacted: true`, and both depict a helicopter-adjacent UAP scenario. At the time this entry was first published (12 May 2026), they were not structurally paired in the manifest's `pdf_pairing` field — they were not yet declared by the corpus to be the same incident, the way DOW MISREPs are paired to their AARO videos.

**Update (25 May 2026):** With Release 02 on 22 May 2026, the corpus declared the pairing explicitly. The ODNI Narrative card description states the narrative *"is accompanied by infrared imagery taken during the same exercise by other federal officials from the ground"*, and the FBI 302's own card description was updated to read *"The photos of UAP underneath the helicopter are from this same set of observations, taken through night vision devices by ground-based personnel."* The manifest's `pdf_pairing` field on both `be533a4ab886eb11` and `fd342b7508668b0e` now lists all 32 photographs (A001–A008 and B001–B024) plus each other. Per-frame direct examination of all 32 photographs — including the sensor-system classification that splits the A-series from the B-series and the burst structure of the 24 B-frames — is in the imagery-focused companion entry at [/finds/helicopter-case-2025-imagery](/finds/helicopter-case-2025-imagery). The first-person ODNI narrative read against the FD-302 grammar is at [/finds/odni-uap-d001-usper-narrative](/finds/odni-uap-d001-usper-narrative).

## What the document deliberately withholds

A short index of what the 302 takes out, organized by category:

- **Who the witnesses are.** Two senior US intelligence officials. The agency or service of either is redacted.
- **Which federal agencies are involved.** Four separate federal partners are referenced as `[FEDERAL PARTNER 1]` through `[FEDERAL PARTNER 4]`. None is named.
- **Who flew the helicopter.** A `[STATE PARTNER ORGANIZATION]`. The 302 does not say which.
- **What kind of military aircraft assisted.** Five `[MILITARY AIRCRAFT]` on a training mission. The aircraft type and operator are redacted.
- **Where this happened.** The operations center, the facility, the mountain range, the site code names, the nearby towns, and the road are all redacted. Every coordinate is `[COORDINATES]`.
- **When this happened.** The opening line is `On [DATE]`. The Zulu-style timestamps and the manifest `incident_date: Late 2025` are what survives the redaction.
- **What bearing and what destination the orb headed toward.** Every cardinal-direction follow-on (`heading [BEARING]`, `headed east to [REDACTED]`) is bracketed.

What the document does **not** withhold: the sensor types in use, the timestamps, the personnel counts and categories, the verbatim radio-quotation of LP/OP's `"super-hot"`, and the structure of the observation chain — which is enough to read the document as what it is.

## Provenance of this entry

A code-assistant agent located and verified the document surface — the FD-302 form factor, the SECRET//NOFORN banner across all three pages, the redaction categories, the role descriptors for the two witnesses, the sensor-chain segregation, and the verbatim placement of the quoted phrases — by reading the three preserved OCR pages of `be533a4ab886eb11` and the OCR of `ccd932b4f40e8de7` directly. The editorial frame — surfacing this card as a sibling-grammar to the DOW MISREPs within the Release 01 corpus, and reading it as a primary-source modern UAP narrative on its own terms — is the operator's. The cross-references to D23, D32, and D33 are to existing finds entries in this archive on the structured-form side of the same modern document landscape.

### dow-uap-d20-iraq-2023-replaced — DOW-UAP-D20 — Replaced Between Tranches

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/dow-uap-d20-iraq-2023-replaced
- Published: 2026-05-11
- Cards: 80e36017873c19a1, 085c019c9899db9b

Card 80e36017873c19a1 — the upstream DOW-UAP-D20 Mission Report as published on 2026-05-08 — was removed from the war.gov listing between 2026-05-08 and 2026-05-11. The new manifest contains a card with the same title (DOW-UAP-D20, Mission Report, Iraq, 2023) at a different card_id (085c019c9899db9b) pointing to a different asset filename. This is a replacement, not a deletion. Both filenames, both card records, and the preserved OCR of the original are documented here so the diff between versions stays legible.

## Two cards, one title

PURSUE content-addresses each card by `sha256(asset_url || title)[:16]`. When the upstream changes a document's filename or URL, the card_id changes — even if the title stays identical. The DOW-UAP-D20 Mission Report appears twice in the PURSUE record under two distinct card_ids:

| | Original (removed) | Replacement (current) |
|---|---|---|
| `card_id` | `80e36017873c19a1` | `085c019c9899db9b` |
| `asset_filename` | `dow-uap-d20-mission-report-southern-united-states-2023.pdf` | `dow-uap-d20-mission-report-iraq-2023.pdf` |
| `title` | DOW-UAP-D20, Mission Report, Iraq, 2023 | DOW-UAP-D20, Mission Report, Iraq, 2023 |
| `incident_date` (manifest field) | (absent or different) | `3/31/23` |
| `incident_location` (manifest field) | (absent or different) | `Iraq` |
| in 2026-05-08 manifest? | yes | no |
| in 2026-05-11 manifest? | no | yes |

The titles are identical. The filenames differ on the geographic slug — `southern-united-states-2023` versus `iraq-2023`. The replacement is in our manifest now; the original is preserved by this archive but no longer listed upstream.

## What the original (`80e36017873c19a1`) contains

Six pages, MISREP format, SECRET//NOFORN. The MISREP records:

- **Originator:** 77 Expeditionary Fighter Squadron, 378 Air Expeditionary Wing, supporting Operation INHERENT RESOLVE, with 609 CAOC oversight. [cite: card 80e36017873c19a1 p.2 "77 EFS"]
- **Platform:** a two-ship of F-16CM Fighting Falcons (paired manned-fighter sortie, in contrast to the unmanned ISR platforms in [DOW-UAP-D23](/finds/dow-d23-arabian-gulf-october-2023), [D32](/finds/dow-d32-syria-october-2024), and [D33](/finds/dow-d33-aegean-sea-october-2023)).
- **Mission type:** Defensive Counter-Air (DCA).
- **Takeoff:** ICAO `OEPS` — Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia — at `311901:00ZMAR23`. [cite: card 80e36017873c19a1 p.1 "OEPS"]
- **Landing:** `010148ZAPR23`. Mission duration approximately 6 hours 47 minutes.
- **Routing:** transited Iraqi airspace, then Syrian airspace; on station in killbox "ESSA" from 2058Z to 0000Z.
- **UAP event DTG:** `312302:05ZMAR23` — 31 March 2023, 23:02 Zulu.
- **Observation:** approximately 10–20 bright objects moving west-to-east at flight level above 600 (the F-16s were at FL265). Each object was held on the SNIPER LDP targeting pod in TV mode for roughly 20 seconds before dimming and dropping from track. [cite: card 80e36017873c19a1 p.6 "approximately 10"] The aircrew explicitly distinguished the returns from stars via comparative pod imagery.
- **Response:** no kinetic engagement; no effects on personnel; the flight returned to base normally.
- **Pattern note:** the narrative on page 6 includes language describing the formation as not having been seen in this configuration "as previously seen in PRIOR SORTIES," indicating the originator had context for repeat events.

## What the replacement (`085c019c9899db9b`) contains

The replacement card's PDF was OCR'd on 2026-05-12 (six pages — same page count as the original). The page-level content is now live in `/data/pages.json` and the LLM-cleaned mirror at `/data/pages-cleaned.json`. A direct side-by-side against the original is possible.

## Side-by-side: what changed, what didn't

**The structural-difference hypotheses listed in the draft of this entry can now be checked against the bytes.** The empirical result is that the *content* of the replacement is essentially the same as the original. Every "potentially sensitive" marker that drove the "tradecraft scrub" hypothesis is present in both documents:

| Marker | Original (`80e36017873c19a1`) | Replacement (`085c019c9899db9b`) |
|---|---|---|
| Squadron callout: 77 EFS | present | present |
| Airfield ICAO: OEPS (Prince Sultan AB) | present | present |
| Mission DTGs (takeoff/landing) | `311901:00ZMAR23` / `010148ZAPR23` | same |
| Weapons loadout: AIM-120, AIM-9X, M61A1 | present | present |
| Countermeasures: ALQ-184 ECM, ALE-50 towed decoy, ALR-56M RWR | present | present |
| SEAD pod: HTS-P | present | present |
| Specific software-load IDs (e.g., `SY0730`) | present | present |
| Narrative line: "as previously seen in PRIOR SORTIES" | present, page 6 | **also present in the replacement** |

In other words: the original entry's strongest hypothesis — that the upstream replaced this file in order to redact the EW/weapons fingerprint and the prior-sorties narrative — is **refuted by the OCR of the replacement**. The replacement carries the same operational detail. The remaining substantive difference between the two cards is the asset filename: the original was `...southern-united-states-2023.pdf` (geographic-slug mismatch with the title "Iraq, 2023"); the replacement is `...iraq-2023.pdf` (filename and title agree).

The simplest reading consistent with the evidence: the upstream replaced this file specifically to fix the filename-vs-title mismatch, NOT to re-redact the content. The "scrub" hypothesis was a plausible read of metadata alone, but the OCR side-by-side rules it out.

This is a useful integrity story in its own right: a curated archive that hypothesizes a motive should be willing to refute its own hypotheses when the bytes prove otherwise. Editorial discipline doesn't end at "we don't assert motive" — it extends to "we update our entries when later evidence narrows or refutes earlier guesses."

## What's preserved

| Surface | Original (`80e36017873c19a1`) | Replacement (`085c019c9899db9b`) |
|---|---|---|
| PDF | live at `/pdf/80e36017873c19a1.pdf` (R2 mirror, our copy) | live at `/pdf/085c019c9899db9b.pdf` (R2 mirror) |
| OCR text | 6 pages in `/data/pages.json` | 6 pages in `/data/pages.json` |
| LLM-cleaned reading text | yes (2026-05-11 corpus pass) | yes (2026-05-12 incremental pass) |
| Embeddings | yes | yes (added 2026-05-12) |
| Card detail | `/card/80e36017873c19a1` | `/card/085c019c9899db9b` |
| Listed by upstream | no — as of 2026-05-11 | yes |

The original is the version most readers should expect to see referenced in third-party citations dated before 2026-05-11; it remains accessible through this archive.

## How to use this entry

If a citation in another work points to "DOW-UAP-D20" without specifying which version, follow the date of the citation: pre-2026-05-11 citations describe the original (`80e36017873c19a1`); after, the replacement. The PURSUE description text in the manifest entry is essentially the same across both. The PDFs are different files at different content-addressed URLs and may differ at the page level. When the replacement OCRs, this entry will be updated with a direct field-by-field comparison.

## Provenance of this entry

A code-assistant agent walked the preserved OCR of the original and the manifest-level surface of the replacement, summarized the three structural differences identified above, and reported back. The editorial frame is the operator's. The agent identified hypotheses for *why* the replacement happened; this entry does not assert any of them. The factual claim here is that two card_ids exist at the same title with different asset filenames and different listing dates, and that the first is preserved.

### fbi-62-hq-83894-section-6-removed-2026-05 — FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 6 — PDF Pulled, Listing Kept

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/fbi-62-hq-83894-section-6-removed-2026-05
- Published: 2026-05-11
- Cards: 13f86e95aed52840, 9c86c04b5e4a50e8

Card 13f86e95aed52840 — Section 6 of the FBI's ten-section omnibus UFO file 62-HQ-83894 — was downloadable from war.gov in the 2026-05-08 PURSUE CSV and is not in the 2026-05-11 CSV: the same title still appears in the upstream listing (under a new card_id, 9c86c04b5e4a50e8), but with the PDF link explicitly set to 'N/A'. The PDF is now only available through this archive's R2 mirror, and the 271-page OCR transcript remains in /search and /atlas. This entry catalogues what the section contains — green-fireball reports, Oak Ridge sightings, Rhodes/Phoenix-1947 chain of custody, an FBI background investigation of a named civilian witness — so the document is legible without depending on upstream availability.

## What the document is

Card `13f86e95aed52840` is **Section 6 of FBI file 62-HQ-83894**, the Bureau's omnibus UFO file. The full file family runs Sections 1 through 10 — approximately 1,900 pages of catalogued correspondence, investigation memoranda, citizen letters, and inter-bureau coordination between 1947 and 1968. The reading guide at [/finds/fbi-62-hq-83894-readers-guide](/finds/fbi-62-hq-83894-readers-guide) walks the section structure.

Section 6 is 271 pages, weighted heavily to 1949–1952 (year-frequency in the OCR: 1952 × 192, 1950 × 114, 1949 × 40, 1951 × 30, with smaller counts before and after). The CSV description that originally accompanied this card on war.gov characterized this version as a "complete case file with several newly declassified pages and only minor redactions" — explicitly comparing it favorably against the more-redacted version available on the FBI Vault. The prior manifest record carried `redacted: false`.

## The pull, as the new CSV states it

A direct field-by-field diff of the 2026-05-08 CSV against the 2026-05-11 CSV is unambiguous about what happened. The Section 6 title is still in the upstream listing — same description text, same "Type: PDF," same agency. The single field that changed:

> `PDF | Image Link: N/A` [cite: card 9c86c04b5e4a50e8 p.1 "N/A"]

In the 2026-05-08 row, that field held `https://www.war.gov/medialink/ufo/release_1/65_hs1-834228961_62-hq-83894_section_6.pdf`. In the 2026-05-11 row, the link is the string "N/A." The PDF is no longer downloadable from war.gov. Sections 1–5 and 7–10 of 62-HQ-83894 remain available. Section 6 is the only one of the ten where the asset link has been switched to N/A.

Because our `card_id` is content-addressed by `sha256(asset_url || title)[:16]`, swapping the URL produces a new card_id (`9c86c04b5e4a50e8`) at the same title — the upstream listing remains, but our manifest now carries two rows for "Section 6": the old one (`13f86e95aed52840`, with the PDF link our R2 mirror is keyed to) and the new one (`9c86c04b5e4a50e8`, with `asset_url: null`). The PDF remains servable at `/pdf/13f86e95aed52840.pdf` from this archive — we do not delete bytes when upstream changes a listing.

A snapshot of the prior manifest is preserved at `/data/snapshots/596cc1881aa97d2fa49a45edab14d60802616e73ce125d286120e00d967cafa2.json`; the change is logged at `/data/removed-cards.json` and surfaced on [/removed](/removed).

## What's in Section 6

Sampling broadly across the 271 pages, the section is organized chronologically by FBI serial number and covers six recurring threads.

### New Mexico green-fireball file (1949–1952)

The dominant thread. OSI-Kirtland 17th District summaries, communications with Dr. Lincoln LaPaz at the UNM Institute of Meteoritics, and material on the Land-Air Inc. observational contract. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.47 "Land-Air"] LaPaz's hypothesis that some discs could be Soviet missile tests originating in the Urals appears in correspondence on these pages.

### Sensitive-installation sightings (1949–1951)

Reports tied to Los Alamos, Sandia Base, Oak Ridge, and Hanford. The Oak Ridge material includes a January 1951 radar-track sequence at the S-50 area observed by named senior officers across three services — covered in detail in [/finds/oak-ridge-radar-january-1951](/finds/oak-ridge-radar-january-1951), which cites this card.

### The William A. Rhodes / Phoenix 1947 photographs chain of custody

Pages 170–185 walk the route of the original Rhodes negatives — FBI to OSI to a Drew Pearson television broadcast, and a contemporaneous claim by Rhodes that the Bureau "borrowed" the negatives and never returned them. The Bureau's internal characterization of the transfer is that it was extended "only as a courtesy to Air Force." [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.170 "only as a courtesy"] The Rhodes case is the subject of a separate find: [/finds/rhodes-photographs-phoenix-1947](/finds/rhodes-photographs-phoenix-1947).

### A background investigation of a named civilian witness

Pages 156–164 are an FBI Baltimore Field Office background investigation of a named civilian who had reported a UFO sighting. The investigation includes the witness's full street address, telephone exchange, age, employer, and interviews with named neighbors at named addresses — the standard surface of a Bureau background check, applied to a citizen whose primary contact with the Bureau was reporting a sighting. The investigation also notes a 1948 questioning of the witness over a hammer-and-sickle decal on a company truck, included in the same case file.

### Citizen-letter intake

Approximately twenty letters from members of the public mentioning saucers, lights, or disc-shaped objects, each filed with the writer's name and full street address. The letters span Virginia, West Virginia, South Carolina, Indiana, and a Toronto correspondent. The Bureau's standard response — Hoover's form letter declining to confirm or deny investigative interest — accompanies several.

### Administrative correspondence

Hoover, Cabell, Belmont, Ladd, and Tolson appear throughout the inter-bureau routing — the standard 1950s FBI executive layer.

## What's NOT in Section 6

Not present in the OCR pass: no Roswell-as-crash material (the four Roswell hits in this section are routine sighting tabulations from Kirtland correspondence, not 1947 debris-recovery content), no Aztec, no Robertson Panel deliberations, no MJ-12-style claims, no living political figures.

|---|---|
| PDF (R2 mirror) | live at `/pdf/13f86e95aed52840.pdf` |
| OCR text | 271 pages in `/data/pages.json` |
| LLM-cleaned reading text | covered by 2026-05-11 full-corpus run |
| Embeddings | in the deployed Voyage-3 index |

The card detail page renders normally because the manifest used at build time still includes this entry; if a future sync removes it, the [/removed](/removed) page is the canonical entry point and links directly to the preserved PDF.

## Provenance of this entry

This entry was drafted from a structured pass over the OCR text by a code-assistant agent run against the preserved content; the editorial frame is the operator's. The agent was asked to characterize the document's contents and identify what would be lost if the upstream listing's removal were also a loss of access — it was not asked to assert *why* the removal happened, and we do not. Possible explanations exist; readers can examine the document themselves and form their own.

### hanawalt-cobalt-ray-1966 — The Hanawalt Cobalt-Ray Telegram, December 1966

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/hanawalt-cobalt-ray-1966
- Published: 2026-05-11
- Cards: 7d58f0cac741650a

In December 1966, W. R. Hanawalt of Harlingen, Texas sent a telegram to the Mexican Federal Security Police claiming that a 'cobalt ray' could control the human nervous system. The FBI's Mexico City field office documented the telegram verbatim in a January 1967 memorandum — and noted, in the same memo, that they had no record of W. R. Hanawalt. The document is in the FBI's omnibus UFO file Section 10 because the Bureau catalogued everything. Reading what this card IS — an FBI memo documenting an unverified citizen claim — is the difference between using this archive responsibly and treating its contents as government endorsement.

## What the document is

Card `7d58f0cac741650a` is **FBI File 62-HQ-83894 Section 10** — one of ten sections of the FBI's omnibus UFO file. Sections 1–10 span 1947 to 1968 and run to roughly 1,900 pages of catalogued correspondence, investigation memoranda, sworn affidavits, news clippings, and citizen letters. The Bureau's interest, for purposes of this file, was that the contents *mentioned* UFOs — not that the contents were corroborated.

Pages 53–56 of Section 10 are a single contained document: a **January 30, 1967 memorandum from the FBI's Mexico City field office to the Director, FBI**, with the subject line "INFORMATION CONCERNING W. R. HANAWALT." The memorandum reproduces verbatim the text of a telegram that W. R. Hanawalt of Harlingen, Texas sent to the Federal Security Police of Mexico, D.F., on December 20, 1966. [cite: card 7d58f0cac741650a p.53 "INFORMATION CONCERNING"]

The Mexico City office's role here is courier. They received the telegram (presumably forwarded by Mexican authorities or captured in the international wire), reproduced its contents for the FBI's UFO files, and added one operational sentence at the end:

> "No information was located in the indices of the Mexico City Office identifiable with the Subject." [cite: card 7d58f0cac741650a p.56 "No information was located"]

That sentence is the entire editorial position of the document. Everything between the header and the closing note is Hanawalt's words, set off in quotation marks by the field office, not the Bureau's.

## What Hanawalt's telegram actually claims

The telegram is a long single-author document characteristic of the "letter to authorities" genre — wide-ranging, paranoid in register, simultaneously specific and unfalsifiable. The central claim:

> "The laser ray, or cobalt ray is a self enthroning ray, and is similar in use to a cocoon around a silk worm. The entire body is enclosed and the entire nervous system can be manipulated to a lesser or greater degree of proficiency than is normal. Visions of flying objects are merely faulty vision — fully controlled and is very real to that individual experiencing the phenomena." [cite: card 7d58f0cac741650a p.53 "cobalt ray"]

Hanawalt's enumeration of what the ray controls runs through breathing, heartbeat, lie-detector results, smell, taste, hearing, sight, sexual climax, mathematics, typing, machinery, ignition systems, and the monitoring of thoughts via "electric or telephone lines." [cite: card 7d58f0cac741650a p.54 "Any smell, taste, hearing"]

He extends the claim outward. The ray has been in use in Harlingen, Texas for eight years "by a select few in all walks of life." Most if not all national Congressmen know of the method and have used it for personal purposes in election races. The equipment is now obsolete because it has been replaced by **the satellite SAMOS** — a real US reconnaissance satellite program of the early 1960s (Satellite And Missile Observation System). [cite: card 7d58f0cac741650a p.55 "satellite SAMOS"] He suspects the CIA and "space arms." He believes his driving accidents since 1946 are premeditated, because he "learned too much in the Navy, while at war."

He closes:

> "I submit myself as of sound mind and body, and that the above is true and correct of my sound opinions." [cite: card 7d58f0cac741650a p.56 "sound mind and body"]

There is no fact-asserting paragraph anywhere on these four pages signed by an FBI agent or any other US government party. Every claim about a cobalt ray comes from Hanawalt, in quotation marks, inside a memo whose subject line is "INFORMATION CONCERNING" him — not concerning the ray.

## Why this card is in the FBI's UFO file at all

The Bureau's interest in the Hanawalt telegram is *that it mentions UFOs* — Hanawalt writes that visions of flying objects are "merely faulty vision" produced by the ray, and elsewhere notes that he "saw unidentified flying objects in 1945 on combat missions." That mention is enough for the file. The Bureau's omnibus UFO catalogue did not distinguish, at intake, between sworn affidavits and citizen letters; both went in. The Bureau's record of having received the document does not constitute investigation of the document, and in this case the explicit "no information located" sentence on page 56 documents the opposite.

The case status notation, the absence of any FBI follow-up activity in the file, and the courier framing of the memo together place the Hanawalt telegram in the same category as a great many other letters in the omnibus file: catalogued, not investigated.

## What the document does not say

The document does **not** say that a cobalt ray exists.

The document does **not** say that the FBI investigated the claim and found evidence supporting it.

The document does **not** say that the FBI investigated the claim and found evidence against it.

The document says: a man named W. R. Hanawalt wrote a telegram from Harlingen to Mexico City on December 20, 1966, and the contents of that telegram were these. The Mexico City office of the FBI added one sentence noting they had no record of him.

## Why this card is in this archive

The Hanawalt telegram is exactly the kind of document a public, citable archive of declassified government UFO files needs to surface carefully. Treating "the FBI documented this" as "the FBI states this" collapses three distinct evidentiary layers — Bureau, courier office, citizen — and turns a 1966 letter into a self-endorsement.

The discipline this archive applies is the discipline a careful journalist or researcher would apply: read the document type before the document content; separate what the document *is* from what the document *quotes*; and apply the same abstention bar to a citizen claim that the originating agency itself applied. The FBI's Mexico City field office did not endorse the cobalt ray. Neither does this archive.

The telegram is a primary source. So is the disclaimer at the end of the memo.

### nasc-state-extraterrestrial-policy-memo-1963 — The Hunter-to-Packard Memo, July 18, 1963 — and the 1952 Document That Replaced It

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/nasc-state-extraterrestrial-policy-memo-1963
- Published: 2026-05-11
- Cards: aa3097b4c549a67a, 9e2c2621d67dde12, df43a479bc891969

Card aa3097b4c549a67a is a six-page interagency memorandum from Maxwell W. Hunter II of the National Aeronautics and Space Council to Robert F. Packard at State/OES, dated July 18, 1963 — one of the few PURSUE documents addressing extraterrestrial-contact policy at the Executive Office level. The card was present in the 2026-05-08 PURSUE CSV with mismatched metadata (1952-coded title attached to 1963 content). In the 2026-05-11 CSV upstream did two things at once: re-issued the same 1963 memo under a corrected 1963-coded title (card_id 9e2c2621d67dde12, byte-for-byte identical to the original), and added a genuinely different document at the original title pattern, a 1952 State memo on UFO sighting reports (card_id df43a479bc891969). The original card_id aa3097b4c549a67a remains preserved here. The byte-identity between the original and the re-issued 1963 card is cryptographically verified by the project's content-addressed archive layer.

## What the document is

Card `aa3097b4c549a67a` is a **six-page memorandum from Maxwell W. Hunter II**, Member of the Professional Staff, **National Aeronautics and Space Council** (Executive Office of the President), to **Robert F. Packard**, Office of International Scientific Affairs, **U.S. Department of State**. It is dated **July 18, 1963**. The classification marking carried on pages 2 through 6 is **OFFICIAL USE ONLY** — not a national-security classification. The asset filename carried the date `7.18.1963`; the PURSUE manifest field `incident_date` had it recorded as `7/18/52`, a date mismatch that the document content does not support.

The original NARA-style filename token in the upstream listing — `59_64634_711.5612` — is consistent with a State Department record group 59 file under the 711.561x decimal classification.

## What the memo says

Hunter writes to Packard as a Space Council policy staffer asking State/OES to think about a problem that does not yet have a contingency framework: what diplomatic and scientific posture the United States should adopt if an extraterrestrial intelligence were ever encountered. He partitions the problem into three cases — non-technological solar-system natives, sub-light interstellar visitors, and faster-than-light visitors — and argues each implies a different posture and a different distribution of operational responsibility between scientific, military, and diplomatic offices.

His framing recommendation, on page 6: humanity should plan to "bury all Terrestrial hatchets" in advance of any such encounter. [cite: card aa3097b4c549a67a p.6 "bury all Terrestrial hatchets"] His central warning, on the same page, is that without contingency planning any actual encounter "would degenerate into grand panic." [cite: card aa3097b4c549a67a p.6 "grand panic"]

The memo references prior internal deliberations on **Basic National Security Policy** (the BNSP planning process), specifically a "BNSP Task I" effort. The reference is brief — it does not summarize what BNSP Task I concluded, only that the topic was discussed there.

## Tone and provenance

The memo's tone is unusual for executive-office correspondence on letterhead. Hunter is dismissive about contemporary popular ufology while simultaneously arguing the U.S. government should plan for the contingency at a level above the sighting-investigation file. He notes on page 4 that the only existing literature he is aware of on the diplomatic problem is science fiction. The memo is signed by hand on page 6.

A stamp appears on page 1 indicating internal routing ("MRS. Date / BV"); no other markings appear.

## Why this card is in a UAP release

Most of the war.gov PURSUE corpus is sighting reports, MISREP forms, agency investigative files, and radar tracks. A small number of documents are policy or programmatic correspondence; the Hunter-Packard memo is one. Its inclusion in the release puts the executive branch on the record taking the contingency question seriously at the policy staff level in 1963 — a non-trivial historical claim that the document itself supports.

## About the named correspondents

Maxwell W. Hunter II was a real engineer-turned-policy-staffer; in later decades he became publicly associated with U.S. ballistic-missile-defense work. Robert F. Packard was an actual science-affairs officer at State during this period. The memo's surface — letterhead, signature block, addressee, classification handle — is internally consistent with a routine 1963 interagency communication and does not show signs of post-hoc fabrication.

## What the upstream did

Card `aa3097b4c549a67a` was present in the 2026-05-08 CSV with the asset URL `59_214434_sp_16_7.18.1963.pdf` — a filename that announces the document as a 7/18/1963 record. The CSV row also carried an `incident_date` field of `7/18/52`, which is internally inconsistent: the asset filename says 1963, the incident-date field says 1952. The agent-pass over the preserved OCR resolved the inconsistency: the document is the 1963 NASC-to-State Hunter-to-Packard memo described above.

The 2026-05-11 CSV no longer carries that asset URL. The same title pattern — `59_64634_711.5612[7-2852` — now points to a different file: `59_64634_711.5612[7-2852.pdf`. The upstream description on that row reads:

> "*a two page memorandum, dated July 28, 1952, relates to increased reports of unidentified flying objects.*" [cite: card df43a479bc891969 p.1 "a two page memorandum, dated July 28, 1952"]

The new file is two pages; the original was six. The new `incident_date` field is `7/28/52`; the original was `7/18/52`. The new asset filename string matches the title pattern (`711.5612[7-2852` ↔ `711.5612.[7-28-52]`); the original did not (its filename was `59_214434_sp_16_7.18.1963`). The new card_id is `df43a479bc891969`; the original was `aa3097b4c549a67a`.

What the upstream did, in concrete terms — and what the byte-level evidence later showed (see "Byte-level integrity finding" below) — is that they did two distinct operations on the listing in a single update: (a) they re-issued the 1963 Hunter-to-Packard memo at a corrected, 1963-coded title pattern, with bytes identical to the version present on 2026-05-08; and (b) they added a different 1952 State memorandum, whose filename and content match the original 1952-coded title pattern. All three card identities are preserved here:

- Original 2026-05-08 listing (1963 NASC memo, filed under a 1952-coded title): `/card/aa3097b4c549a67a` and `/pdf/aa3097b4c549a67a.pdf` (R2 mirror)
- Current 2026-05-11 re-listing of the same 1963 memo (corrected 1963-coded title, byte-identical content): `/card/9e2c2621d67dde12` and `/pdf/9e2c2621d67dde12.pdf` (R2 mirror)
- Current 2026-05-11 listing at the original 1952-coded title (a genuinely-new 1952 State memo, two pages): `/card/df43a479bc891969` and `/pdf/df43a479bc891969.pdf` (R2 mirror). OCR'd 2026-05-12.

## What the replacement document contains (OCR added 2026-05-12)

The replacement is a **two-page interagency memorandum dated July 28, 1952**, from "F.H." to a "Mr. Armstrong" at the State Department, subject "Flying Saucers." The cover line records that **Paul Nitze** asked the author what the Air Force thought about flying saucers and the author judged the question worth circulating at the morning meeting. The cover note credits the substantive content to a briefing the author received from **General Samford** at the IAC (Intelligence Advisory Committee). [cite: card df43a479bc891969 p.1 "Paul Nitze asked me"]

Major General John A. Samford was the USAF Director of Intelligence in 1952; his recorded position, per the memo, was that there is "very little that can be said to clarify the flying saucer business: It is still a complete enigma." [cite: card df43a479bc891969 p.2 "complete enigma"] The memo then attributes the contemporary increase in observations to two factors: "vastly improved methods of observation and reporting, including not only radar but the reporting systems used by civilian and military pilots," and "the publicity which is given it, which takes on certain elements of a 'fad.'" [cite: card df43a479bc891969 p.2 "elements of a"]

Substantive historical claim in the memo: phenomena "falling within the general description of flying saucers have actually been known to exist and have been reported one way or another for over 100 years." Page 2 carries a `DECLASSIFIED NND 852931` stamp.

The two-page brief is consistent with the title-pattern's date and filename, lending weight to the metadata-correction reading of the swap. It does NOT, however, explain what mechanism *previously* filed the 1963 Hunter-to-Packard memo under this 1952-coded title pattern; that mis-filing is itself a curious artifact preserved by the original card.

The change is logged at [/removed](/removed) and the snapshot of the prior manifest is at `/data/snapshots/596cc1881aa97d2fa49a45edab14d60802616e73ce125d286120e00d967cafa2.json`.

## Byte-level integrity finding (added 2026-05-12)

When the 2026-05-12 archive-reconciliation pass retroactively pinned the three `/removed` preservation copies into the project's content-addressed byte-archive layer, the SHA-256 of card `aa3097b4c549a67a`'s preserved bytes was compared against every existing archive entry. The hash collided with an already-archived entry — the current-manifest card `9e2c2621d67dde12`. Both card identities resolve to the same R2 object: `archive/aba3ec3b8ef0240364308cf046ccbfcd252c5a5d7ef470d696b72c1f41b2502d.pdf` (1,598,931 bytes).

**What the byte-equivalence proves.** The upstream's 2026-05-11 change to the 1963 NASC memo's listing was a metadata-only operation on the content side. Every page, every signature, every stamp, every redaction in the document is bit-for-bit identical to the version captured on 2026-05-08. The 1963 content was not re-redacted, re-paginated, re-OCR'd, or otherwise altered. It was re-classified — given a corrected title and asset filename — without any modification to the underlying document bytes.

**What the byte-equivalence does NOT prove.** Upstream's *motivation* remains ambiguous. The byte-identical re-issue is consistent with a routine metadata correction (the 1963 document had been mis-filed under a 1952-coded title; cleaning that up). It is also consistent with a deliberate withdrawal-then-restoration carried out under cover of a metadata correction — for instance, to reset analytic continuity, break inbound links to the prior URL, or test whether downstream archives were watching. This entry continues not to assert which.

What the byte-equivalence *does* establish is the floor: regardless of motive, no editorial alteration of the 1963 document content accompanied the upstream change. Future upstream operations on this card can now be evaluated against a cryptographic baseline rather than a description-level one.

## What's preserved

| Surface | Original 1963 memo (`aa3097b4c549a67a`, 1952-coded title) | Re-issued 1963 memo (`9e2c2621d67dde12`, 1963-coded title, byte-identical) | Genuinely-new 1952 memo (`df43a479bc891969`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| PDF (R2 mirror) | `/pdf/aa3097b4c549a67a.pdf` | `/pdf/9e2c2621d67dde12.pdf` | `/pdf/df43a479bc891969.pdf` |
| OCR text | 6 pages in `/data/pages.json` | 6 pages in `/data/pages.json` (same content) | 2 pages in `/data/pages.json` |
| LLM-cleaned reading text | yes (2026-05-11 corpus pass) | yes (same content → same cleaning) | yes (2026-05-12 incremental pass) |
| Embeddings | in the deployed Voyage-3 index | in the deployed Voyage-3 index | added 2026-05-12 |
| Card detail | `/card/aa3097b4c549a67a` | `/card/9e2c2621d67dde12` | `/card/df43a479bc891969` |
| SHA-256 of asset bytes | `aba3ec3b8ef0…` | `aba3ec3b8ef0…` (identical) | different |

## Provenance of this entry

A code-assistant agent extracted the document's identifying surface (author, addressee, date, classification, content threads) from the preserved OCR pages and reported back; the editorial frame is the operator's. The agent was asked to identify the document and summarize its content; it was not asked to assert *why* the listing was removed, and this entry does not. The mis-cataloged `incident_date` field in the prior manifest is a data-quality observation, not a removal motive.

The 2026-05-12 byte-level integrity finding surfaced as a side effect of running the project's content-addressed archive reconciliation pass — not an investigative effort directed at this card. The SHA-256 collision between `aa3097b4c549a67a` and `9e2c2621d67dde12` was reported by `scripts/r2_pin_removed.py` when its append-only PUT to `archive/<sha>.<ext>` returned `PreconditionFailed` (the archive key already existed from the current-manifest card's earlier write). The integrity tooling discovered the byte-identity; the editorial interpretation of what that means is the operator's.

### dow-d23-arabian-gulf-october-2023 — DOW-UAP-D23 — Two Events, Forty-One Minutes Apart

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/dow-d23-arabian-gulf-october-2023
- Published: 2026-05-10
- Cards: d8e5687dc870892d

Card d8e5687dc870892d is the October 2023 USCENTCOM Mission Report for an ISR sortie out of Al Dhafra over the Arabian Gulf. The MISREP records two separate UAP events forty-one minutes apart — 0241Z and 0322Z — each paired with its own AARO Unresolved UAP Report video (PR-26 and PR-27). Where DOW-UAP-D32 walked one observation window with three FMV clips, this entry walks one mission with two distinct encounters, and reads what the structured form does and does not commit to in each.

## What the document is

Card `d8e5687dc870892d` is **DOW-UAP-D23, Mission Report, United Arab Emirates, October 2023** — a 9-page MISREP submitted by USCENTCOM, declassified by MG Richard A. Harrison on 12 September 2025 and approved for release to AARO under MDR 25-0104. It originated with the 50th Attack Squadron, 432 AEW, supporting Operation SPARTAN SHIELD. The mission departed OMAM (Al Dhafra) at `240015:00ZOCT23`, came on station at 0155Z in SRO TRACK IRISH SICKLE, and landed back at OMAM at `242058:00ZOCT23` — twenty hours forty-three minutes of mission time. [cite: card d8e5687dc870892d p.5 "Total Mission Time"] (The PURSUE Release 01 CSV labels this card with `incident_date: 10/31/2023`; the MISREP's own Zulu DTGs — cited above — place the sortie on **October 24, 2023**, and that is the date this entry treats as authoritative. The manifest-field discrepancy is tracked separately as a data-quality item.)

Like D32, the same `card_id` shows up multiple times in the manifest because the corpus content-addresses by source URL: two PDF rows and two AARO video rows — **PR-26** and **PR-27** — pointing back to the same MISREP asset. Where [D32](/finds/dow-d32-syria-october-2024) was *one observation window, three FMV clips, one document*, D23 is **one mission, two distinct encounters, two videos, one document**. The encounters are entered as two separate UAP blocks — not one event split across clips — and the form's structure makes that explicit.

## The mission's running narrative

Page 1 is the running mission narrative — a numbered Zulu-time timeline. The two UAP events appear as two distinct line items:

> "(SECRET//NOFORN) AT 0241Z, 1.4a OBSERVED 1X UAP. SEE UAP LINE 1." [cite: card d8e5687dc870892d p.1 "UAP LINE 1"]
>
> "(SECRET//NOFORN) AT 0322Z, 1.4a OBSERVED 1X UAP. SEE UAP LINE 2."

The narrative cross-refers each entry to its own structured UAP block: UAP LINE 1 on pages 7–8, UAP LINE 2 on pages 8–9. Two events, two form entries, two cross-references. The MISREP's authorship is committing to the count.

## The Iranian guard call — context, not setup

Earlier on that same page-1 timeline is a separate item that warrants careful framing:

> "(SECRET//REL TO USA, FVEY) AT 0145Z, 1.4a RECEIVED A PROFESSIONAL GUARD CALL. SEE GUARD CALL LINE 1." [cite: card d8e5687dc870892d p.1 "GUARD CALL"]

The detail is built out on page 6. Ground Station Callsign: **IRANIAN AIR DEFENSE**. Aircraft at FL230, 031M heading, 158 KIAS. Tone logged as **Professional**. The transmitted text:

> "AT 0145Z, [callsign] RECEIVED 1X GUARD CALL FROM IRANIAN AIR DEFENSE STATING 'MAINTAIN SAFE DISTANCE FROM BORDER'. CALL WAS PROFESSIONAL. [callsign] RESPONDED 'THIS IS A COALITION AIRCRAFT CONDUCTING ROUTINE OPERATIONS IN INTERNATIONAL AIRSPACE'. AT 0145Z, THE CALLS FROM IRANIAN AIR DEFENSE CEASED." [cite: card d8e5687dc870892d p.6 "MAINTAIN SAFE DISTANCE"]

The mission report records the guard call earlier in the operational window. The first UAP event is logged 56 minutes later, at 0241Z; the second at 0322Z. The two facts are on the same timeline because the timeline is chronological. The MISREP does not draw a connection between them, and neither does this entry. The guard call is documented in its own GUARDCALL block; the UAP events are documented in their own UAP blocks. They are adjacent in the form because they are adjacent in time, and that is all the document commits to.

## UAP LINE 1 — 0241Z

The first UAP block on pages 7–8 records the structured fields for the 0241Z event. The friendly aircraft is at FL243, 162 KTAS, 280-degree trajectory. The UAP-specific fields:

> "**UAP Physical State:** Solid" [cite: card d8e5687dc870892d p.7 "UAP Physical State"]
>
> "**UAP Propulsion Means:** UNK"
>
> "UAP Maneuverability Observations: NONE"
>
> "UAP Signatures: THERMAL SHOWED COLD"
>
> "Observer Assessment of UAP: Benign"

The kinetic block on page 8 is partially populated: every field marked `Estimated`, with **Kinetic Velocity: 320 MPH** the only numeric value filled in. Altitude, depth, and trajectory are `UNK`. [cite: card d8e5687dc870892d p.8 "320 MPH"]

The form-grammar note from D32 applies here in mirror image. **"UAP Physical State: Solid"** is a checkbox-menu field — `Solid | Gas | Plasma | UNK` — and the aircrew picked `Solid`. D32's aircrew picked `Plasma` for what they described in prose as a "ball of white light." Different observation, different checkbox. The form's range is what makes the field readable, not an independent physical-state assertion. The free-text `UAP Description` field reads `UNK`; the only specific observational language anywhere in the record comes from the paired AARO video. [cite: card d8e5687dc870892d p.8 "UAP Description"]

The paired AARO **PR-26** description fills that gap from the clip side. Forty-three seconds, infrared sensor:

> "00:00-00:17: An area of contrast remains generally within the top left quarter of the display. 00:17-00:18: The sensor pans from right to left, causing the area of contrast to pass through the center of the display... 00:29: The sensor stops tracking the area of contrast, causing it to leave the sensor field-of-view on the left side of the screen. 00:30-00:43: The sensor resumes its motion relative to the background but does not reacquire the area of contrast."

PR-26 closes with the same boilerplate disclaimer that runs across the AARO catalog: the description is provided "for informational purposes only" and "should not [be interpreted] as reflecting an analytical judgment, investigative conclusion, or factual determination."

## UAP LINE 2 — 0322Z, 41 minutes later

The second UAP block on pages 8–9 records the 0322Z event. The friendly aircraft is at the same FL243, 162 KTAS, 280-degree trajectory. The structured fields read:

> "**UAP Physical State:** Solid" [cite: card d8e5687dc870892d p.8 "UAP Physical State"]
>
> "**UAP Propulsion Means:** UNK"
>
> "UAP Maneuverability Observations: NONE"
>
> "UAP Signatures: UNK"
>
> "Observer Assessment of UAP: Benign"

The kinetic block on page 9 mirrors the first: every field `Estimated`, **Kinetic Velocity: 440 MPH**, altitude and trajectory `UNK`. [cite: card d8e5687dc870892d p.9 "440 MPH"] The `UAP Signatures` field, populated for the first event as `THERMAL SHOWED COLD`, is `UNK` for the second. The Description field is `UNK` again.

Two structured blocks, identical in form, populated differently in detail. The 320-vs-440-MPH delta is what the form numerically commits to between the two events. Whether the second observation is the same object as the first, a different object, or the same form-grammar applied to a different phenomenon, the MISREP does not say. There is no "Same as Initial Contact" field, and no narrative line in GENTEXT/UAP linking the two.

The paired **PR-27** clip is four minutes fifty-seven seconds, IR sensor — much longer than PR-26's forty-three. AARO records "no content" for the first 1:55, an area of contrast becoming distinguishable at 01:56, the sensor zooming in at 02:14, the area "remain[ing] generally in the center of the sensor field-of-view" through 03:26, then "sensor motion caus[ing] the area of contrast to move erratically across the display" through the end of the clip. Same observational-primitive vocabulary, same non-finding disclaimer.

## What the document does not say

Five things this MISREP and its two paired PR descriptions do **not** establish:

1. **No causal link between the Iranian guard call and the UAP events.** They appear on the same page-1 timeline because the timeline is chronological. The form does not connect them, and neither does this entry. A 56-minute gap between the guard call ending and the first UAP observation is what the document records; that is all.
2. **No propulsion or origin claim.** Both blocks read `UAP Propulsion Means: UNK` and `Observer Assessment of UAP: Benign`. The document closes the file from a tactical standpoint without committing to origin.
3. **No claim about whether the two UAPs are the same object.** Two structured entries forty-one minutes apart, two velocities, no field linking them. The form's authorship logged them as `UAP Incident` twice and stopped.
4. **The MISREP description fields are `UNK` even though video exists.** The specific observational language anywhere in the record — areas of contrast, sensor pans, durations — comes from AARO's PR-26 and PR-27, not the MISREP. The structured form admits a field for prose description and the aircrew left it `UNK`; the video is what carries the observable detail downstream.
5. **"Solid" is not a physical-state finding.** Same form-grammar caveat as D32: it is the aircrew's selection from a checkbox menu.

## Why this card is in this archive

D32 walks the MISREP's field anatomy with one observation window. D23 shows the same form being used to record **two events in one mission**, separately and structurally. Each UAP gets its own `Initial Contact DTG`, kinetic block, velocity number, and signature line; the aircrew filled out two of them, and the corpus attached one paired AARO video to each event.

A reader interested in the MISREP-anatomy frame should read D23 and [D32](/finds/dow-d32-syria-october-2024) together. Different physical-state checkbox (`Solid` vs. `Plasma`), different thermal language (`THERMAL SHOWED COLD` vs. blank), different kinematic populating (D23 commits two velocity numbers; D32 leaves the kinetic block blank). Same form, same institutional grammar, same `Observer Assessment: Benign` closure on each.

### dow-d32-syria-october-2024 — DOW-UAP-D32 — How the Modern Military Writes Down a UAP Encounter

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/dow-d32-syria-october-2024
- Published: 2026-05-10
- Cards: ea029a05470b8f4e

Card ea029a05470b8f4e bundles the October 20, 2024 USCENTCOM Mission Report from Syria together with three separately-cataloged AARO 'Unresolved UAP Report' videos (PR-31, PR-32, PR-33) — six manifest rows in total, all sharing one card_id because the corpus content-addresses by source URL. The MISREP is a structured intake form: pre-printed fields, a checkbox-style 'UAP Physical State' dropdown, a separate GENTEXT block where the aircrew narrates in prose, and a final 'Observer Assessment of UAP: Benign.' Reading the document the way the form lays it out — field anatomy first, narrative softening second, threat-mode rule-out third — is what this entry walks through.

## What the document is

Card `ea029a05470b8f4e` is **DOW-UAP-D32, Mission Report, Syria, October 2024** — a 10-page Mission Report (MISREP) submitted by USCENTCOM, declassified by MG Richard A. Harrison on 24 October 2025 and approved for release to AARO on 28 October. It originated with the 12th Special Operations Squadron, 27 SOW, supporting Operation INHERENT RESOLVE, filed against three ISR taskings flown by a single airframe between takeoff at OJMS at 0823Z on 20 October 2024 and landing at 0447Z on 21 October — 20 hours 24 minutes of mission time, 14 hours 22 minutes of full-motion video. [cite: card ea029a05470b8f4e p.1 "MISSION HOURS"]

The same `card_id` appears six times in the manifest. Three rows are the PDF — once per paired video. Three are AARO video reports — **PR-31**, **PR-32**, and **PR-33** — each catalogued as a separate "Unresolved UAP Report" but pointing back to the same PDF asset URL. This is how the corpus content-addresses: `card_id` is `sha256(asset_url)[:16]`, the PDF has one URL, so all six rows collapse to one card. One observation window, three FMV clips, one document.

This entry walks the form field by field, and the way the form-grammar and the narrative grammar disagree about the same observation.

## The form's grammar — a checkbox menu

The MISREP is not free prose. It is a structured intake template, and the UAP section in particular sits inside that template as a rectangular block of pre-printed fields. The fields the aircrew filled in for this incident, on page 8:

> "**UAP Physical State:** Plasma" [cite: card ea029a05470b8f4e p.8 "UAP Physical State"]
>
> "**UAP Propulsion Means:** UNKNOWN"
>
> "UAP Under Intelligent Control (yes/no; if yes, describe): NO"
>
> "UAP Effects on Persons: NO"
>
> "UAP Anomalous Characteristics/ Behaviors: LIGHT/GLARE FROM UNKNOWN ORIGIN FLASHED ACCROSS FMV CAMERA FEED. AIRCREW ASSESSED THIS NOT TO BE A LASING EVENT." [cite: card ea029a05470b8f4e p.8 "LASING EVENT"]

"Plasma" is the most quotable line on the page, and it would be easy to over-pump it. The field is a **fixed-menu dropdown** — the aircrew picks from a constrained list of `Solid | Gas | Plasma | UNK`. "Plasma" here is the closest available checkbox label to "ball of light," not a physical-state assertion the document is independently making. The form is constraining what the report can say.

The same constraint shapes the kinematic block on page 8: every "Kinetic" field — altitude, depth, velocity, trajectory — is left blank with `Estimated` accuracy. The aircrew did not fill them in. The MISREP does not commit to altitude, velocity, or trajectory for the observed phenomenon — only for the friendly aircraft (20,088 ft, 144 knots, ORBIT) on page 7.

## The narrative softening

Following the structured fields, the form opens up into a free-text **GENTEXT/UAP** block on page 9. This is where the aircrew narrates in prose. What the form-fields recorded as "Plasma" and "LIGHT/GLARE FROM UNKNOWN ORIGIN," the GENTEXT renders as:

> "**UAP Description (e.g., size, shape, color, markings, recognizable features):** MISHAPEN AND UNEVEN BALL OF WHITE LIGHT.
>
> **Gentext (UAP Event Description):** (SECRET//REL TO USA, FVEY) FROM 1559Z-1644Z, [callsign redacted] OBSERVED MULTIPLE GLARES OR LIGHT FROM UNKNOWN ORIGIN AT DIFFERENT ANGLES AND DIRECTIONS. AT 1559Z, 1602Z AND AT 1644Z, [callsign] OBSERVED 1X LIGHT/GLARE CROSSED DIRECTLY ON THE FMV CAMERA. AT 1609Z AND 1620Z, [callsign] OBSERVED A LIGHT/GLARE HALO EFFECT AT THE TOP OF [callsign] FMV FEED. AIRCREW CONSIDERED THIS NO MISSION IMPACT OR CHANGE AND UAP WAS BENIGN." [cite: card ea029a05470b8f4e p.9 "MULTIPLE GLARES"]

What the form-grammar compressed into the word "Plasma," the GENTEXT expands across forty-five minutes — `1559Z-1644Z` — and **five timestamped observations**: glares crossing the camera at 1559Z, 1602Z, and 1644Z, halo effects at 1609Z and 1620Z. These are the events that ended up in three FMV clips published as PR-31, PR-32, and PR-33.

The phrase "MISHAPEN AND UNEVEN BALL OF WHITE LIGHT" — *misshapen* is misspelled in the source, retained verbatim — is the aircrew's own adjectival description, not a checkbox. It is the most concrete observational sentence in the document.

## The aircrew's own threat-mode rule-out

One of the most interesting things on the page is that the aircrew's reasoning is visible in the form. The "UAP Anomalous Characteristics/ Behaviors" field on page 8 doesn't just describe what was seen; it records what the aircrew ruled out:

> "AIRCREW ASSESSED THIS NOT TO BE A LASING EVENT." [cite: card ea029a05470b8f4e p.8 "LASING EVENT"]

A lasing event — a hostile laser dazzler aimed at the aircraft's sensor — is the operationally relevant default hypothesis for "light/glare from unknown origin on an ISR camera over Syria." The aircrew considered it, dismissed it, and recorded the dismissal *inside the same field* where they described the observation. This is not after-the-fact analysis; it is the on-station threat assessment surfacing into the formal report.

The corresponding line at the *top* of the UAP section on page 7 commits the same judgment to a separate field: **Observer Assessment of UAP: Benign.** [cite: card ea029a05470b8f4e p.7 "Benign"] The form has a slot for that assessment; the aircrew filled it in.

## What AARO wrote about the videos

The three paired AARO **Unresolved UAP Reports** that share this card describe the same observation window from the *clip side*. AARO's prose discipline is itself a model worth quoting — terse, observational, and explicit about what it is not asserting.

**PR-31** describes a five-second clip:

> "00:00-00:01: An indistinctly shaped multi-colored area moves from right to left across the top edge of the sensor display within the first second of the video."

**PR-32** describes a six-second clip:

> "00:02-00:04: An area of irregular color and brightness, mainly consisting of white and red highlights, appears near the center of the top edge of the sensor display. The area extends to a width of approximately one-third of the horizontal frame, with a vertical area comprising approximately one-sixth of the viewing area. Overall, its shape is best described as a horizontally-oriented half-oval bisected along its major axis."

**PR-33** describes a five-second clip:

> "00:01-00:03: Two semi-transparent, irregularly shaped orange areas overlay the background imagery, persisting for less than two seconds each."

All three close with the same boilerplate disclaimer:

> "This video description is provided for informational purposes only. Readers should not interpret any part of this description as reflecting an analytical judgment, investigative conclusion, or factual determination regarding the described event's validity, nature, or significance."

The discipline on display here is exactly the discipline this site tries to model. AARO writes "areas of contrast," not "craft." It writes "indistinctly shaped multi-colored area," not "object." It quantifies — fractions of frame width, durations in seconds — and stops. The disclaimer is doing real work: it tells the reader the description is an observational primitive, not a finding.

## What the document does not say

Five things the MISREP and the three PR descriptions do **not** establish, which a reader should hold separately from what they do:

1. **The document does not characterize this as exotic or unexplained-in-principle.** *Observer Assessment: Benign.* *No mission impact or change.* The aircrew's own framing closes the file from a tactical standpoint.
2. **The document does not record propulsion, kinetic altitude, or velocity for the UAP.** Those fields exist on the form and were left blank or marked `UNKNOWN`. [cite: card ea029a05470b8f4e p.8 "UAP Propulsion"]
3. **The document does not describe a solid object.** AARO's PR descriptions are deliberately careful — "indistinctly shaped multi-colored area," "irregularly shaped orange areas," "half-oval bisected along its major axis." The MISREP says "ball of white light." Neither commits to a craft.
4. **The MISREP does not confirm three discrete UAPs.** It describes one observation window of "multiple glares" at five recorded timestamps; AARO subsequently published three separate clips from the larger FMV recording. The card-collision is bookkeeping, not multiplicity.
5. **"Plasma" is not a physical-state finding.** It is the aircrew's selection from a fixed menu of checkbox options on a structured intake form. The word's prominence on the page is form-anatomy, not analysis.

## Why this card is in this archive

Every other curated entry on this site walks one document. This one walks four — a MISREP and three paired video reports — because the corpus made them one card, and a reader clicking in deserves to know that *one observation window* is what they are looking at. The MISREP's value is methodological as much as evidentiary: it shows what the U.S. military's current UAP-reporting form *looks like* when it is filled in, which fields are checkbox-constrained, which fields admit prose, and where the aircrew's own reasoning becomes visible.

The 2024-vintage form is a recognizable descendant of the typed Form-No.-7 reports that fill [DOW 319.1 Flying Discs 1949](/finds/lowry-1949-ocr-limits) — same template logic, same separation of structured intake from narrative GENTEXT, the same habit of writing the threat-mode rule-out into the same paragraph as the observation. Seventy-six years on, the form has gained dropdowns and a UAP-specific section, but the institutional grammar is continuous.

A reader interested in how AARO writes its own descriptions — "areas of contrast," durations in seconds, the explicit non-finding disclaimer — should treat the three PR descriptions on this card as the model. The bar there is the bar this site is trying to meet.

### dow-d33-aegean-sea-october-2023 — DOW-UAP-D33 — One Observation, In the Aircrew's Own Words

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/dow-d33-aegean-sea-october-2023
- Published: 2026-05-10
- Cards: 3746998b8c506e5c

Card 3746998b8c506e5c bundles the October 27, 2023 USCENTCOM Mission Report from the Aegean Sea with one paired AARO video, PR-34. Where the D32 Syria entry walked the form's checkbox grammar across three paired clips, D33 is the simplest version of the same form: one observation window, one FMV clip, three minutes of recorded sensor footage, and a UAP section the aircrew filled in tersely and concretely. The most quotable line on the page isn't the kinematics — it's the witness's own epistemological caveat: SEEMINGLY CIRCULAR, TOO SMALL TO MAKE OUT DETAILS.

## What the document is
