Card `3746998b8c506e5c` is **DOW-UAP-D33, Mission Report, Greece, October 2023** — a 7-page MISREP filed by the 33 SOS, declassified by MG Richard A. Harrison on 22 January 2026 and approved for release to AARO under USCENTCOM MDR 26-0019. The mission was an ISR sortie out of LGLR on the Greek mainland: takeoff at 2339Z on 26 October 2023, landing at OJMS at 1309Z on 27 October — 13 hours 30 minutes of mission time, 6 hours 29 minutes of FMV. The UAP observation lasted three minutes. [cite: card 3746998b8c506e5c p.1 "MISSION HOURS"]

The same `card_id` appears twice in the manifest — one row for the PDF, one for the paired AARO **Unresolved UAP Report PR-34** — because the corpus content-addresses by source URL and both rows point at the same asset. After the [D32 Syria entry](/finds/dow-d32-syria-october-2024) — three clips in a single document — D33 is the cleaner shape: one observation, one clip, one short GENTEXT paragraph. The interest here is not in form-anatomy abstraction (D32 walks that) but in how *terse* the aircrew were and how visible their own epistemological care is in the fields they did fill in.

## The form fields, as filled in

The MISREP's UAP section sits on pages 6 and 7. Most of the kinetic and signature fields are left blank or marked `UNK`. The fields the aircrew did commit to are short and specific:

> "**UAP Maneuverability Observations:** Sharp 90 degree turns" [cite: card 3746998b8c506e5c p.6 "Sharp 90 degree turns"]
>
> "**UAP Physical State:** Solid"
>
> "UAP Propulsion Means: UNK"
>
> "UAP Under Intelligent Control (yes/no; if yes, describe): NO"
>
> "**Observer Assessment of UAP: Benign**"

"Sharp 90 degree turns" is a striking phrase, and a reader should hold it carefully — it is the **aircrew's own characterization** entered into a free-text field, not an instrument measurement. The corresponding kinematics block on page 7 leaves altitude, depth, and trajectory blank (each marked `Estimated` accuracy with no value), and fills only one number:

> "**Kinetic Velocity Accuracy:** Estimated
>
> **Kinetic Velocity:** 80 MPH" [cite: card 3746998b8c506e5c p.7 "80 MPH"]

What the document is willing to commit to numerically is one estimated velocity figure.

Where D33 differs from D32 inside the same form is also worth noting. The Physical State dropdown — `Solid | Gas | Plasma | UNK` — reads "Plasma" on the Syria card and "Solid" on this one. Same constrained menu, different selections by different aircrews looking at different things.

## The aircrew's own description

The most quotable line on the document is also the most editorially careful one. In the GENTEXT/UAP block on page 7, where the form opens up into prose, the aircrew were given a "UAP Description" field — size, shape, color, markings, recognizable features — and chose to write:

> "**UAP Description (e.g., size, shape, color, markings, recognizable features):** SEEMINGLY CIRCULAR, TOO SMALL TO MAKE OUT DETAILS" [cite: card 3746998b8c506e5c p.7 "SEEMINGLY CIRCULAR"]

That is the editorial gem of the card. The witness was offered the form's most descriptive slot and used it to tell the reader where their own confidence ran out. *Seemingly* circular, not circular. *Too small to make out details*, not "smooth, featureless, metallic." The hedge is on the page; the aircrew calibrated their own visual confidence inside the field meant to extract it.

The narrative GENTEXT immediately following is similarly disciplined:

> "AT 0035Z [callsign] WAS EN ROUTE TO THEIR TARGET WHEN THEY SPOTTED A UAP FLYING JUST ABOVE THE SURFACE OF THE OCEAN WATER. THE UAP TOOK MULTIPLE 90 DEGREE TURNS AT AN ESTIMATED 80 MPH. AT 0038Z, [callsign] LOST THE UAP FROM THEIR FEED." [cite: card 3746998b8c506e5c p.7 "MULTIPLE 90"]

Three minutes — 0035Z to 0038Z. *Multiple* turns, the count is not given. *An estimated 80 MPH*, the qualifier is in the prose. *Lost the UAP from their feed*, not "lost the target" or "broke contact" — the loss is described as a sensor event, not a kinematic one. Every quantitative claim is hedged on the page where it appears.

## What AARO wrote about the video

The paired **PR-34 Unresolved UAP Report** describes the 2 minute 57 second FMV clip from the clip side, with AARO's standard prose discipline:

> "00:04: An area of contrast enters the sensor field-of-view from the bottom left quarter of the screen.
>
> 00:07-00:19: The area of contrast moves back and forth horizontally across the field-of-view as the sensor pans to track it.
>
> ...
>
> 02:22: The area of contrast becomes indistinguishable against the background, and the reticle drops its lock.
>
> 02:27-02:57: After losing lock, the sensor rapidly cycles zoom levels and contrast thresholds."

AARO's vocabulary stays at "area of contrast" throughout — no "object," no "craft," no "vehicle." The 90-degree turns the MISREP narrates do not surface in this text as turns; they surface as horizontal motion across the field-of-view between 00:07 and 00:19. The closing boilerplate disclaimer — "should not be interpreted as reflecting an analytical judgment, investigative conclusion, or factual determination" — is the same one AARO appends to every PR description.

## A second mission report, two days later

A separate MISREP, **DOW-UAP-D35** ([card `c788c17e8cc32230`](/card/c788c17e8cc32230)), covers a 29 October 2023 mission also over the Aegean Sea. Its description records the UAP as "small and circular" and as flying near the surface of the ocean; its paired video, PR-35, is 24 seconds long and shows the area of contrast becoming indistinguishable as the background scene transitions from water to land. D35 is a separate card and a separate observation. The MISREPs do not assert that the two events involved the same phenomenon, and this entry does not either. Two filings, same general area, two days apart. That is what the corpus contains.

## What the document does not say

Five things the D33 MISREP and the PR-34 description do **not** establish, that a careful reader should hold separately from the things they do:

1. **"Sharp 90 degree turns" is not an instrument measurement.** It is a phrase the aircrew typed into a free-text field on a structured intake form.
2. **"80 MPH" is explicitly an estimate.** The form's `Kinetic Velocity Accuracy` slot reads `Estimated` for that figure. [cite: card 3746998b8c506e5c p.7 "Kinetic Velocity Accuracy"]
3. **The document does not identify the object's origin or propulsion.** `UAP Propulsion Means: UNK`. `UAP Under Intelligent Control: NO`.
4. **The document does not characterize the object as exotic.** *Observer Assessment of UAP: Benign.*
5. **The document does not claim D33 and any other mission's UAP are the same object.** The D35 cross-reference above is to a separately-filed report covering a different date, not a continuation of this one.

## Why this card is in this archive

The [D32 Syria entry](/finds/dow-d32-syria-october-2024) is about how a structured intake form constrains what an aircrew can say. D33 is the cleanest version of the same form: one observation, one short GENTEXT paragraph, one paired clip, most kinetic and signature fields left empty.

The methodological lesson on the page is not "Sharp 90 degree turns" — that phrase, by itself, is the easiest thing to lift out of context and over-quote. The lesson is what the aircrew did with the "UAP Description" field. Given a slot for size, shape, color, markings, and recognizable features, they wrote `SEEMINGLY CIRCULAR, TOO SMALL TO MAKE OUT DETAILS` — and stopped. The hedge is in the form. A reader who treats that line as the shape of an honest aircrew description has the right baseline for reading every other UAP narrative this corpus contains.

### apollo-17 — Apollo 17 Crew Debriefing — What's Actually There

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/apollo-17
- Published: 2026-05-09
- Cards: 0b298cfc9c65a4d6

The Apollo 17 Technical Crew Debriefing is in the PURSUE archive. It's two pages. The 'unusual sightings' Cernan, Evans, and Schmitt described to NASA in January 1973 are reentry plasma, an aircraft carrier seen through fog, and the famous Apollo light flashes — three different known phenomena. We're including this entry to demonstrate the editorial bar: the documents say what they say, not what they're rumored to.

## Why this entry exists

Of the 222 cards in the current PURSUE manifest (plus 3 more we preserve on /removed), the **Apollo 17 Technical Crew Debriefing** is one of the shortest — exactly two pages — and one of the most asked-about. Apollo astronauts are folkloric witnesses; the corner of the internet that cares about UAP often quotes Apollo crew members to imply concealed encounters.

Anyone clicking into [the card](/card/0b298cfc9c65a4d6) deserves to know what the document actually contains. So:

## What the document actually says

Page 1 is a cover sheet — title, indexing data, a declassification stamp dated 5/6/2026 ("E.O. 13526, Sec 3.3(a) / NASA Declassification Guide"). [cite: card 0b298cfc9c65a4d6 p.1]

Page 2 is the substantive content, an excerpt from a longer mission debriefing that addresses three discrete phenomena. [cite: card 0b298cfc9c65a4d6 p.2]

### Reentry "tunnel"

Command Module Pilot **Ronald Evans** describes what he saw through the rendezvous window after the heat-shield fireball decreased:

> "…after the brightness of the fireball decreased, I could look back up through the rendezvous window and see what to me was kind of like a tunnel with a bright spot in the middle of the tunnel. Way down the tunnel, way back behind, I could see the fireball." [cite: card 0b298cfc9c65a4d6 p.2 "tunnel with a bright spot"]

This is plasma sheath geometry during reentry — well-documented across the Apollo program and not at all unusual. The crew is describing the optical interior of the ionization trail behind the command module as it slows in the upper atmosphere.

### "Tin can"

Mission Commander **Eugene Cernan** offers a one-liner about post-splashdown:

> "The only unusual sighting I can recall during landing or recovery is when the CMP looked out the window and saw the superstructure of an aircraft carrier and said, 'Oh, we've got a tin can with us.'" [cite: card 0b298cfc9c65a4d6 p.2 "tin can"]

Evans replies, in the same exchange:

> "Well, it was kind of foggy on the windows." [cite: card 0b298cfc9c65a4d6 p.2 "foggy on the windows"]

The "unusual sighting" was an aircraft carrier briefly mis-identified through fogged-up windows. Both astronauts are laughing about it on the record.

### Light flashes

Lunar Module Pilot **Harrison Schmitt** describes the Apollo light flashes:

> "We had light flashes just about continuously during the whole flight when we were dark adapted. I had one which I thought was a flash on the lunar surface. That one period of time when we had the blindfolds on for the ALFMED experiment there were just no visible flashes, although that evening, that night, before I went to sleep I noticed that I was seeing the light flashes again." [cite: card 0b298cfc9c65a4d6 p.2 "light flashes"]

These are the **Apollo light flashes**, a phenomenon studied since Apollo 11 and attributed to cosmic ray interaction with the retina or with the visual cortex of dark-adapted astronauts. ALFMED — the Apollo Light Flash Moving Emulsion Detector — was a *deliberate experiment* on Apollo 17 to characterize them, not an investigation of an unknown.

## What this isn't

The Apollo 17 debriefing in PURSUE is a small, mundane document. It contains:

- A **known optical effect** during reentry.
- A **misidentification** corrected immediately on the record.
- The **Apollo light flashes**, a phenomenon under active scientific investigation at the time and well-explained today.

It does not describe: spacecraft. It does not describe: lunar artifacts. It does not describe: anything unexplained that survived first-pass analysis at NASA in January 1973.

The fact that this document is filed under PURSUE's UAP release is itself informative. It tells us the Department of War's release criteria were broad — they included material that *mentioned* unusual visual phenomena even when those phenomena had benign explanations. That's a feature, not a bug; readers want full disclosure, not curated highlights.

But it cuts both ways. Documents being in this archive does not, by itself, make them mysterious. The bar this site holds itself to — every claim cites; abstention is fine; the documents say what they say — applies most clearly to entries like this one, where the easy thing would be to lean into the famous-astronaut framing.

## What to read instead

Readers looking for substantive primary-source UFO testimony from the same archive should start with [the Muroc AAF sightings of July 8, 1947](/finds/muroc-1947) — five sworn witness statements about objects that *were* unexplained, in a file that the FBI kept open for sixty years.

### dow-incidents-1-100 — DOW Box 7 — The Numbered Incidents, 1947–1948

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/dow-incidents-1-100
- Published: 2026-05-09
- Cards: b60b84a66715204a

The Department of War's Box 7 contains 100 numbered Unidentified Flying Object incident reports filed in CHECK-LIST format — the same standardized intake sheet, with the same 26 numbered fields, used across the first eighteen months of organized U.S. military UFO reporting. We pick six representative incidents to characterize the corpus shape: a famous early sighting, a multi-witness pilot report, a brief civilian report that closed quickly, a fatal-pursuit case, a meticulously-investigated photographer report, and a mass observation.

## What this card is

Card `b60b84a66715204a` is the Department of War's **Box 7, Incident Summaries 1–100** — 209 declassified pages comprising the first hundred numbered Army Air Forces / Air Defense Command "Unidentified Flying Object" incident reports, almost all dated between June 1947 and early 1948.

Almost every entry uses an identical printed form: **CHECK-LIST – UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECTS**, 26 numbered fields. The fields are:

1. Date
2. Time
3. Location
4. Name of observer
5. Occupation of observer
6. Address of observer
7. Place of observation
8. Number of objects
9. Distance of object from observer
10. Time in sight
11. Altitude
12. Speed
13. Direction of flight
14. Tactics
15. Sound
16. Size
17. Color
18. Shape
19. Odor detected
20. Apparent construction
21. Exhaust trails
22. Weather conditions
23. Effect on clouds
24. Sketches or photographs
25. Manner of disappearance
26. Remarks

The form's existence is itself the story. Within months of the first publicly-reported "flying disc" sighting, the Army Air Forces had standardized intake to the point that a station mechanic in Newfoundland filling out his statement and a test pilot at Muroc filling out his were giving answers to the same 26 fields in the same order. What a witness *didn't* say is preserved as `N/S` (Not Stated) — many fields on many forms come back N/S, which itself is data.

We pick six incidents below to characterize the file's range. Reports we cite are quoted verbatim including the form's idiosyncratic spacing.

## Incident #1: Muroc, July 8, 1947

Incident #1 in this filing system is the same Muroc Army Air Field event preserved in the [FBI's 62-HQ-83894 Section 3](/card/99c12a9c49a91750) as five sworn affidavits — and treated separately on this site as [The Muroc AAF Sightings, July 8, 1947](/finds/muroc-1947). Here, in CHECK-LIST form, the same incident reads as a tabular intake:

> "1. Date | 8 July 1947 | Incident # 1
> 2. Time | 0930
> […]
> enroute to his office and before entering heard one of the local aircraft in the traffic pattern. Looking up he observed the aircraft and slightly to the left he saw 2 silver objects of either spherical or disc-like shape moving about 300 MPH at approximately 8000 ft heading about 320° due north. He immediately called S/Sgt Gerald E. Nauman, T/Sgt Joseph Ruvolo and Miss Jannette Marie Scotte. Witnesses all verified the sighting and the direction of the objects - all three stated that the objects were moving toward Mojave, Calif." [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.3 "silver objects"]

The CHECK-LIST narrative follows the witness through their attempts to verify what they had seen:

> "Witness was sure it was not an optical illusion or that the objects were not weather balloons since they traveled against prevailing wind and since the speed at which they traveled and the horizontal direction taken indicated that they were not weather balloons. Furthermore they could not remain at the same altitude so consistently if they were weather balloons. Witness then attempted to get personnel (medical officers) to further varify the sighting…" [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.3 "weather balloons"]

Compare this with the same witness's sworn affidavit version in , which is first-person legal testimony rather than third-person form-fill ("Looking up, as I always do I observed the aircraft, and looked slightly to the left, whereupon I observed two (2) silver objects…"). Same incident, two filing systems, two literary registers.

## Incident #4: Captain John Paul Stapp, Muroc, July 8, 1947

Two and a half hours after Lt. McHenry's 09:30 sighting at the Billeting Office, Captain John Paul Stapp — at the time a flight test officer at Muroc — filed a separate incident report from a different location on the same base:

> "1. Date | 8 July 1947 | Incident # 4
> 2. Time | 11:50
> 3. Location | Area # 3, Rogers Dry Lake, California.
> 4. Name of observer | Captain John Paul Strapp
> 5. Occupation of observer | Flight Test
> 7. Place of observation | Observation Truck, Area #3, Rodgers Dry Lake, Calif.
> 8. Number of objects | One (1)
> 9. Distance of object from observer | 20,000 feet
> 10. Time in sight | 90 seconds
> 12. Speed | slower than the maximum velocity P-80 aircraft
> […]
> 14. Tactics | rotation or oscillation of slow type (suggested by 2 fins or nobs on the upper surface which crossed each other at intervals
> 18. Shape | resembled a parachute canopy at first then assumed ovular shape
> 20. Apparent construction | It presented a distinct ovular outline, with two (2) projections on the upper surface which might have been thick fins or nobs. These crossed each other at intervals, suggesting either rotation or oscillation for slow type." [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.11 "Strapp"]

(The CHECK-LIST form spells the observer's surname "Strapp" once and "Stapp" elsewhere. Captain Stapp later became famous as the rocket-sled-test pioneer who in 1954 voluntarily underwent 46 g of deceleration at Holloman AFB; in July 1947 he was already at Muroc as a test officer.)

## Incident #17: Kenneth Arnold, near Mt. Rainier, June 24, 1947

Two weeks before Muroc — and twelve days before the press release at Roswell that retracted within hours — civilian pilot **Kenneth Arnold** flew past Mt. Rainier, Washington, and reported nine objects in formation. This is the sighting that gave the English language the term "flying saucer."

The CHECK-LIST form for Incident #17 is among the most spare in the box:

> "1. Date | 24th June 1947
> 2. Time | 1500
> 3. Location | Mt. Ranier, Washington
> 4. Name of observer | Kenneth Arnold
> 5. Occupation of observer | Dealer in fire control supplies holds private pilot's license
> 6. Address of observer | Box 387, Boise, Idaho
> 8. Number of objects | 9
> 9. Distance of object from observer | 20 to 25 miles
> 10. Time in sight | 2-1/2 to 3 minutes
> 11. Altitude | 9,500 ft
> 12. Speed | Approx 150 MPH
> 16. Size | Approximately that of DC-4 - 45 to 50 ft
> 17. Color | mirror like
> 18. Shape | Approximately circular" [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.36 "Kenneth Arnold"]

The narrative text on the following page reads:

> "Pilot Kenneth Arnold was flying his plane at an altitude of approximately 9,200 feet. He trimmed out plane in direction of Yakima, Washington which was almost directly east of his position and sat in his plane observing the sky and the terrain. […] A bright flash suddenly reflected on the plane. Upon looking to the left and to the north of Mt. Rainier he observed a chain of 9 peculiar looking craft flying from north to south at approximately 9,500 ft elevation and going seemingly in a definite direction of about 170°. Thought at first they were jet aircraft but noticed that every few seconds 2 or 3 of them would dip or change their course slightly just enough to cause the sun to strike them at an angle which reflected brightly on his plane. As they approached Mt. Rainier he could observe their outlines against the snow quite plainly, but couldn't find any tails. Clocked speed and found it to be approximately 150 MPH." [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.37 "Mt. Rainier"]

The CHECK-LIST file reports a clocked speed of approximately 150 MPH — a value sometimes contested in popular accounts of the Arnold sighting that quote much higher figures. The Army Air Forces' filed-of-record number is 150.

## Incident #26: Robert W. Leidy, Newfoundland, July 10, 1947

The corpus is not all military pilots and base personnel. Two days after Muroc, a Pan American Airways station mechanic named Robert W. Leidy — APO 864, Newfoundland — filed a much briefer report:

> "1. Date | 10 July 1947 | Incident # 26
> 2. Time | Between 3:00 and 5:00 PM in the afternoon
> 3. Location | Pan American Airways, Harmon Field, Newfoundland
> 5. Occupation of observer | Station Mechanic
> 7. Place of observation | Traveling in a car returning from fishing.
> 12. Speed | Terrific rate of speed in a circle because of the arcs in the path.
> 14. Tactics | Definite trail and caused clouds to break open as it went through. It looked to be traveling in a circle and left sharp edges to cloud
> 17. Color | No difference in color looked as if object broke the cloud and left this opening.
> 21. Exhaust trails | bluish streak" [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.50 "Harmon Field"]

Most fields on the Leidy form return `Not Stated`. He was driving back from fishing; he saw something move through clouds; he reported what he could. The form preserves both the data points he could give and the gaps where he could not.

## Incident #30: Captain Charles E. McGee, Lockbourne AAB, January 7, 1948

Six months later, the form has not changed but the witnesses are increasingly uniformed. Captain Charles E. McGee, Assistant Operations Officer at Lockbourne Army Air Base in Columbus, Ohio, filed Incident #30 in the file the same day Captain Thomas Mantell crashed and died near Fort Knox, Kentucky, while pursuing an object in his P-51:

> "1. Date | 7 January 1948 | Incident # 30
> 2. Time | 1925 EST
> 3. Location | Lockbourne Army Air Base, Columbus, Ohio
> 4. Name of observer | Charles E. McGee, Capt. USAF
> 5. Occupation of observer | Asst. Operations Officer (Pilot)
> 7. Place of observation | Runway 23 Overhead approach
> 9. Distance of object from observer | first 4-5 miles Southwest of Base, second time 6-7 miles West and moved westerly in a hovering manner
> 14. Tactics | Flashed on and off, on westward flight appeared to be fading and descending
> 16. Size | Large size of a flood light
> 17. Color | white later yellowish to orange
> 18. Shape | Oval as if looking at spot light
> 25. Manner of disappearance | descending and burning out" [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.56 "Lockbourne"]

A separate CHECK-LIST in the same section — Incident **#30c**, also January 7, 1948 — captures DF Operator Mr. Eisele at the Lockbourne control tower seeing what is plausibly the same object 15 minutes earlier:

> "Direction of flight | Appeared to hover but performed eliptical, counter-clock wise course when it descended to horizon (4″) remained stationary (3″) returning original position (3″) […]
> 16. Size | About size of runway light when viewed from 500 ft - apparently enormous - see 9 above
> 17. Color | Red to amber-yellow
> 18. Shape | Circular" [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.60 "Eisele"]

Following pages in the same section preserve PFC Stanley Oliver's statement from the Godman Field control tower at Fort Knox about a separate 1330 CST sighting on the same day, with the surviving narrative noting Col. Hix's office's report of an unidentified object "supposedly some 250 ft to 300 ft in diameter" sighted over Mansville, Ky. — material that became the **Mantell incident** when Captain Thomas Mantell was scrambled to intercept and crashed pursuing it. [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.70 "Godman Field"] [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.80 "Mantell"] The CHECK-LIST file preserves the separate intake forms; it does not synthesize them into a single narrative.

## Incident #40: William Albert Rhodes, Phoenix, July 7, 1947

Incident #40 is the William Albert Rhodes sighting at Phoenix on July 7, 1947 — one of the few early incidents accompanied by photographic evidence:

> "1. Date | 7 July 1947 | Incident # 40
> 2. Time | 1600
> 3. Location | Phoenix, Arizona
> 6. Address of observer | 4333 N. 14th St., Phoenix, Arizona
> 12. Speed | 400-600 MPH
> 14. Tactics | Spiraled down from 5000′ to 2000 ft and then ascended at 45° angle
> 15. Sound | Noise like jet on approach - no sound heard while in view
> 16. Size | 20-30 ft
> 17. Color | grey
> 18. Shape | elliptical
> 24. Sketches or photographs | Photos (2)" [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.88 "Phoenix"]

The narrative on the page that follows is unusually detailed and specifies a hypothesis Rhodes himself considered:

> "Object appeared elliptical in shape and had a diameter of 20-30 feet. When first seen it was at about 5,000 ft and traveling from 400 to 600 MPH. Its grey color rendered it difficult to perceive at a distance as it blended with the clouds. […] The object had what appeared to be a cockpit canopy in the center which extended toward the back and beneath the object. […] He also stated that he thought the object was the Navy's new 'Flapjack Plane' but altered his opinion since the object seemed to have no landing gears…" [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.89 "Flapjack Plane"]

The "Flapjack Plane" reference is to the Chance Vought V-173 / XF5U experimental aircraft — a documented contemporary candidate that the witness himself raised and rejected on the form.

## A multi-witness mass observation (around Inc #69)

The file's later pages include a much different shape of incident: a **multi-witness, multi-pass mass observation** at Twin Falls, Idaho, in which three witnesses progressively counted formations of objects passing overhead in groups of three, five, seven, and finally a flight of "35 to 50":

> "Mrs Hedstrom saw the first object traveling at a terrific rate of speed in a northeasterly direction. It was out of sight before Mr. Hedstrom & their neighbor Mrs. Shultz could see anything. While discussing this sighting all 3 saw 10 similar objects proceed rapidly in the same direction in the form of a triangle. As they were disappearing 3 of the objects on the left flank peeled off and proceeded in a more northerly direction. The remaining objects appeared to close ranks and proceeded on a NE course. Five minutes later they saw another group of 3 objects proceeding in the same direction in triangular formation. Three to 5 minutes another triangular formation of five or six objects were observed going in the same direction. Then a few minutes later the three witnesses saw large group of objects (some 35 to 50 of them) flying in a triangular formation in the same direction. Approximately 20 or 25 minutes after this group of objects were observed similar objects were noted coming back over the city in a Southwesterly direction. Generally they were in groups of 3, 5 and 7 and followed each other at approximately 5-minute intervals. Mrs. Hedstrom then called Detective Richard A. Frazier of the Twin Falls Police Dept., a next door neighbor…" [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.140 "Hedstrom"]

The narrative ends mid-sentence on the bottom of the page; the next page in the corpus is heavily faded and the continuation is partially illegible. (See [Lowry 1949 — what bad OCR looks like](/finds/lowry-1949-ocr-limits) for more on what survives transcription and what doesn't.)

## What the file does and doesn't establish

These are intake forms, not adjudications. The CHECK-LIST does not say *what the object was*; it says *what the witness reported*. Many cases close with the form filed, no follow-up narrative, no investigator's conclusion. The Stapp form notes "rotation or oscillation of slow type"; it does not assert the object actually rotated. The Arnold form records "Approximately circular"; it does not endorse the literal saucer shape that became the era's lasting figure of speech.

What the box *does* establish, when read as a whole:

- A standardized military intake form for "unidentified flying object" reports existed in the U.S. Army Air Forces by mid-1947.
- Test pilots, station mechanics, control tower operators, civilian pilots, civilian housewives, and police officers were all filed under the same form, with the same 26 fields.
- Many incidents had multiple corroborating witnesses; many had only one.
- A non-trivial fraction of fields on most reports come back `N/S` (Not Stated). The reports preserve that absence.
- Cross-references between incidents (e.g., "See Legge account (Incident 60) and Albert Samms' account (Incident 60b)" [cite: card b60b84a66715204a p.130 "Legge"]) show the file was consciously linked, not just sequentially numbered.

Box 8 (incidents 101–172, card `7fd3d2656cbc83a6`) and Box 9 (incidents 173–233, card `be226374e719c729`) continue the same numbering and the same form. This entry covers Box 7 only. Future curated entries may walk through specific notable incidents from those continuations.

### fbi-62-hq-83894-readers-guide — FBI 62-HQ-83894 — A Reader's Guide

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/fbi-62-hq-83894-readers-guide
- Published: 2026-05-09
- Cards: bcf2e688dfbc220d, 4844321219e306af, 99c12a9c49a91750, 5ecebc7c28a8d8c7, b246c782b16be168, 13f86e95aed52840, f85532f0514320be, ad721de274bb7d6c, 8bfd94484138d59b, 7d58f0cac741650a

The FBI's omnibus UFO file is the largest single archive in PURSUE: ten cards, ~1,900 declassified pages spanning the first twenty years of the American 'flying disc' era. The structure is filing-system order — serials roughly 1 through 540 — not topical. This entry is a navigation aid: what lives in each section, who the recurring correspondents are, where to look up specific 1947 cases versus 1950s saucer-club correspondence versus J. Edgar Hoover's standing-policy form letters of the 1960s.

## Why a reader's guide

FBI file **62-HQ-83894** is what the FBI calls an *omnibus* file: not a single investigation but a topical bucket the Bureau used to collect everything that came in about "flying discs," "flying saucers," and "unidentified flying objects" between 1947 and 1968. PURSUE includes the file in ten parts, one per FBI section, with the FBI's own serial-number ranges preserved on the cover sheets:

| Section | Card | Pages | Serials | Rough date range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `bcf2e688dfbc220d` | 185 | 1–52 | June 1947 – Aug 1947 |
| 2 | `4844321219e306af` | 194 | 53–100 | Aug 1947 – late 1947 |
| 3 | `99c12a9c49a91750` | 190 | 101–130 | 1947–1948 (Muroc material) |
| 4 | `5ecebc7c28a8d8c7` | 214 | 131–185 | 1948–1949 (Project SIGN era) |
| 5 | `b246c782b16be168` | 209 | 186–245 | 1949 |
| 6 | `13f86e95aed52840` | 271 | 246–301 | 1949–1952 |
| 7 | `f85532f0514320be` | 205 | 302–343 | 1952–1954 |
| 8 | `ad721de274bb7d6c` | 217 | 344–384 | 1954–1957 |
| 9 | `8bfd94484138d59b` | 290 | 385–447 | 1958–1963 |
| 10 | `7d58f0cac741650a` | 184 | 448– | 1963–1968 |

Each section opens with the FBI's standard 4-series cover sheet (4-596, 4-895, 4-896, 4-564 — the form numbers are visible at the top). Most cover sheets carry the same authority statement:

> "Declassification authority derived from FBI Automatic Declassification Guide, issued May 24, 2007."   

Many serials are 1947 contemporaneous; the declassification stamp is from 2007. We are looking at material that took **sixty years** to clear inside the filing system.

## Section 1 (`bcf2e688dfbc220d`) — June–August 1947, the deluge

The file opens at the moment "flying disc" became a national news story. Section 1 is heavy on civilian correspondence, newspaper clippings (one page reproduces a full Sunday photo spread captioned *"Who, what, where, why are flying disks? The year's biggest mystery produced these Sunday photos while reports came from everywhere and everyone that the saucers were everywhere"* [cite: card bcf2e688dfbc220d p.50 "flying disks"]), and the Bureau's first attempts to acknowledge how much of this material to take seriously.

A representative early Hoover-office memorandum forwards material to the War Department:

> "There are attached hereto copies of a letter received from the above-captioned individual, together with copies of a newspaper clipping enclosure, concerning 'flying discs.' Mr. Reibold's letter has been acknowledged and he has been advised that copies of his letter have been furnished to you for your consideration." [cite: card bcf2e688dfbc220d p.10 "Reibold"]

The cover memo is "BY SPECIAL MESSENGER" to "Director of Intelligence, War Department General Staff, The Pentagon" dated **August 5, 1947**, six weeks after the Kenneth Arnold sighting.

Many pages in this section are heavily faded carbon copies. Approximately a third of the section's pages have OCR confidence below 50, with a number falling back to the LLM-vision pipeline that returns annotations like `[ILLEGIBLE - mostly blank page with faded stamped text at bottom]`. (See [Lowry 1949 — what bad OCR looks like](/finds/lowry-1949-ocr-limits) for a separate entry on OCR limits.)

## Section 2 (`4844321219e306af`) — August 1947 onward

Section 2 is dense with field-office teletypes. This is where you find:

- An **August 5, 1947, URGENT teletype from FBI Detroit** about a Dow Chemical Company employee who brought claimed "flying disc" debris to the company's physics laboratory. [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.8 "Dow Chemical"]
- An anonymous **July 5, 1947 telegram** received in Washington advising that Major Paul Gaynor of AAF Headquarters consult one Richard F. Shaver of Lily Lake, Illinois, "WHO MAY HAVE UMPORTANT INFORMATION CONCERNING THEIR ORIGIN." [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.20 "Shaver"]
- A handwritten letter from **A. Courtney Parker, Superintendent of Schools** in Strafford, Vermont, dated September 17, 1947, describing what he called "a so-called flying saucer" seen at 3:40 PM while watching honey bees on Rix Ledges north of Lebanon, New Hampshire. [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.100 "Strafford"]
- An **August 14, 1947 internal memo** "relative to the reported air crash of two AAF officers investigating flying disc complaints," with the recommendation that the Liaison Section pass it to AAF Intelligence. [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.50 "reported air crash"]
- An **August 6, 1947 SAC San Francisco teletype** noting that "LT. COL. DONALD SPRINGER A-TWO HAMILTON FIELD, IN CHARGE OF INVESTIGATION BY A-TWO IS THOUGHT BY A-TWO TO BE RETURNING FROM KELSO, WASHINGTON AREA…" [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.150 "SPRINGER"] — Springer is the same officer whose 4th Air Force memo cover-letters the Muroc affidavits in Section 3.

## Section 3 (`99c12a9c49a91750`) — late 1947 – 1948, including the Muroc affidavits

This is the section that contains the [Muroc AAF sworn statements of July 8, 1947](/finds/muroc-1947) — five Army Air Forces personnel describing two separate disc sightings hours apart at the dry-lake test base that became Edwards AFB. The full file index, witness affidavits, and the Lt. Col. Donald Springer cover memo all live in pages 60–72 of this section.  

The Muroc material is not unique to Section 3 — the same incident also appears as **Incident #1** in the AAF's separately-organized check-list reports (see [DOW Box 7 incident summaries](/finds/dow-incidents-1-100)) — but the FBI version preserves the original sworn-affidavit form, in which the witnesses' words are first-person legal testimony rather than a standardized intake form's bullet points.

## Section 4 (`5ecebc7c28a8d8c7`) — 1948–1949, Project SIGN era

Section 4 covers the period when the Air Force's first formal UFO study, **Project SIGN** (later renamed GRUDGE), was active at Wright-Patterson. A representative page is the FBI Laboratory's worksheet for an examination conducted **September 22, 1948** at the request of the Commanding General, Air Materiel Command, of soil samples submitted under "Project 'SIGH'":

> "Examination requested: Micro (Petrographic-Geologic). Examination by: JEVOUS. Result of Examination: Returned 10/18/48 Reg mail." [cite: card 5ecebc7c28a8d8c7 p.60 "SIGH"]

(The "SIGH" spelling appears to be a contemporaneous typist error for "SIGN.")

This section also contains the file's **April 27, 1948 United Press dispatch** datelined Dayton, Ohio, headlined *"new Data, Ideas About Flying Saucers And Death of Pilot Who Chased One,"* which is the contemporary press treatment of the **Mantell incident** — Captain Thomas Mantell's January 7, 1948 fatal crash near Fort Knox while pursuing a sighted object. [cite: card 5ecebc7c28a8d8c7 p.150 "Mantell"]

## Section 5 (`b246c782b16be168`) — 1949

Section 5 has the **July 12, 1949 Tolson-to-Director memorandum** that captures the Bureau's stance toward independent UFO informants:

> "You inquired as to what was being done with reference to the information concerning flying saucers, which information was furnished by Ernest Cuneo. […] a letter is being prepared for the Los Angeles Office suggesting that they make a discreet check of the background of the individual who wrote the letter to Winchell and thereafter interview him for details." [cite: card b246c782b16be168 p.10 "Cuneo"]

The same section contains an **OSI Serial 38-49 dated 23 June 1949**, "Subject: Unidentified Flying Objects - Report Of," which gives the kind of latitude/longitude precision that distinguishes military reports from civilian ones:

> "Location of objects when first observed: 42°38′ N, 119°43′ W. Location of objects when last seen: 42°28′ N, 119°48′ W." [cite: card b246c782b16be168 p.30 "42°38"]

## Section 6 (`13f86e95aed52840`) — 1949–1952, including formal reporting policy

Section 6 includes a key piece of correspondence: the **letter from Major General C. P. Cabell**, Department of the Air Force Headquarters, to Hon. J. Edgar Hoover transmitting the Air Force's instructions for "Reporting of Information on Unconventional Aircraft":

> "The inclosed letter, subject: 'Reporting of Information on Unconventional Aircraft,' is forwarded for your information and any cooperation you may be able to extend. As indicated in the letter it is desired to place this subject in its proper perspective as part of the normal USAF requirement for information of air technical intelligence interest." [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.10 "Cabell"] 

It also contains a multi-page **17th District OSI summary table** of "Sightings of Unknown Aerial Phenomena" — a tabular log of 1949–1950 observations across Sandia Base, Roswell, Albuquerque, Los Alamos, Alamogordo, and other New Mexico locations, columns for *Date, Time, Number Observed, Apparent Direction of Flight, Color, Shape, Manner of Disappearance, Reliability*, and so on. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.50 "Unknown Aerial Phenomena"]   The section continues through the **February 10, 1951 Knoxville report** on "UNIDENTIFIED OBJECTS OVER OAK RIDGE AREA, PROTECTION OF VITAL INSTALLATIONS" [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.100 "OAK RIDGE"] and Hoover's August 8, 1952 referral to the Air Force of a letter from one Florence Whitish of Charleston, South Carolina:

> "Miss Whitish's communication has been acknowledged and she has been informed of this referral. No investigation is contemplated with regard to this matter." [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.200 "Whitish"]

This sentence-pattern — *acknowledged, referred to Air Force, no FBI investigation* — recurs in the file with such regularity that it becomes the practical answer to the question the file's existence raises.

## Section 7 (`f85532f0514320be`) — 1952–1954, the saucer-letter era

Section 7 is dominated by **citizen letters to the Director, FBI** — handwritten and typed — from members of the public proposing methods to catch, study, communicate with, or surrender to flying saucers. A representative example is the **January 24, 1953 letter from Los Angeles** addressed to Hoover:

> "This is being written to you so that it may be forwarded to President Eisenhower if you feel it advisable; and to prevent any security leaks if such transmission of message is to be accomplished. PURPOSE — A PLAN FOR BRINGING DOWN ONE OF THE STRANGE AIR VEHICLES AS SIGHTED OVER JAPAN AND ELSEWHERE IN THE WORLD; AND THEN TO BE STUDIED BY OUR SCIENTISTS." [cite: card f85532f0514320be p.100 "Eisenhower"]

A later page in the same section contains a **June 18, 1954 SAC Seattle teletype** documenting the Bureau's working understanding of how the Air Force ran the matter internally:

> "OSI advises us that they have no interest whatsoever themselves in connection with these matters and that Operations of the Air Force doesn't even advise them. Colonel S. W. RAYNOR, District Commander, OSI, states that there is an evaluation at Wright-Patterson Field where the data is correlated, that the reports are handled from the Air Force here to that point in a routine fashion and that OSI gives no credence whatsoever to it because they have never had any previous experience of any kind as to anything arising out of the situation." [cite: card f85532f0514320be p.200 "RAYNOR"]

## Section 8 (`ad721de274bb7d6c`) — 1954–1957

Section 8 contains a **July 28, 1955 Cincinnati press clipping** preserved in the file, headlined *"See 'Em? --- Saucers Cover City"* — three discs reportedly sighted in formation over Cincinnati, with the additional reportage that "Stringfield said Cincinnati is supposed to be a magnetic fault line and that perhaps the saucers come here to recharge." [cite: card ad721de274bb7d6c p.50 "Stringfield"] (Leonard Stringfield was a prominent civilian UFO researcher of the period; the press clip is preserved without Bureau commentary.)

The same section has the **April 20, 1955 letter from Air Force Headquarters** to Hoover regarding one Charles A. Yost of the OC Research Laboratory, St. Clair Shores, Michigan, forwarded by the Director of Special Investigations, Alaskan Air Command. [cite: card ad721de274bb7d6c p.100 "Yost"] It closes with a **November 8, 1957 SAC Houston teletype** about an object "BETWEEN SIZE OF GOLF BALL AND BASKETBALL" found in the yard of a Houston resident's home. [cite: card ad721de274bb7d6c p.200 "GOLF BALL"]

## Section 9 (`8bfd94484138d59b`) — 1958–1963

Section 9 contains an internal-policy memorandum *"Memorandum to Mr. Donahoe, RE: FLYING SAUCERS"* that lays out the Bureau's actual standing arrangement:

> "Neither Agents Handbook nor manuals contain instructions regarding handling of reports of sightings of unidentified flying objects although policy has been well established by above Bureau bulletins and SAC Letters and no problems have arisen in connection with this matter. Air Force has on several occasions assured that Bureau will be advised of any developments of interest to us. Last such assurance given 11-12-57 (62-83894-387). Our liaison with Air Force on this matter is with OSI although within Air Force this matter is handled by Air Technical and Intelligence Center, Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio." [cite: card 8bfd94484138d59b p.50 "Donahoe"]

The section also contains the **George W. Van Tassel investigative file** — a multi-page report on the founder of the Giant Rock contactee gatherings:

> "they have the power to know your thoughts just as JESUS did. He said this is their means of communication and many of the space people are mute, but they train a certain number of them to speak earth languages." [cite: card 8bfd94484138d59b p.150 "Van Tassel"]

The Bureau's interest in Van Tassel is documented as an investigative subject; the document does not draw conclusions about the truthfulness of his claims.

The section closes with **Hoover's July 13, 1964 form letter** to one Hayden Hewes of the "Interplanetary Intelligence of Unidentified Flying Objects" in Oklahoma City:

> "It has been the FBI's long-standing policy not to conduct investigations regarding information this Bureau receives about unidentified flying objects since such matters are not within our jurisdiction. All such data is immediately sent to the Department of the Air Force for its consideration." [cite: card 8bfd94484138d59b p.250 "long-standing policy"]

This is the Bureau's stock answer for the entire 1960s.

## Section 10 (`7d58f0cac741650a`) — 1963–1968, the wind-down

Section 10 is thin compared to the earlier sections. It contains **convention programs from civilian flying-saucer conferences** ("COMING 1966 FLYING SAUCER CONVENTIONS") [cite: card 7d58f0cac741650a p.10 "CONVENTIONS"], a **October 10, 1967 Dallas memorandum** about an anonymous informant routed to OSI Tinker AFB [cite: card 7d58f0cac741650a p.100 "Tinker AFB"], and an extended citizen letter combining UFO claims with Cold War warnings ("Russia is well aware of this fact and has capitalized upon this fact. They have in this way been able to penetrate our Radar System undetected.") [cite: card 7d58f0cac741650a p.130 "Russia"].

A second Hoover policy form letter appears in this section, dated after his prior communication had been "destroyed":

> "[my position on UFOs] has not changed since I wrote to you on January 26, 1965. Also, it is contrary to my long-standing policy to express an opinion on such matters. Since my prior communication to you has been destroyed, I am enclosing another for your files…" [cite: card 7d58f0cac741650a p.33 "January 26, 1965"]

After 1968, the file goes quiet. Project Blue Book closed in 1969, and the FBI's omnibus UFO file did not re-open as such.

## What the file is, and what it isn't

This file is **the FBI's correspondence and field-office traffic on the subject**, not an FBI investigation of UFO reality. The Bureau's posture is consistent across two decades: receive, acknowledge, refer to the Air Force, do not investigate. Field offices forward; the Director's office signs the form letter; the matter goes to OSI or to ATIC at Wright-Patterson.

The file *contains* primary-source UFO testimony — most notably the [Muroc affidavits](/finds/muroc-1947) preserved in Section 3 — but the file is not those affidavits. It is the entire administrative record around how the Bureau decided to handle them, which is by **passing them on**.

For a journalist or researcher: if you want the witness statements, go directly to the section that contains them (the Muroc affidavits are in Section 3, pages 60–72; the William Albert Rhodes Phoenix sighting affidavit material is referenced through both this file and the parallel DOW Box 7 incident summaries). If you want to understand FBI policy toward the topic, read Hoover's 1964 form letter in Section 9 first; everything else is variation on its theme.

### kenneth-arnold-june-24-1947 — Kenneth Arnold, June 24 1947 — In His Own Words

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/kenneth-arnold-june-24-1947
- Published: 2026-05-09
- Cards: 4844321219e306af

Kenneth Arnold's typed account of his June 24, 1947 sighting over the Cascade Mountains is preserved in FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 2 as a copy attached to a CIC field report. It runs across pages 164–166. What's striking on the page — separate from the 'flying saucer' mythology that grew up around it — is how procedural the statement is: timed measurements, parallax estimates, comparison with a DC-4 he could see at the same time, and a direct rebuttal of the reflection-and-mirage hypothesis offered to him by 'a number of news men and experts' before he sat down to write.

## What the document is

Pages 164–167 of FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 2 (card `4844321219e306af`) are a typed copy of Kenneth Arnold's own written account of his June 24, 1947 sighting, signed at the bottom of page 167. The copy is attached to a 16 July 1947 memorandum from S/A Frank M. Brown of the 4th Air Force CIC documenting interviews with Boise-area aviation contacts about Arnold's reliability. [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.168 "Idaho Daily Statesman"]

A separate biographical statement ("Some Life Data on Kenneth Arnold") is on page 163. [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.163 "LIFE DATA"] The sighting account that follows is what this finds entry is about.

## What Arnold says he was doing

Arnold opens by establishing that the day's flight was a marine search, not a UFO observation. On Tuesday, June 24, 1947, he had finished his work for Central Air Service at Chehalis, Washington, and took off about 2:00 p.m. for Yakima — but delayed an hour to look for a large marine transport reported down near the southwest side of Mt. Rainier. [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.164 "marine transport"]

He flew at approximately 9,500 feet, made one westward sweep of the high plateau, came back through a 360-degree turn over Mineral, Washington, climbed back to roughly 9,200 feet, and trimmed his airplane for Yakima. He notes the air was smooth that day, and that there was a DC-4 visible to his left and rear at approximately 14,000 feet. [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.164 "DC-4"]

Two or three minutes into that course a bright flash reflected on his airplane. He looked for the source of the reflection and saw nine objects flying north-to-south past Mt. Rainier.

## The procedural observations

Arnold's narrative does not describe the objects in dramatic terms. It describes what he did to estimate their parameters:

- **Distance.** He estimates his distance from the formation at twenty to twenty-five miles, with the angle almost at right angles to his course. [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.165 "twenty to twenty-five miles"]
- **Size, by parallax.** He compared the formation against the DC-4 to his left at the same time, using a Zeus fastener or cowling tool held up at arm's length. The objects appeared smaller than the DC-4 but spanned roughly as wide as the DC-4's outboard engines.
- **Speed, by stopwatch.** He timed the formation's transit between Mt. Rainier and Mt. Adams using his sweep second hand: one minute and forty-two seconds. [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.165 "forty-two seconds"]
- **Formation length, by ridge measurement.** He notes that as the lead object cleared a snow-covered ridge between the two mountains, the trailing object was just entering it on the other side. He measured the ridge at approximately five miles, and concludes the formation was at least that long.

He also notes what made him uneasy about the observation: as he watched the objects flip and flash in the sun, he could make out no tails on them, and "any pilot would justify more than a second look at such a plane." 

## The reflection-or-mirage rebuttal

The most methodologically interesting passage on the page is Arnold's response to skeptical hypotheses he had been offered between landing at Yakima and writing the statement. He identifies the source as "news men and experts":

> "A number of news men and experts suggested that I might have been seeing reflections or even a mirage. This I know to be absolutely false, as I observed these objects not only through the glass of my airplane but turned my airplane sideways where I could open my window and observe they with a completely unobstructed view. (Without sun glasses)" [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.165 "reflections or even a mirage"]

He is documenting that he had already test-falsified the reflection hypothesis at the time, in flight, by physically banking his airplane and opening the window — and that he had repeated the observation without intervening glass and without polarized lenses.

## What Arnold does not claim

The statement is striking for what it doesn't reach for. Arnold does not say what the objects were. He explicitly declines to: he writes that he has based the article on "positive facts" and that as far as guessing what he observed, it is "just as much a mystery to me as it is to the rest of the world." [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.167 "positive facts"]

He also notes — preserved in the FBI's copy — that despite openly inviting an investigation by the Army and the FBI as to the authenticity of his story or his physical and mental capabilities, he had received no interest from either Bureau. [cite: card 4844321219e306af p.167 "openly invited"] The CIC field interview that the statement is attached to (S/A Frank M. Brown's memo of 16 July 1947) is, in effect, that follow-up — three weeks late, by way of an aviation editor at the *Idaho Daily Statesman*.

## Why this entry is in this archive

The Arnold sighting is the historical anchor of modern UFO reporting; the term "flying saucer" entered American English through press coverage of it. What's preserved in FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 2 is something more specific than the cultural fact: it is Arnold's own typed account, in his own structure, with his own reasoning about what he saw and how he tried to falsify alternate explanations on the spot.

A reader interested in the Army Air Forces' separate, contemporaneous filing of the same incident — Incident #17 on the standardized CHECK-LIST form, with a recorded "clocked speed" of approximately 150 MPH that contradicts the much higher figures often quoted in popular accounts — should compare the [DOW Box 7 incident summaries](/finds/dow-incidents-1-100). Same observation, same observer, two filing systems, two literary registers.

### lapaz-green-fireballs-1948-1950 — Lincoln LaPaz and the Green Fireballs (1948–1950)

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/lapaz-green-fireballs-1948-1950
- Published: 2026-05-09
- Cards: 13f86e95aed52840

Between December 1948 and May 1950, Dr. Lincoln LaPaz — Director of the Institute of Meteoritics at the University of New Mexico — compiled a sequence of seven reports for the 17th District Office of Special Investigations on the bright green horizontally-moving 'fireballs' observed near Los Alamos, Sandia, and other New Mexico installations. His May 23, 1950 Seventh Report, preserved in FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 6, lists eleven specific differences between these phenomena and ordinary meteors and recommends a structured scientific project. He does not call the fireballs 'unidentified objects.' He calls them 'anomalous luminous phenomena' and treats them as a problem in observational astronomy.

## What the document is

Pages 24–40 of FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 6 (card `13f86e95aed52840`) are a single transmittal: a 25 May 1950 cover memo from **Lt. Col. Doyle Rees**, Commanding Officer of the 17th District OSI at Kirtland AFB, addressed to Brigadier General Joseph F. Carroll, Director of Special Investigations, USAF. Subject: *Summary of Observations of Aerial Phenomena in the New Mexico Area, December 1948 – May 1950*. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.24 "Aerial Phenomena"]

Attached to the cover memo are LaPaz's "Seventh Report" of 23 May 1950 (pages 27–31), a frequency-distribution graph (page 32), a one-page analysis of a photograph by Cpl. Lertis E. Stanfield (page 33), and a tabular summary of sightings beginning at page 34.

The 17th District's responsibility for tracking these phenomena had been formalized at a December 1948 liaison meeting that included Fourth Army, AFSWP, the FBI, AEC, the University of California, the Air Force Scientific Advisory Board, AMC, and OSI. The cover memo records that no logical explanation was offered at that meeting; participants concluded only that the phenomena "existed" and should be studied scientifically until satisfactorily explained. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.25 "phenomena existed"] The same memo notes the District's concern about "continued occurrence" of such phenomena near sensitive military and government installations.

## LaPaz's eleven differences

The Seventh Report's central section is a numbered enumeration of how the green fireballs depart from typical meteor behavior. The first ten were carried forward from his Second Report of 20 December 1948; the eleventh was added in 1950 from a frequency analysis just completed.

The differences are observational, not interpretive. They are stated as comparisons with the cataloged behavior of meteors:

- **Path geometry.** Most December fireballs traveled in horizontal paths; genuine meteors rarely do. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.27 "horizontal nature"]
- **Altitude.** Meteor heights are typically of the order of forty or more miles; the December 12 fireball's calculated height was much lower.
- **Velocity.** The December 12 fireball's calculated velocity was lower than typical meteors but considerably greater than V-2 rockets, jet aircraft, or conventional flares.
- **Acoustic signature.** Meteorites penetrating to comparable altitudes are always accompanied by very violent noises; no noises were reported for the December fireballs. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.27 "violent noises"]
- **Approach direction.** Genuine meteors arrive from all points of the compass with equal frequency; the green fireballs concentrated in approach sectors from the north half of the sky. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.28 "north half"]
- **Color.** Laboratory test identified the color as consistent with copper-salt emission in a blowpipe flame — rare for genuine meteors.
- **Time-of-day distribution.** A frequency-versus-local-time analysis showed the fireballs' maximum at approximately 2030, coincident with neither the meteor maximum (~0300) nor the meteorite-fall maximum (~1600). [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.29 "2030"]

The full numbered list (and the contemporaneous correspondence around it) runs across pages 27–31.

## What LaPaz recommended

LaPaz did not propose a single explanation for what the fireballs were. His Seventh Report incorporates a long passage from his own 20 February 1950 letter to Dr. P. H. Wyckoff at the Atmospheric Physics Laboratory, in which — having reviewed all available data — he concludes the fireballs "fall into one of two categories": meteorite falls (the majority), and U.S. guided missiles undergoing tests. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.30 "meteorite falls"] The same letter recommends placing Dr. Fred Whipple, Dr. Peter Millman, Dr. L. A. Manning, and Dr. William Crozier in charge of various components of a structured fireball project (radar tracking, dust collection, ground search). LaPaz offers to serve as voluntary consultant. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.31 "voluntary basis"]

## The sighting tables

Pages 34–40 are a CONFIDENTIAL columnar log of "Sightings of Unknown Aerial Phenomena" reported by the 17th District. Each entry records date, time, number of observers, observer reliability rating (VR Very Reliable, R Reliable, Unk Unknown), location, apparent direction of flight, altitude, color, course (horizontal-to-vertical), apparent speed, and manner of disappearance. A representative entry from December 5, 1948 records two reliable observers near Las Vegas, New Mexico observing a whitish-orange object slightly above 9,000 feet for a few seconds, descending slightly before disappearing. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.35 "Las Vegas"]

Many entries are categorized in a footnote-keyed evaluation column — `(1)` Green Fireball Phenomena, `(2)` Disk or Variation, `(3)` Probable Meteor. The tables span December 1948 through early 1949 across Las Vegas (NM), Albuquerque, Sandia Base, Los Alamos, Roswell, Alamogordo, Phoenix, El Paso, and Window Rock (AZ), among others.

A separate one-page item, "Sighting No. 175," documents an analysis of a photograph taken at Datil, New Mexico by Cpl. Lertis E. Stanfield of Holloman AFB on 24–25 February 1950. LaPaz's analysis concludes: based on the angular diameter (approximately 1/4 of a degree) and angular velocity (greater than half a degree per minute), the photographed object was not the moon, not Venus or any other planet, and not a bright fixed star slightly out of focus. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.33 "Stanfield"]

## What the file establishes

The 25 May 1950 transmittal does not establish that the green fireballs are exotic. It establishes that:

- A credentialed astronomer with a research-mathematics background at the New Mexico Proving Grounds was attached to the 17th District as voluntary consultant for the duration of the investigation.
- He was, by his Seventh Report, comfortable categorizing the phenomena into terrestrial categories (meteorite, missile test) but was not comfortable closing the file without structured radar-and-dust observation by a named scientific team.
- The 17th District itself was treating the recurring observations as a matter for "scientific" study — its phrase — rather than as a public-relations problem or a hoax problem.

LaPaz's report is a working scientist's primary document. It catalogs differences, recommends instrumentation, identifies named collaborators, and quantifies what is missing. The reader can examine the eleven enumerated differences and the eighteen-month sighting table directly and form their own assessment of how secure each entry is.

For the broader institutional context — how the FBI was reading these reports as they arrived from OSI and other agencies — see the [reader's guide to FBI 62-HQ-83894](/finds/fbi-62-hq-83894-readers-guide), Section 6.

### lowry-1949-ocr-limits — DOW 319.1 — When the Documents Don't Cooperate

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/lowry-1949-ocr-limits
- Published: 2026-05-09
- Cards: 218e167fbd265d91

Card 218e167fbd265d91 is the Department of War's Flying Discs 1949 file — 143 pages of mostly carbon-copy correspondence between Air Force Flight Service Centers, Air Materiel Command, and Wright-Patterson AFB. The OCR pipeline succeeded on most pages but failed on roughly a quarter of them, falling back to LLM-vision and returning [ILLEGIBLE] markers. This entry is about that failure mode: what bad OCR looks like, why it happens, and what the reader can and cannot recover from a 75-year-old typewritten carbon.

## Why this entry

Most curated finds on this site cite documents that are *recoverable* — the OCR pipeline read them, the words on the page line up with the words in the search index, you can quote them. This entry is about a card where that breaks down.

`218e167fbd265d91` is **DOW 319.1 Flying Discs 1949** — 143 declassified pages comprising correspondence routed between U.S. Air Force Flight Service Centers (Lowry, Olmsted, McChord, others), Air Materiel Command, and Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, dated mostly 1949 with some 1948 and 1950 material. The file is presumably the working dossier of a Flight Service unit responsible for compiling sighting reports per **Flight Service Regulation 200-4** of 2 November 1948.

The reason this card is worth its own entry is that **roughly a quarter of its pages are too degraded for the primary OCR engine to handle**. They fall back to a vision-language-model pipeline that returns annotations like `[ILLEGIBLE]`, `[REDACTED]`, and shape descriptions instead of transcribed text. A reader who clicks into this card looking for evidence will encounter both kinds of pages and should be calibrated for what they're seeing.

## What the file is, when it is recoverable

The cleanest pages in the file are individual flight-service Form-No.-7 reports. A representative example is page 1, the cover transmission from **Lowry Flight Service Center, Lowry Air Force Base, Denver, Colorado, dated 9 January 1950**, signed by Lt. Col. Robert M. McLeod:

> "In compliance with Flight Service Regulation 200-4, dated 2 November 1948, Subject: 'Unidentified Flying Objects,' the following report is submitted.
> 2. On the night of 6 January 1950, two objects were sighted over Kansas City, Kansas, and Olathe, Kansas. They appeared to be motionless over Clathe for ten to fifteen minutes, then moved off very fast.
> 3. The weather at Kansas City was clear with twelve miles visibility.
> 4. The incident was witnessed by James F. Grey, 6200 Hadley St., Raytown, Missouri, phone FL 2744; and Robert Van De Vyvere, 5532, Raytown Road, Missouri. Both are employed at Bendix Aviation, Kansas City, Kansas, and the former is a pilot.
> […]
> 6. Two objects were sighted, both spherical in shape. They appeared to be the size of old fashioned street lights about two blocks distant. They were a brilliant white, emanating orange and red flashes." [cite: card 218e167fbd265d91 p.1 "Kansas City"]

This is what *recoverable* looks like — clean transcription, full witness names and addresses, weather, flight regulation cited, a working chain of custody back to "Fairfax AFB Operations, Kansas City, Kansas." The OCR engine reports 95% confidence on this page. Researchers can quote it.

A second representative recoverable page is the **September 22, 1949 Olmsted Flight Service Center report** of an object sighted thirty miles northeast of Griffiss Air Force Base, Rome, New York:

> "Date of Sighting: 20 September 1949 […] Where Sighted: Thirty North East, Griffiss Air Force Base, Rome, New York […] (1) Type aircraft, speed, altitude, direction of flight. C-45, 160 [knots], 10,000, 250 degrees" [cite: card 218e167fbd265d91 p.3 "Griffiss"]

A page later, the same Olmsted form continues into negative-evidence fields:

> "11. Effect on clouds: Unknown
> 12. Lights: None
> 13. Support: None
> 14. Propulsion: Appeared to be rocket or jet
> a. Propeller or jet: Appeared to be rocket or jet
> b. Rotor: None
> c. Aerodynamic vanes: None observed
> d. Visible exhaust or jet openings: None observed
> 15. Control and stability: None observed" [cite: card 218e167fbd265d91 p.5 "Effect on clouds"]

This is recoverable because the original was a clean carbon, the form is a typeset template with limited handwriting, and Surya's typewriter-character recognition handles 1940s monospace cleanly.

## What the file is, when it is not recoverable

Now the same file's **page 2** — the routing slip that sits behind the McLeod cover transmission described above:

> "TRANSMITTED
> JAN 9 4 00 PM '50
> LOWEY
> FLIGHT SERVICE CENTER
> [ILLEGIBLE - faded text throughout middle section]
> FLIGHT:
> [ILLEGIBLE - faded text]
> [Several paragraphs of heavily faded and illegible typewritten text]
> [ILLEGIBLE - bottom section contains faded text]
> DENLEH' COГOBVДO
> ГOMБA VIБ LOHCE БУДЕ
> ГOMБA ERIГIГIРI ЗЕВДICE CEИДЕБ" [cite: card 218e167fbd265d91 p.2 "LOWEY"]

That last block of text is not Cyrillic. It is the LLM-vision pipeline attempting to transcribe an upside-down, mirror-image, heavily-faded carbon impression where individual character glyphs have degraded toward a state in which the model's tokenizer is reaching for whichever character set best matches what looks like a series of curls and dots. "DENLEH' COГOBVДO" is almost certainly a partly-rotated rendering of *DENVER, COLORADO*; "ГOMБA" and similar tokens are almost certainly faded artifacts of the form's printed *FORM* and similar header text. The page is unrecoverable; the model's best-effort produces glyph-soup.

The pipeline exposed `[ILLEGIBLE]` and `[REDACTED]` markers so that downstream search and LLM consumers don't accidentally confuse model hallucination with archival text.

A second, more compact example is page 21:

> "TRANSMITTED
> AUG 10 3 [illegible] PM '49
> FILED SENT RETURN
> WM. ROOHOOFER FIELD" [cite: card 218e167fbd265d91 p.21 "ROOHOOFER"]

"WM. ROOHOOFER FIELD" is not a real Air Force installation. Surya's confidence score is 45 on this page, and the LLM has rendered what is presumably a faded date stamp in the form `WM. ROOFNOFER` or `MCCHORD` (it is in fact almost certainly *McCHORD FIELD* — a 1949 Air Force base near Tacoma, Washington — but the model is not certain enough to commit). The reader should treat this page as: a routing slip exists; it is dated approximately August 10, 1949; it appears to involve a Flight Service installation; nothing more.

## Where the LLM-vision fallback succeeds

It is worth noting where the LLM pipeline does *better* than the OCR engine, which is when the page is not text at all. Page 70 of this file is an annotated photograph of an aircraft, with the surviving caption text:

> "Chance-Vought V-173 or XF5U-1
> U.S. Navy
> Incl. 1" [cite: card 218e167fbd265d91 p.70 "Chance-Vought"]

The Chance-Vought V-173 (and its larger sibling, the XF5U-1 "Flying Flapjack") was a U.S. Navy experimental disc-shaped aircraft of the 1940s — exactly the kind of contemporary candidate flight-service investigators would have included as Inclosure 1 to demonstrate that not everything disc-shaped was unexplained. Surya would not have transcribed the photograph at all; the LLM's vision component identifies what the photograph shows and renders the caption text. This is the kind of page where the fallback adds value.

The same fallback can also handle ambiguity cleanly. Page 119 of the file:

> "[Page appears to be a heavily faded carbon copy or poor quality scan of a declassified document. Most text is illegible due to fading.]
> [At top of page, two black dots marking holes for file fasteners]
> [Several lines of text in upper portion are too faded to read with certainty]
> [Middle section contains what appears to be a table or columnar data, but text is too faded to transcribe accurately]
> [At bottom of page, two circular stamps/marks are visible:]
> Left stamp (circular): [ILLEGIBLE - appears to be a date stamp, possibly reading 'NOV 1 1904']
> Right stamp (larger circular): [ILLEGIBLE - contains text arranged in circular pattern around the perimeter, text too faded to read]
> [Additional text below stamps, appears reversed/upside down]: 'RECORDED' and 'HAS HEREIN CONTAINED'
> [Arrow marker visible in upper right corner]" [cite: card 218e167fbd265d91 p.119 "ILLEGIBLE"]

This is the model doing what it should: describing the page's structure, flagging stamps it can identify versus stamps it cannot, noting orientation issues. The "NOV 1 1904" reading is nearly certain to be wrong (this file is 1949 material), and the model says "possibly reading." That hedge is correct behavior.

## What the file does not recover

The most useful thing this entry can offer a working researcher is the **distribution**, so they know what to expect:

- 143 total pages
- 109 transcribed by Surya (76% of the file). Median Surya confidence: **93**.
- 34 fell through to LLM-vision (24% of the file). Median LLM-vision confidence: **25**.
- 31 pages have an overall confidence below 50 — i.e., the OCR system itself is flagging "this page is mostly unrecoverable."

Approximately one in five pages in this file is *partially* unrecoverable in a way that loses content the original document presumably contains. We do not know what those pages say. The full PDF on war.gov has the same physical degradation; an in-person archivist with a high-resolution scan and a magnifying glass might do better than either OCR or vision-LLM, but that is not a service this site provides.

The reader should *not* assume that the readable pages on this card are representative of the full file's content. There is content the corpus does not preserve, and the absence is not random — it concentrates on routing slips, file covers, and intra-office memoranda where carbon copies were produced casually, while the principal incident reports (those signed by colonels for forwarding to Air Materiel Command) are typically much cleaner.

## What this means for citing the corpus

A small piece of practical guidance for anyone planning to cite material from PURSUE in published work:

1. **Check the engine and confidence on every page you cite.** Surya at 90+ confidence on a 1947–1968 typewritten page is high-quality transcription. LLM-vision at confidence 25 with `[ILLEGIBLE]` markers is *not* a quote; it is the model describing a page it could not read.
2. **Quote verbatim, including OCR oddities.** If the form spells the surname "Strapp" once and "Stapp" elsewhere, both spellings are part of the historical record. Don't silently correct.
3. **When in doubt, link to the page and let the reader see the source themselves.** That is what the citation format on this site is for.
4. **`[ILLEGIBLE]` is data.** A page being mostly unreadable tells you something about the original document's condition. Quote the markers if they're load-bearing for your argument.

For the larger primary-source-rich material — the [FBI omnibus file](/finds/fbi-62-hq-83894-readers-guide), the [Muroc affidavits](/finds/muroc-1947), the [DOW Box 7 incident summaries](/finds/dow-incidents-1-100) — the OCR is mostly clean and quotable. This card is the unusual one. We are flagging it now so a researcher who clicks into it knows what they are looking at, and so the broader principle — *the corpus is honest about its own limits* — is on the record alongside the [other meta entries](/finds/whats-not-uap).

### muroc-1947 — The Muroc AAF Sightings, July 8, 1947

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/muroc-1947
- Published: 2026-05-09
- Cards: 99c12a9c49a91750, bcf2e688dfbc220d

On the same day Roswell Army Air Field publicly announced and then retracted a 'flying disc' recovery, five Army Air Forces personnel at Muroc — the dry-lake test base that would become Edwards AFB — gave sworn statements about two separate disc sightings hours apart. The FBI investigation file is in the corpus.

## What the documents say

On Tuesday, July 8, 1947, two unusual sightings happened a few hours apart over Muroc Army Air Field — the high desert flight-test installation that Hollywood and the Army Air Forces both like, now known as Edwards AFB.

The same day, *roughly 800 miles east in New Mexico*, the public information officer at Roswell Army Air Field issued — and within hours retracted — a press release announcing the recovery of a "flying disc."[^roswell-context]

The Muroc events stayed quieter, but five Army Air Forces personnel filed sworn affidavits about them within two weeks. The FBI investigation file, opened on July 8 by Air Defense Command and forwarded to FBI San Francisco on August 26, 1947, is in this corpus. [cite: card 99c12a9c49a91750 p.60]

## The 09:30 sighting

1st Lieutenant **Joseph C. McHenry**, Billeting Officer at Muroc, gave his statement on July 11, 1947. It opens with a line that has the specific texture of contemporaneous testimony rather than later reconstruction:

> "Someone will have to show me one of these Disc before I will believe it." [cite: card 99c12a9c49a91750 p.66 "show me one of these Disc"]

He had said this minutes earlier in the Post Exchange. He then walked back to his office:

> "Looking up, as I always do I observed the aircraft, and looked slightly to the left, whereupon I observed two (2) silver objects of either a spherical or disc-like shape, moving about three hundred (300) miles an hour, or perhaps less, at approximately eight thousand (8000) [feet]…" [cite: card 99c12a9c49a91750 p.66 "silver objects"]

McHenry called other personnel out from the Billeting Office. Three of them — **T/Sgt Joseph Ruvolo**, **Secretary Jannette Marie Scott**, and **S/Sgt Gerald E. Nauman** — gave their own sworn statements on July 14, 1947, all describing the same two silver disc-like objects, all giving the same speed range (300–400 mph) and same altitude (~8,000 ft), all noting the absence of any audible engine sound.

Scott's affidavit:

> "On Tuesday morning 8 July 1947, at approximately 10:00, while typing some cards, and taking care of my routine work, Lieutenant McHenry called me, along with T/Sgt. Joseph Ruvolo and S/Sgt. Gerald E. Nauman, to the front of B.O.Q. 'A' Bldg. Pointing up in a direction directly above me he asked us to explain what we saw. There were two, silver colored disc like objects flying toward Mojave, California, one directly back of the other, at a speed of about 300 to 400 miles per hour, having an altitude of approximately 8000 feet." [cite: card 99c12a9c49a91750 p.71 "silver colored disc"]

Nauman's:

> "I have 20-20 vision and I am positive these two (2) objects could not have been Aircraft, weather balloons or birds." [cite: card 99c12a9c49a91750 p.72 "20-20 vision"]

McHenry's account adds a second observation moments later:

> "Upon further investigation, two (2) of us at the same time sighted another object of a silver spherical or disc-like nature at approximately eight thousand (8000) feet, traveling in circles over the North-end." [cite: card 99c12a9c49a91750 p.67 "traveling in circles"]

He notes specifically that the object's "circle was too tight and too severe a plane to be any aircraft that I know of." [cite: card 99c12a9c49a91750 p.67 "too tight and too severe"]

## The noon sighting

Around 12:00, **Major Richard R. Shoop**, Office of the Chief of Tech. Engineering Division, was called outside by **Colonel Gilkey**, the Commanding Officer of Muroc. Shoop's statement, taken July 11, 1947:

> "I observed between five (5) and eight (8) miles to the North what appeared to be a thin metallic object. It appeared to be metallic because the method in which it was flying caused the sun to reflect like an apparently aluminum colored surface. The object moved from an intermediate altitude in an oscillating fashion, almost to the surface of the ground and then started climbing again. It climbed to a fairly high altitude and moved off slowly into the distance. The object appeared to be the size of a pursuit airplane but did not have the shape of a conventional plane. The time that the object was in view was approximately eight (8) minutes. This same object was seen by my wife at the same time." [cite: card 99c12a9c49a91750 p.64 "thin metallic object"]

Colonel Gilkey himself, interviewed orally by Captain Harry D. Black (Intelligence Officer, Muroc) on August 11, 1947, later believed his observation might have been "paper" — a more conservative read that's preserved in the file alongside the original sworn affidavits. [cite: card 99c12a9c49a91750 p.63 "paper"]

## What the documents don't say

These are eyewitness reports, not photographs, not radar tracks. Nobody at Muroc on July 8, 1947 had a camera pointing at the sky for the right eight minutes. The cover memo from Lt. Col. Donald Springer (4th Air Force, Hamilton Field, August 18, 1947) marks the case status as "Pending" and notes "No further investigation of these incidents is being considered by this headquarters." [cite: card 99c12a9c49a91750 p.61 "No further investigation"]

The objects were not identified. The witnesses were not contradicted. The case was closed.

## Why it's in the corpus

The Muroc incident sits inside FBI file **62-HQ-83894 Section 3** — one of ten sections of the FBI's omnibus UFO file, ~1,900 pages spanning 1947 to 1968. The investigation memo is dated 1947; the FBI declassification stamp is dated *May 24, 2007*. Sixty years inside the filing system before declassification; another nineteen before the Department of War surfaced it as part of PURSUE in 2026.

If a UFO researcher is going to challenge how solid the public record actually is, the Muroc affidavits are exactly the kind of primary source that document review needs to engage with. Multiple witnesses. Sworn statements. Same day. Same place. Same description. No identification.
