[^roswell-context]: This is well-documented context, not a claim from the corpus. The Roswell press release ("RAAF Captures Flying Saucer On Ranch in Roswell Region") was published in the *Roswell Daily Record*, July 8, 1947; the retraction came hours later from 8th Air Force HQ in Fort Worth.

### oak-ridge-radar-january-1951 — Oak Ridge, January 1951 — Radar Lock, Three Passes, No Visual

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/oak-ridge-radar-january-1951
- Published: 2026-05-09
- Cards: f85532f0514320be

FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 7 contains a Department of Defense Office of Public Information statement summarizing the Air Force's working understanding of unidentified aerial phenomena as of the early 1950s. Embedded in its 'Radar Sightings' section is a single-paragraph case study from January 1951 near Oak Ridge, Tennessee, in which two Air Force aircraft obtained a radar lock on an unidentified target and made three intercept passes — each one led by the radar trace toward a specific point on the ground. The Air Force presents the incident not as a mystery but as evidence for temperature inversion reflection.

## What the document is

The relevant pages live in FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 7 (card `f85532f0514320be`), pages 71–74. They are a Department of Defense Office of Public Information statement, dated to the early 1950s, written for use in answering public inquiries about Air Force investigations of unusual aerial phenomena. The cover bears the file enclosure stamp "62-83894-320 ENCLOSURE." [cite: card f85532f0514320be p.71 "OFFICE OF PUBLIC INFORMATION"]

The statement narrates the project history familiar from Air Force public communications of the period: a Wright-Patterson study set up December 30, 1947; 375 reported sightings investigated through December 27, 1949; a transition to "normal intelligence function" at the Air Technical Intelligence Center thereafter. By the time of writing, "about 1500 reports" had been investigated.

The "Radar Sightings" section on page 73 is where the document does something a curated finds entry should pause on: it explains the *mechanism* the Air Force believes accounts for many radar contacts, and offers a concrete case as illustration.

## The mechanism the document is teaching

The statement opens its radar discussion with what reads as a position paper on a known atmospheric phenomenon. It states that some unusual radar images are reflections of ground objects from a layer of warm air above the earth — a temperature inversion. [cite: card f85532f0514320be p.73 "temperature inversion"] Such reflections, the document notes, can be as sharp as returns from an aircraft, with apparent speeds ranging from zero to "fantastic," and apparent motion in all directions. The institutional consequence is given in one sentence: such radar sightings have resulted in hundreds of "fruitless intercept efforts." [cite: card f85532f0514320be p.73 "fruitless intercept efforts"]

This is an unusually direct statement for the period. The Air Force is acknowledging on the record, in a public-information document filed inside an FBI omnibus file, that hundreds of attempted intercepts of radar-only contacts had produced no closure on the supposed target.

## The Oak Ridge case as illustration

Immediately following that admission, the document offers a single illustrative case:

> "Bearing out the theory of temperature inversion reflection is an incident which occurred in January 1951 near Oakridge, Tennessee. Two Air Force aircraft attempted to intercept an unidentified 'object' and actually established a radar 'lock' on the object. Their altitude at the time was 7,000 feet. The unidentified object, according to their radar, appeared to be at an elevation of ten to 25 degrees. Three passes were made in an attempt to close on the object. In each instance the pilots reported that their radar led them first upward and then down toward a specific point on the ground." 

What is documented is unambiguous. There were two aircraft. They obtained a radar lock — the document uses the word and puts it in scare quotes only on second mention. They flew three intercept passes. On each pass, the radar trace led them upward then back down toward the ground. The interpretation offered is that this geometry — a fixed point on the ground producing a return that only appears to climb and descend with the interceptor's own approach — is consistent with a temperature inversion bending the radar return from a stationary ground object.

No visual confirmation is recorded. The document does not say what was on the ground at the apparent termination point of the trace.

## What the document doesn't claim

The Oak Ridge paragraph is presented as supporting evidence for a mechanism, not as a debunking of the original incident. The paragraph does not say:

- That the pilots concluded at the time their target was a temperature inversion artifact.
- That a ground source was identified after the flights.
- That every subsequent radar-only interception in the file is similarly explained.

What it does say is that this geometry — climb-then-dive toward a ground point, repeated across three passes — is the geometry the Air Force was using as an internal training example for *why* radar-only contacts at unusual altitudes shouldn't always be taken at face value.

The same page goes on to acknowledge ionized clouds and thunderstorm activity as causes for some unidentified radar returns. The next page also clarifies that attempts at interception are "not made every time" an unidentified image briefly appears on a scope, because current Air Force interceptors require predictable target tracking to be effective. [cite: card f85532f0514320be p.74 "not made every time"]

## Why the case is in this archive

The Oak Ridge incident does not survive in this file as a pilot's debriefing or an OSI investigative report; what survives is its use, four-plus years later, as a *teaching case* in an unclassified Air Force public-information statement. The entry is therefore methodologically valuable on two levels: it preserves a primary description of an actual three-pass intercept attempt at 7,000 feet against a radar contact, and it preserves the Air Force's own institutional reasoning about what that case is evidence *of*.

A reader is in a position to examine both layers. The radar lock and the climb-then-dive geometry are observed facts. The temperature-inversion attribution is the analytical frame the Air Force assigned. The two are separable.

For the broader pattern of Air Force / FBI / OSI correspondence about Oak Ridge — a recurring location across Section 4 (the Presley photograph hoax of July 1947) and Section 6 (the February 10, 1951 Knoxville report on "UNIDENTIFIED OBJECTS OVER OAK RIDGE AREA, PROTECTION OF VITAL INSTALLATIONS") — see the [reader's guide to FBI 62-HQ-83894](/finds/fbi-62-hq-83894-readers-guide).

### presley-oak-ridge-photographs-1947 — Presley's Oak Ridge Photographs (July 1947) — Forensic Analysis of a False Positive

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/presley-oak-ridge-photographs-1947
- Published: 2026-05-09
- Cards: 5ecebc7c28a8d8c7

In July 1947 William Presley of 218 Illinois Avenue, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, photographed what he reported as a flying object. The photographs and negatives were forwarded to the Atomic Energy Commission, then to the Air Materiel Command's Technical Intelligence Division at Wright-Patterson. Colonel C. D. Gasser's 10 February 1949 letter back to AEC, preserved in FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 4, walks through the physical analysis of the negatives in three numbered observations and recommends declassification. The interesting feature of the document is not that the photographs were debunked. It is the methodical, observation-by-observation register in which the debunking is written.

## What the document is

FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 4 (card `5ecebc7c28a8d8c7`) preserves, on pages 109–113, a small cluster of correspondence about photographs taken in July 1947 by William Presley of Oak Ridge, Tennessee:

- **Page 109** — A 18 February 1949 memorandum from SAC Knoxville to the FBI Director, transmitting a copy of a letter from Colonel C. D. Gasser to G. J. Rathman of the AEC's Security Division. The cover memo summarizes the result: the photographs "are the result of accident or purposeful hoax and are not actually photographs of a 'flying saucer'." [cite: card 5ecebc7c28a8d8c7 p.109 "accident or purposeful hoax"]
- **Pages 112–113** — The full text of Gasser's 10 February 1949 letter, marked "C O P Y" in vertical marginal letters, explaining the basis of the analysis.

Gasser's title at the time is given as "AMC Engineering Field Officer" at NEPA Project, P. O. Box E, Oak Ridge — meaning he was the Air Materiel Command's man on the ground for engineering matters at the Atomic Energy Commission's Oak Ridge installation.

## The chain of analysis

Gasser's letter establishes the chain of custody and the analytical authority concisely. The photographs were originally received by Major D. J. Grant on site, then forwarded by Gasser's office to the Air Force office of the Chief, Technical Intelligence Division, AMC, Wright-Patterson AFB. The body of the letter quotes Wright-Patterson's analysis verbatim. [cite: card 5ecebc7c28a8d8c7 p.112 "Technical Intelligence Division"]

The analysis itself is written as three discrete numbered observations of the negatives:

**Observation 1 — Surface relief on the emulsion.** Examined under strong incident light, the emulsion is "raised" at the location of the reported sphere relative to the rest of the negative. The conclusion is that a drop of warm water or developer struck the film at that point and rolled down the surface. [cite: card 5ecebc7c28a8d8c7 p.112 "raised at that point"] The diagnostic step is mechanical: tilt the negative under raking light and observe whether the sphere belongs to the silver image or to the surface relief. The letter reports that it belongs to the latter.

**Observation 2 — Continuity across two frames.** When the two negatives are placed side by side with the edges aligned, the so-called "trail" is continuous from one negative onto the next. [cite: card 5ecebc7c28a8d8c7 p.112 "rolled on from one negative"] This observation is independent of the first: a real airborne object photographed in a 35mm camera would not produce a single continuous mark crossing the dead space between adjacent frames.

**Observation 3 — Trail in the unexposed margin.** The conclusive finding is given on page 113:

> "Still further proof is shown on the fogged edge of the negative containing only the trail. This is proven by the fact that the trail extends beyond the normal format of the negative. In other words, there is a trail of that section of the negative which was not exposed in the camera." [cite: card 5ecebc7c28a8d8c7 p.113 "not exposed in the camera"]

The "trail" extends into a region of the negative that was never exposed in the camera at all — physically outside the lens's image circle. Whatever produced the trail interacted with the emulsion *during processing*, not during exposure.

A fourth, briefer observation closes the analysis by pointing to the number of unevenly developed sections of the negative.

## The recommendation

Gasser's letter does not stop at attribution. It recommends declassification of the entire matter and that Mr. Presley be advised of the nature of the images if and when the negatives are returned to him. [cite: card 5ecebc7c28a8d8c7 p.113 "declassified"] The intended outcome is that the original photographer be told what the analysis found.

The FBI's cover memo on page 109 records, separately, that Colonel Gasser personally advised that while the photographs are not real, his statements concerning the existence of flying saucers and the opinions previously expressed by him "nevertheless stand as previously stated." [cite: card 5ecebc7c28a8d8c7 p.109 "nevertheless stand"]

That sentence is unusual to find preserved in an FBI summary memo. It marks an explicit separation between the analysis of one specific piece of physical evidence and the analyst's broader views on the underlying topic. Gasser is on the record as the colonel who concluded these particular negatives were artifacts; he is also on the record as someone whose other professional views about the existence of flying saucers were not retracted by that finding.

## What the document establishes about institutional method

The Presley case produced what is, by 1949 standards, a textbook small forensic examination:

1. Physical chain of custody from observer to AEC to AMC field office to Wright-Patterson.
2. Three independent observations of the negatives, each diagnostic on its own.
3. A specific causal mechanism (a drop of warm water or developer rolling down the emulsion during processing) that accounts for all three observations together.
4. A recommendation to declassify and to notify the original photographer.

What the document does *not* do is treat Presley as a hoaxer. The cover-memo phrase "accident or purposeful hoax" preserves both possibilities; the technical analysis does not require Presley's intent in the production of the artifact, only the developer drop's contact with the film. The negatives could be the result of a careless film-processing step that left a marker at the moment a curious citizen submitted them up the chain.

The value of the entry is that the corpus contains, in its own pages, a complete forensic refutation of one of its July 1947 photographs — written in 1949, at a level of methodological care equivalent to what a contemporary archival analysis might produce. The same release that contains [LaPaz's catalog of differences from meteor behavior](/finds/lapaz-green-fireballs-1948-1950) and the [January 1951 radar-lock teaching case](/finds/oak-ridge-radar-january-1951) also contains this letter. The archive's institutional record on photographic evidence is not credulous.

For the broader context of FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 4, see the [reader's guide](/finds/fbi-62-hq-83894-readers-guide).

### rhodes-photographs-phoenix-1947 — The Rhodes Photographs (Phoenix, 1947) — Custody, Not Verdict

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/rhodes-photographs-phoenix-1947
- Published: 2026-05-09
- Cards: 13f86e95aed52840

On July 7, 1947, William Albert Rhodes photographed two unidentified objects over Phoenix, Arizona. He delivered the negatives to Army Air Forces Intelligence on August 30, 1947, with the explicit understanding he would probably never get them back. He didn't. What survives in FBI 62-HQ-83894 Section 6 is not a verdict on the photographs but a five-year paper trail of memos between the Bureau, OSI, and Air Force A-2 trying to figure out who currently has them and what Drew Pearson is allowed to broadcast.

## What the document is

FBI omnibus file 62-HQ-83894 Section 6 (card `13f86e95aed52840`) preserves a cluster of memoranda dated June 1952 about photographs taken by **Dr. William Albert Rhodes** of Phoenix, Arizona. The trigger for the 1952 memos was a phone call: Fred Blumenthal, in the office of syndicated columnist Drew Pearson, called Special Agent Wick on June 4, 1952, asking whether Rhodes was correct that the FBI had borrowed his negatives and refused to return them. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.180 "borrowed his negatives"]

The Bureau's internal answer, drafted that same day for Mr. Tolson, retraces an institutional history that by then was already five years old.

## The original delivery

The Bureau's June 4, 1952 memo to Mr. Tolson reconstructs the original transaction. On the morning of August 30, 1947, Rhodes delivered the negatives to the Phoenix Office, where they were accepted with the understanding that they were being given to Mr. Fugate as a representative of Army Air Forces Intelligence, and that there was — in the file's own phrase — "little, if any, chance" of Rhodes getting them back. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.182 "little, if any, chance"]

The agent who collected them was **George Fugate, Jr.**, working under Colonel Donald Springer of A-2, Fourth Air Force, Hamilton Field — the same Springer whose cover memos appear elsewhere in this file, including the [Muroc affidavit transmittal](/finds/muroc-1947). The Phoenix Office assisted Fugate in talking with Rhodes, not in investigating the photographs themselves.

## The recurring custody question

The 1952 memos summarize an ongoing back-and-forth that the Bureau had conducted without resolution since 1949:

- **June 8, 1949** — OSI representative Lynn C. Aldrich, Phoenix, contacted the Phoenix Office because Rhodes had requested the negatives' return. Aldrich noted that Fugate's recollection of the matter was "hazy." [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.172 "hazy"]
- **April 17, 1950** — Rhodes told the Phoenix Office that *True Magazine* would like the photographs. Phoenix referred him to OSI at Fourth Air Force Base, San Francisco, "since they had been made available to this agency by the Phoenix Office on August 30, 1947." [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.172 "True Magazine"]

Each contact returns the same answer: the Phoenix Office gave the material to the Army Air Forces in 1947, and the question of where the negatives now reside is somebody else's question.

## The June 1952 follow-up

The June 10, 1952 memorandum from W. A. Branigan to Mr. Belmont recommends the Bureau Liaison contact OSI directly — not to investigate the photographs but to determine whether OSI provided them to Pearson's office. The memo notes that Pearson, on his June 8 television program, demonstrated photographs of flying discs but says it is "not known" whether those are the same photographs as the ones in the captioned case. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.173 "television program"]

Seven days later, V. P. Kear's June 17 follow-up memo records the result of the inquiry. Lieutenant Colonel Leroy Barnard and Lieutenant Colonel E. M. Neville of OSI were both contacted; both advised that no inquiries had been received by OSI from Blumenthal. [cite: card 13f86e95aed52840 p.174 "no inquiries had been received"] A separate inquiry to Air Force Intelligence A-2 (Colonel C. M. Young) confirmed that no inquiry had reached the Director of Intelligence either. The chain of custody, as far as the Bureau could reconstruct it, did not lead to Pearson.

## What the file establishes

The Rhodes photographs themselves are not in this section of the file. They are referenced only as having been transmitted in 1947 to Army Air Forces Intelligence, with subsequent custody questions routed through OSI and A-2. What the section preserves is the institutional shape of the custody question itself — the back-and-forth between a witness who wanted his negatives back, a Phoenix Office that had passed them along five years earlier, and a Bureau that needed to answer Drew Pearson's office without making operational claims it could not source.

The Bureau's internal recommendations across the June 10 and June 17 memos are procedural: ask OSI, ask A-2, document the answers. There is no editorial framing of the underlying photographs as authentic, fraudulent, or significant. The file is doing institutional bookkeeping on physical objects whose disposition was, at the time of the memo, not fully resolved within the document itself.

For a reader, the value of the entry is not the original sighting; it is the archival record of how documentary control over flying-disc evidence worked across multiple agencies and years.

For the broader institutional context of FBI 62-HQ-83894, see the [reader's guide](/finds/fbi-62-hq-83894-readers-guide).

### whats-not-uap — What's Not Actually UAP in the PURSUE Archive

- URL: https://pursueindex.com/finds/whats-not-uap
- Published: 2026-05-09
- Cards: 17a8cc07fd8c694f

The PURSUE archive contains 161 documents. Not all 161 are about UAP. The most striking example is DOW-UAP-D48, a 181-page 1996 launch-range safety report on space booster failure modeling. We flag this not to undermine the archive but to set expectations: the Department of War's release criteria were broader than 'UAP material' alone.

## The premise

A reader scanning PURSUE assumes every document is about Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena. The Department of War filed it under that release; the manifest titles use the `DOW-UAP-D##` prefix; the press will frame the whole package as "UAP files."

That's not quite the shape of what's here.

## DOW-UAP-D48: a 1996 launch-range safety report

The card titled **"DOW-UAP-D48, Department of the Air Force Report, 1996"** is in fact:

> **"Modeling Unlikely Space-Booster Failures in Risk Calculations"**, Research Triangle Institute (RTI) Report No. RTI/5180/77-43F, September 10, 1996, prepared for the U.S. Air Force 45th Space Wing (Patrick AFB, FL) and 30th Space Wing (Vandenberg AFB, CA) Safety Offices. [cite: card 17a8cc07fd8c694f p.1]

Authors: **James A. Ward, Jr.** and **Robert M. Montgomery** of RTI's Center for Aerospace Technology, Launch Systems Safety Department. [cite: card 17a8cc07fd8c694f p.2]

The abstract begins:

> "Missile and space-vehicle performance histories contain many examples of failures that cause, or have the potential to cause, significant vehicle deviations from the intended flight line. In RTI's risk-analysis program, DAMP, such failures are referred to as Mode-5 failure responses. Although Mode-5 failure responses are much less likely to occur than those that result in impacts near the flight line, risk-analysis studies are incomplete without them." [cite: card 17a8cc07fd8c694f p.4 "Mode-5 failure responses"]

181 pages of statistical risk modeling for Atlas and Titan launch vehicle failures. Tables of "Mode-5 Shaping Constants." References to Lockheed Martin internal data, USAF accident reports, the General Dynamics Atlas Flight History through 1965. [cite: card 17a8cc07fd8c694f p.181]

There is no UAP content in this document.

The connection to PURSUE is presumably that **failed launch vehicles can produce anomalous visual phenomena that get reported as UAP** — a tumbling booster reentering the atmosphere is exactly the kind of thing a witness on the ground might describe as a maneuvering disc. Range-safety risk analysis is the engineering domain that quantifies how often that happens and what trajectories it can take.

So the document is *adjacent* to UAP — useful background for anyone analyzing claimed sightings near the Eastern Range or Vandenberg launch corridor — but it is not itself UAP material.

## Why surface this

Two reasons:

**1. Reader trust.** If you've come to PURSUE expecting "the Pentagon's UFO files," you will hit DOW-UAP-D48 eventually and feel either confused or misled. Telling you up front that not every document in the archive is what its filename suggests defuses that. The archive is real; the labels are sometimes inherited from filing systems older than the release; we're going to keep flagging the surprises rather than letting them become someone else's "gotcha."

**2. It tells us something about the release criteria.** The Department of War's PURSUE process appears to have included documents that *touched* UAP investigation infrastructure — including the safety/range-control engineering side — not only the witness statements and mission reports that are the obvious core. That broader scope is interesting. It implies that the DoD's internal UAP working groups have been pulling from launch range data, accident investigations, and safety analyses to inform their own assessments. That's a methodology question worth surfacing for anyone studying how the U.S. government actually approaches UAP characterization.

## What we're not claiming

- We are not claiming DOW-UAP-D48 is "fake," "filler," or "intentionally misleading." It's an unredacted public document the U.S. Air Force paid for, and it's been out for nearly thirty years. Its inclusion is presumably deliberate.
- We are not claiming the rest of the archive is similarly thin. The Apollo 17 debriefing is short and mundane (see [Apollo 17 — what's actually there](/finds/apollo-17)). The FBI's omnibus 62-HQ-83894 file is ~1,900 pages of investigative material spanning two decades (see [the Muroc affidavits](/finds/muroc-1947) for one of its most concrete cases).
- We are not flagging this as the only "non-UAP" document in PURSUE. As the curated finds set grows, we'll annotate others if and when they're worth pointing out.

The thousands of OCR'd pages in this corpus include genuine primary-source UFO investigation files. They also include a 1996 booster-failure risk model. Both are worth knowing about. Reader, calibrate accordingly.
